Help them see the difference between builders — who layer net-new investment on top of existing capabilities and compound advantages with every model upgrade — and buyers optimizing for investor narrative. Test whether AI budget is additive or cannibalized from product, engineering, or core domain teams; that single signal separates durable competitive advantage from a vendor logo on a slide deck.
when_to_apply: A company I'm evaluating just announced a big AI partnership right after a stock drop — is this real or panic spending?
I need to figure out whether my employer's AI reorganization will make us stronger or is just theater for the board
An enterprise customer is claiming they're 'AI-first' now and I need to assess whether they'll actually integrate or just bolt on a vendor
I'm advising a board that wants to respond to AI disruption pressure and I need to distinguish genuine investment from reactive spending
Two competitors both announced AI strategies — how do I tell which one will actually compound and which is performative?
principles: Net-new investment layered on top of existing capabilities signals genuine positioning for the transition
AI budget cannibalized from product, engineering, or core domain teams signals optimization for investor narrative rather than competitive advantage
Builders develop compounding advantages with every model upgrade; buyers get a vendor logo on a slide deck
The gap between these two responses becomes visible in every metric that matters within 12 months
Defensive AI postures adopted under stock pressure often make companies more vulnerable to actual disruption later

source_posts.title: A $3 million karaoke company just triggered a global logistics selloff + the 3 categories that tell you whether to panic or buy

frameworks.example_application: This company announced a $200M 'AI transformation' two weeks after their stock dropped 18% on disruption fears. The tell: the AI budget was carved from their core engineering and product teams, not layered on top. They're buying, not building. In 12 months, they'll have a partnership logo on their investor deck and fewer engineers who understand their own product. Meanwhile, their competitor quietly hired 40 ML engineers funded by new budget and is retraining models on proprietary logistics data — that's the builder, and the gap between them will be irreversible by Q3.
do_not_use_when: A pre-revenue startup is deciding whether to build AI capabilities in-house or use APIs, where competitive signaling is irrelevant and resource constraints dominate the decision.
A regulated industry firm (healthcare, defense) is evaluating AI vendors where procurement rules, compliance requirements, and certification timelines override build-vs-buy logic entirely.
A company has already committed to an AI platform and the user needs implementation advice, not a diagnostic on whether the decision was strategically sound.
A non-profit or government agency is announcing an AI initiative where investor optics don't exist and the framework's core signal — budget cannibalization for narrative — doesn't apply.
frameworks.description_original: A diagnostic distinction that separates companies genuinely integrating AI into workflows (builders) from companies announcing AI partnerships for investor optics (buyers), used to assess whether an organization's AI response will create durable competitive advantage or just a press release.

frameworks.name: The Five Levels of Vibe Coding
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user's question touches on AI coding adoption, tool maturity, or team productivity. Classify the user's actual situation into Levels 0–5 using the bottleneck as your diagnostic signal — keystrokes, task scope, diff-reading throughput, or specification quality. Challenge the common assumption that daily Copilot or Cursor use means operating above Level 2, and surface whether the real constraint is tools or organizational and psychological change.
when_to_apply: My team uses Copilot and Cursor daily but I'm not sure we're actually getting the productivity gains we should be
We're evaluating an 'agentic coding' tool that claims to handle full features autonomously — how do I assess whether that's real?
I need to build an AI adoption roadmap for our engineering org and I don't know what the actual milestones look like
Developers on my team resist letting AI write whole features — they insist on reviewing every diff — and I'm trying to figure out if that's the right call or the bottleneck
We want to get to autonomous code generation but I don't know what organizational changes are required beyond just buying better tools
principles: Each level represents a fundamentally different human-AI relationship, not just a quantitative improvement in tool use
The bottleneck shifts at each level: from keystrokes (Level 0) to task scope (Level 1) to diff review (Level 2-3) to specification quality (Level 4-5)
Most self-identified 'AI-native' developers cluster at Level 2, not Level 3-5 where they believe they operate
Advancing beyond Level 3 requires organizational and psychological change, not just better tools
Level 5 requires that no human writes code and no human reviews code — the factory evaluates outcomes, not implementation
steps: Level 0 (Spicy Autocomplete): AI suggests next lines; human still writes all software. This matters because it reveals that the bottleneck is still keystrokes — the AI is 'a faster tab key' — and the human-AI relationship hasn't actually changed the nature of the work; the human still writes software, the AI just reduces friction within that unchanged process.

Level 1 (Coding Intern): AI handles discrete, well-scoped tasks; human reviews all output and retains architecture. This matters because it distinguishes bounded task delegation from mere autocompletion — the bottleneck shifts from keystrokes to task scope — but architecture, judgment, and integration remain entirely human, meaning the developer's cognitive load hasn't fundamentally changed.

Level 2 (Junior Developer): AI handles multi-file changes across a codebase; human reads every diff. This matters because this is where 90% of self-identified 'AI-native' developers actually cluster while believing they operate at Level 3–5, and the tell is that the bottleneck is diff-reading throughput — the human still reads every diff — which caps how much AI-generated output the team can absorb.

Level 3 (Developer as Manager): Human directs AI and reviews output; AI does all implementation; human day is diffs. This matters because this is where the relationship flips — you're no longer writing code with AI help but directing AI and judging its output — yet almost everyone tops out here because advancing further requires organizational and psychological change (trusting outcomes over inspecting implementation), not better tools.

Level 4 (Developer as PM): Human writes a specification, leaves, returns to evaluate whether outcomes are correct; no diff reading. This matters because the bottleneck shifts entirely from code review to specification quality — 'how precisely you can describe what should exist' — and reaching this level requires a degree of trust in the system and a quality of specification writing that almost no one has developed yet, which is why skipping this distinction causes teams to overestimate their maturity.

Level 5 (Dark Factory): Specification in, working software out; no human writes code, no human reviews code; humans approve outcomes only. This matters because it reveals the endpoint where the entire organizational structure built for humans writing code becomes friction rather than support — as demonstrated by StrongDM's three-engineer team — and the foundation is entirely human work: specification discipline, behavioral scenario design, and outcome evaluation, not more engineers or better AI tools.

source_posts.title: The dark factory is real, most developers are getting slower, and your org chart is the bottleneck (plus 5 prompts to get from level 2 to 5)

frameworks.example_application: This team says they're 'fully AI-native' but every PR still gets a line-by-line human diff review and developers manually architect all modules before handing tasks to Copilot. That's Level 2 — Junior Developer — not Level 4 where they claim to be. The tell is that the bottleneck is still diff-reading throughput, not specification quality. Moving to Level 3 requires the team to stop reading every line of generated code and start managing AI output the way a manager reviews a developer's work. That's a psychological shift — trusting outcomes over inspecting implementation — and no tool upgrade will get them there without it.
steps_original: Level 0 (Spicy Autocomplete): AI suggests next lines; human still writes all software
Level 1 (Coding Intern): AI handles discrete, well-scoped tasks; human reviews all output and retains architecture
Level 2 (Junior Developer): AI handles multi-file changes across a codebase; human reads every diff
Level 3 (Developer as Manager): Human directs AI and reviews output; AI does all implementation; human day is diffs
Level 4 (Developer as PM): Human writes a specification, leaves, returns to evaluate whether outcomes are correct; no diff reading
Level 5 (Dark Factory): Specification in, working software out; no human writes code, no human reviews code; humans approve outcomes only
do_not_use_when: The user is a solo developer asking whether to use Copilot for a personal side project, where team-level organizational change advice is irrelevant.
The user's concern is AI-generated code introducing security vulnerabilities in a regulated environment, requiring a risk/compliance lens rather than a maturity taxonomy.
The user is evaluating AI coding tools purely on cost and licensing terms, not on capability tiers or workflow integration depth.
The user leads a non-engineering team using AI to automate document drafting or data analysis, not software development, so the developer-centric levels don't map.
frameworks.description_original: A six-tier classification system (Level 0–5) that maps where a developer or team actually stands in their AI-assisted development practice, from line-by-line autocomplete to fully autonomous software factories.

frameworks.name: Delegation Bet vs. Coordination Bet
frameworks.description: Use this framework to diagnose whether a user's agent architecture matches their actual workflow structure — apply it when they're choosing between agent approaches or troubleshooting adoption friction. Help them see the difference between a delegation bet (autonomous output, correctness drives value) and a coordination bet (connectivity drives value via network effects) by testing whether their work is fundamentally independent or interdependent. Push them to recognize that tool choice reshapes organizational culture, making a mismatch an operational restructuring problem, not a software swap.
when_to_apply: We're deciding between an autonomous coding agent like Codex and an integrated agent system like Claude with MCP — how do we choose?
Our AI agent deployment is producing good outputs but the team spends more time copy-pasting results between tools than they save
Leadership wants to adopt AI agents org-wide but different teams have fundamentally different workflow structures
We picked an AI agent platform six months ago and now switching feels impossibly expensive — was our initial choice wrong?
Should we invest in building agent-to-agent coordination infrastructure or just give each team member a powerful autonomous assistant?
principles: Delegation bet: one sufficiently capable agent working alone produces trusted output without supervision — value comes from correctness and autonomy
Coordination bet: real work is fundamentally interdependent and agents must talk to each other and integrate with existing tools — value comes from connectivity and coordination
The architectural starting point shapes every downstream feature, default, and assumption, making the approaches remain distinct even as they partially converge
Integration ecosystems compound via network effects — each new tool connection makes the whole system more useful — while isolated architectures do not benefit from this flywheel
The tool choice reshapes organizational structure (delegation culture vs. coordination culture), making switching later an operational restructuring rather than a software migration
Both patterns are valid; the error is applying the wrong pattern to a workflow, not choosing one over the other universally

source_posts.title: Codex 5.3 vs. Opus 4.6: Why your AI agent choice compounds faster than you think + the workflow audit that prevents the wrong one

frameworks.example_application: This team's work is fundamentally interdependent — a single research task touches the CRM, three Slack channels, a shared doc, and a project tracker before it's 'done.' That's a coordination bet, not a delegation bet. Deploying Codex-style autonomous agents here means the team will manually stitch outputs back into their tools, which is slower than the original workflow. The right move is an integration-first agent architecture where value compounds through connectivity — each new tool connection makes every workflow faster. Choosing the delegation path would feel productive for the first week and create operational drag for the next twelve months.
do_not_use_when: The user is evaluating a single AI writing assistant for personal productivity, where no multi-tool workflows or team coordination exist to integrate with.
The user's core problem is poor output quality from their current agent, not architectural fit — delegation vs. coordination framing won't fix a capability gap.
The user is a startup with one engineer and no existing tooling stack, so network-effect and switching-cost assumptions built into this framework don't yet apply.
The user is asking whether to build AI agents at all versus hire humans, making the delegation-vs-coordination distinction premature and potentially misleading.
frameworks.description_original: A distinction between two fundamentally different AI agent philosophies — autonomous delegation (hand off a task and walk away) versus integrated coordination (agents working inside existing tools and talking to each other) — that determines which organizational muscle to build.

frameworks.name: Infrastructure Inversion Pattern
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is positioning around AI infrastructure timing, build-vs-buy, or platform strategy. Classify their situation into one of three positions — platform builder, defensible tenant, or vulnerable tenant — then sort their claims against the dumb-pipe versus intelligent infrastructure distinction to show where value capture actually lands and whether the window for platform-building is still open.
when_to_apply: We're debating whether the massive AI infrastructure spending is a bubble or whether we should be investing even more aggressively
Our product is built on top of a foundation model API and I'm trying to figure out if we're building value or just renting someone else's platform
Should we build our own infrastructure layer now or wait until the technology matures and build applications on top of whoever wins?
I'm trying to understand why this technology investment cycle might play out differently from the dot-com fiber overbuild
Our board thinks we can catch up on AI infrastructure in 2-3 years — I need to explain why the window might already be closing
principles: Every major economic era begins with massive infrastructure overbuilding followed by investor panic before the infrastructure's true use is discovered
Infrastructure is never built for the thing that makes it valuable—it's built for what the builders imagine, then used for what the next generation imagines
Platform builders capture the economics of everything built on top; companies that wait become tenants paying the platform's margins
The structural difference between dumb-pipe infrastructure (railroads, fiber) and intelligent infrastructure (AI models) changes who captures downstream value
When infrastructure is vertically integrated with the intelligence it delivers, builders can capture application-layer value, not just hosting fees
The window for platform-building compresses with each successive infrastructure cycle: railroads took 20 years, fiber took 10, AWS took 6, AI is moving in ~18 months
The penalty for underbuilding in an infrastructure inversion is permanent—you cannot catch up after the window closes

source_posts.title: $185 billion is the down payment — the 4 skills that survive when agents code for months

frameworks.example_application: The $185 billion flowing into AI infrastructure isn't a bubble — it follows the same pattern as railroads, fiber optic, and cloud. But unlike fiber (a dumb pipe where the builders went bankrupt while Google and Netflix captured the value), AI infrastructure is vertically integrated with intelligence. The model builders aren't laying cable for someone else to use — they're building the intelligence layer itself, which means they capture application-layer economics too. A company building SaaS features on top of OpenAI's API is a vulnerable tenant: the platform builder can ship their feature as a checkbox. The 18-month window for establishing a defensible position — through proprietary data, workflow integration, or building your own infrastructure layer — is compressing faster than any prior cycle, and the penalty for waiting is permanent tenancy.
do_not_use_when: The user is evaluating a specific vendor contract for cloud hosting costs, where the question is operational procurement, not strategic platform positioning.
The user is asking about infrastructure investment in a regulated utility or physical commodity sector where intelligent vertical integration is legally prohibited or structurally impossible.
The user is a startup with under 12 months of runway deciding whether to build vs. buy a data pipeline, where survival constraints override platform-timing strategy.
The user is analyzing a past infrastructure cycle (e.g., railroads in the 1880s) for academic or historical research, not to inform a current investment or build decision.
frameworks.description_original: A classification framework that identifies which position an entity occupies in a platform-building cycle—platform builder, defensible tenant, or vulnerable tenant—and predicts value capture based on whether the infrastructure being built is a 'dumb pipe' or an integrated intelligence layer.

frameworks.name: Four Skills That Survive Infrastructure Inversion
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is questioning where to invest professional development time or what skills retain value as AI automates execution-layer work. Evaluate their situation against the four criteria—taste, exquisite domain judgment, phenomenal ramp, and relentless honesty about value migration—then surface the likely inversion: most users are allocating time toward execution skills that are depreciating fastest. Push them to explicitly inventory which hours they spend on judgment versus execution before proposing any reallocation.
when_to_apply: I'm trying to figure out where to invest my learning time when AI capabilities seem to shift every week
I spend most of my day on execution tasks and I'm starting to wonder if that's a career risk
We're hiring for a role that's going to be heavily augmented by AI agents — what should we screen for?
Someone on my team insists their value is in the craft of writing code, not in the judgment around what to build and why
I'm advising someone who wants to wait until AI 'stabilizes' before adapting their workflow
principles: Taste—the ability to distinguish competent from excellent output by hard-won instinct—becomes exponentially more valuable when the cost of generating options drops to zero
Exquisite domain judgment means specific, contextual, intuitive knowledge of how a domain actually works, accumulated through experience that cannot yet be replicated from training data
Phenomenal ramp is the meta-skill: the ability to absorb capability changes at speed so all other skills remain applicable as the frontier moves weekly
Relentless honesty about value migration requires actively inventorying which parts of your work are judgment versus execution and reallocating time before the market forces it
Most people's time allocation is inverted—they spend the majority of hours on execution skills that are depreciating fastest
Waiting for AI to 'settle down' before rebuilding professional infrastructure is equivalent to waiting for cloud to 'prove itself' in 2008—you pay a compounding learning-curve tax

source_posts.title: $185 billion is the down payment — the 4 skills that survive when agents code for months

frameworks.example_application: This senior engineer spends 70% of their time writing implementation code and 30% on architecture reviews and quality judgment calls. That ratio is inverted — the 70% is the fastest-depreciating slice of their portfolio. The architecture taste and domain judgment (knowing which database choice will cause pain at scale in this specific regulatory environment) are the appreciating assets. The immediate reallocation: shift to 30% execution / 70% judgment, using AI agents for the implementation layer, and invest freed hours into phenomenal ramp — staying current with how agent capabilities change the architecture options weekly. The fourth skill — relentless honesty about value migration — is the one that makes this reallocation happen at all, because without it, the engineer tells themselves 'I'm a better coder than any AI' and misses the window.
do_not_use_when: The user is a student choosing between two undergraduate majors, where foundational skill-building matters more than repositioning deprecating execution skills.
The user's organization has explicitly banned AI tool adoption, making infrastructure-inversion assumptions structurally invalid for their context.
The user is asking how to evaluate a specific AI vendor's product capabilities, which requires feature analysis rather than human-skill positioning advice.
The user is navigating a short-term layoff and needs immediate job-search tactics, not a multi-year professional reallocation strategy.
frameworks.description_original: A rubric of four human capabilities—taste, exquisite domain judgment, phenomenal ramp, and relentless honesty about value migration—that retain or appreciate in value when AI agents automate execution-layer work.

frameworks.name: Inference Gap Analysis
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is reasoning about AI infrastructure economics, capex rationality, or compute cost forecasting. Help them see the difference between training-era and inference-era economics by testing whether their model accounts for continuous, compounding inference load from agentic workflows — not just bursty training spend. If their analysis treats capex as excessive, surface how agent workloads multiplying across enterprise workflows make those numbers look undersized, not inflated.
when_to_apply: I keep seeing analysts argue that AI infrastructure spending is a bubble — are they missing something?
We're trying to forecast compute costs for deploying autonomous agents across our enterprise and the numbers seem impossibly large
Why do AI infrastructure spending estimates keep getting revised upward every quarter?
Our capacity planning assumes chatbot-level inference loads but we're moving to agentic workflows — how far off are we?
Evaluating whether hyperscaler capex announcements are rational given current AI revenue
principles: Training compute is expensive but bursty and front-loaded; inference compute is cheaper per unit but continuous and scales with deployment
A human interacting with a chatbot generates modest inference load; an autonomous agent performing a workflow generates continuous inference at orders of magnitude higher volume
Agent workloads multiply inference demand across every enterprise workflow simultaneously, not just individual user sessions
Analysts who correctly called the bubble were analyzing training economics; they were wrong because the actual demand driver is inference for agents
The shift from training-era to inference-era spending makes previously 'excessive' capex numbers look undersized when modeled against agentic workloads

source_posts.title: $185 billion is the down payment — the 4 skills that survive when agents code for months

frameworks.example_application: The bearish thesis on $185B in AI capex looks airtight if you model training economics — training runs are bursty, front-loaded, and plateau once a model ships. But that's the wrong demand curve. A single enterprise deploying 10,000 autonomous agents running continuous multi-step workflows generates inference load that dwarfs anything a million chatbot users produce. The analysts who called it a bubble were right about training math and catastrophically wrong about which compute era we're entering. That $185B isn't excess — it's the down payment on inference infrastructure that doesn't exist yet.
do_not_use_when: The user is evaluating AI infrastructure costs for a narrow, fixed-scope internal tool with no planned agentic expansion, making inference scaling arguments irrelevant.
The user is asking whether a specific AI startup's valuation is justified based on its training IP and model differentiation, not infrastructure deployment economics.
The user operates in a regulated industry where agentic workflows are prohibited, so inference scaling assumptions underlying the framework cannot apply.
The user is a financial analyst already focused on inference-era metrics and needs sector-specific revenue comps, not a conceptual reframe of training versus inference economics.
frameworks.description_original: A distinction between training-era and inference-era infrastructure economics that explains why bubble analyses built on training-cost math systematically underestimate agent-driven compute demand.

frameworks.name: The 70/30 Rule for Human-Agent Delegation
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is struggling with agent adoption, override behavior, or autonomy scoping — it reframes the problem around the research-backed insight that people default to 70% human control and 30% agent delegation. Shift their framing from "capability bottleneck" to "trust bottleneck" by challenging the assumption that better outputs will drive adoption. Push them toward governance-first design: agents draft and execute, humans decide and send.
when_to_apply: We built a fully autonomous agent workflow and adoption is much lower than expected despite strong capability metrics
Deciding how much autonomy to give an AI agent that handles tasks with social consequences like emails, calendar management, or client communication
Our team keeps manually overriding or ignoring the agent's outputs even though they're usually correct
Where exactly should I place human approval gates in an agentic workflow — I don't want to bottleneck everything but I can't let it run free
Planning a phased rollout of an AI agent and need to decide what to automate now versus what to keep human-controlled
principles: People will choose a less competent human helper over a more competent AI helper when stakes are real — this is psychological, not rational
Design for 70/30 by default: agent executes, human decides
Build approval gates so agents draft and humans send, agents research and humans decide, agents monitor and humans act
Trust is the actual bottleneck, not capability — governance must precede autonomy expansion
Increase delegation incrementally as operating history and trust accumulate, not based on capability alone

source_posts.title: 160,000 developers are building digital employees, not chatbots + the 4 prompts I use to deploy agents safely

frameworks.example_application: The conventional assumption is that the email-drafting agent should send autonomously because it achieves 95% quality parity with human-written emails. That's wrong here because the cost of a bad email is social and reputational — exactly the domain where people choose a less competent human over a more competent AI. The architecture should be agent-drafts, human-sends: the agent composes and suggests timing, but the send button stays with the person. Adoption will climb because the user feels control over the risk surface, and over three months of operating history with zero embarrassing sends, the approval gate can be relaxed to auto-send for routine confirmations while keeping human review on anything external or senior-facing.
do_not_use_when: The agent handles fully automated backend data pipelines with no social consequences where human review adds latency but zero trust or adoption value.
Low adoption stems from poor UX or a broken integration, not autonomy anxiety — the 70/30 lens misdiagnoses a technical problem as a psychological one.
The user is designing agent delegation for a regulated process where compliance mandates specific human sign-off percentages, making the 70/30 default irrelevant.
The team is deciding whether to build an AI agent at all, not how to structure one — this framework assumes deployment is already chosen.
frameworks.description_original: Reframes agent deployment design around the research-backed finding that people want 70% human control and 30% agent delegation, rather than the 0/100 full-autonomy architecture most agent systems default to.

frameworks.name: Network Intelligence Framework
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user needs to extract strategic value from their LinkedIn network for job searching, warm introductions, reference selection, or relationship revival. Classify each connection across six dimensions — half-life score, reciprocity debt, vouch score, resurrection potential, network archetype, and warm-path ranking — then sort the user's vague claims about "who they know" into concrete, prioritized action lists. Push back on the assumption that connection count signals network health; what matters is decay-adjusted warmth and reciprocity balance.
when_to_apply: I'm about to start a job search and I have no idea which of my 800 LinkedIn connections would actually help me
I need a warm intro to a specific company but I can't figure out who in my network is closest to them
I haven't talked to most of my professional contacts in years and I need to figure out which relationships are worth reviving
I need to pick references but I'm not sure who would actually advocate strongly for me versus just confirm dates
I exported my LinkedIn data and I want to turn it into an actual strategic asset instead of a vanity metric
principles: Relationships decay over time using half-life mathematics; every week without contact erodes relationship strength
Reciprocity imbalances reveal who you can ask favors from (those who owe you) vs. who you should give to first (those you owe)
Vouch likelihood is a composite signal combining message depth, recency, recommendations, endorsements, and shared tenure—not just connection status
Dormant conversations with built-in re-engagement hooks are lower-effort and higher-probability than cold outreach
Network archetype determines optimal strategy; generic advice fails because different network shapes require different approaches
For niche target companies, relevance outweighs warmth in warm-path scoring (70% weighting); for well-known companies, warmth matters more
Your data should serve your questions, not the platform's engagement metrics
steps: Export LinkedIn data archive (connections, messages, endorsements, recommendations, positions, skills, profile CSVs). This matters because the author argues we have been "passive consumers of our own data," seeing only what platform product teams decided we should see; exporting raw data lets you ask your own questions—"the ones they'd never build a button for"—rather than accepting LinkedIn's engagement-optimized interpretation of your network.

Calculate relationship half-life scores: initial strength × 0.5^(T/180), adjusted +90 days for shared company history, +60 days for deep message threads, -60 days for shallow interactions. This matters because the author identifies "relationship decay" as a specific insight LinkedIn could surface but won't; without decay-adjusted scoring, you treat a connection from five years ago the same as one from five months ago, missing that every week without contact erodes relationship strength.

Build reciprocity debt ledger: assign point values to given/received recommendations (5 pts) and endorsements (1 pt); compute net balance per connection to identify ask-list vs. give-first contacts. This matters because the author calls out "reciprocity imbalances" as a hidden insight LinkedIn withholds; the example application shows three people who wrote recommendations and received nothing back—those must be give-first priorities before any asks, or you risk damaging relationships by requesting favors from people you already owe.

Compute vouch scores (0–100) per connection: message depth (up to 40 pts) + recency (20 pts if <6 months, 10 pts if 6–12 months) + recommendations written for you (20 pts each) + endorsements per 3 (10 pts) + shared company tenure (15 pts). This matters because the author explicitly distinguishes "who would actually vouch for you" from mere connection status; the example reveals that only 12 out of an entire network scored above 60, exposing how thin a reference list really is versus the illusion of a large connection count.

Scan message history for resurrection opportunities: flag threads with unscheduled catch-ups, unanswered help requests, unfulfilled offers, and job-change re-entry points. This matters because the author identifies "dormant conversations with built-in re-engagement hooks" as a category of insight LinkedIn will never surface; these are lower-effort and higher-probability than cold outreach—the example's winning warm path was an unanswered coffee offer from four months ago, not a new cold message.

Classify network archetype (Thought Leader, Insider, Connector, Climber, Builder) based on inbound connection rates, company concentration, title density, and startup vs. enterprise mix. This matters because the author's principles state that "different network shapes require different approaches" and generic advice fails; the example shows a Connector archetype has high diversity but shallow depth, which demands a fundamentally different strategy than an Insider with deep concentration at one company (inferred).

Run warm-path discovery for any target company: rank connections by combined relevance score (domain keywords, adjacent companies, investor/founder roles) × warmth score, weighted 70% relevance for niche targets. This matters because the author's core case study is surfacing "a second-degree connection to a company where I had zero obvious ins—and why LinkedIn will never build this feature"; the example proves the strongest path isn't the closest friend but a relevance-weighted second-degree contact at a competitor, which no platform search would reveal.

Map each analysis output to a concrete action: half-life → who to contact this week; reciprocity ledger → who to ask for favors; vouch scores → reference list qualification; resurrection list → quick-win outreach; archetype → strategy selection; warm path → introduction request. This matters because the author frames all six analyses as needing to be "mapped to a concrete job-search action"—without this translation step, the data remains an intellectual exercise rather than a working system you can deploy tonight, reproducing the passive-consumer relationship the entire framework exists to replace.

source_posts.title: Cold applications have a <2% response rate now + the warm path system that replaces them (includes a guide and prompts!)

frameworks.example_application: This network is a Connector archetype — high diversity across companies and industries, but shallow message depth with most connections. The vouch score list is thin: only 12 connections score above 60, and 8 of those are from the same former employer. The reciprocity ledger shows three people who wrote recommendations and received nothing back — those are the give-first priorities before any asks. For the target company (a Series B climate-tech startup), the warm-path scoring weights relevance at 70%: the strongest path isn't the closest friend but a second-degree connection who spent three years at a competitor and has a live message thread with a resurrection hook — an unanswered coffee offer from four months ago.
do_not_use_when: The user wants to grow their LinkedIn following for thought leadership, not navigate a job search or warm introductions.
The user has fewer than 50 connections, making decay math and archetype classification statistically meaningless at that scale.
The user needs a reference for an academic program, where institutional credibility and credentials outweigh network warmth signals.
The user is hiring and wants to evaluate candidates' LinkedIn profiles, not assess their own network for outbound job-search use.

frameworks.name: Context Gap Analysis for Human-AI Complementarity
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when quality is degrading despite good intentions — reframing the user's instinct to treat it as a people problem into a context problem. Challenge their assumption that better training or accountability will close the gap; push them to prove whether the context required to prevent failure can realistically be held in a single mind at decision time. What this reveals that generic advice misses: where the cognitive limit is structural, and whether the right enforcement mechanism is even targeting an articulable rule.
when_to_apply: The same quality standards keep slipping despite everyone agreeing they matter and knowing the rules
We're trying to decide which parts of our review or QA process to give to AI versus keep as human judgment
Quality degrades gradually across a large codebase or content surface and nobody can monitor all of it
Our best people catch things that average performers miss, and we want to scale that attention without depending on heroics
Recurring failures keep happening that aren't really about skill — the information existed, it just wasn't in the right person's head at the right moment
principles: Most quality failures are context problems, not people problems — the information needed to prevent failures exists but isn't held in mind at the moment of decision
AI has structural advantage where tasks require holding more context than humans can manage, applying rules consistently at scale, and catching deviations without fatigue
Humans retain structural advantage for novel decisions, business trade-offs, cross-system judgment, and knowing when rules should be broken
Expertise narrows the context gap but does not close it — building quality systems around heroic attention does not scale
Every enforcement system needs a designed exception mechanism, or engineers will create informal workarounds that defeat the purpose
Enforcing the wrong rules at scale is worse than not enforcing them — bad patterns in pockets may contain local wisdom that contradicts a flawed standard
steps: Step 1 — Identify your entropy: Find where things degrade despite good intentions — where agreed-upon principles don't get followed, where quality drifts over time without any single bad decision causing it. Frame this as a context problem, not a people problem. This matters because the author argues most architectural failures aren't dramatic collapses from bad judgment but 'slow rot' — good engineers operating under cognitive constraints where 'each individual change made sense, each passed review,' yet together they created messes no single person could see forming. Skipping this reframing traps you in a people-problem diagnosis that leads to training and accountability interventions that can never fix a structural issue.

Step 2 — Map the cognitive constraint: Determine what a person would need to hold in mind simultaneously to prevent that degradation. Ask whether a reasonable, competent person can realistically maintain that context. If the context required exceeds what any single mind can hold at decision time, you have found a structural cognitive limit. This matters because the author identifies lost context — not lost skill — as the root cause: 'the information needed to prevent the problem existed. It was just spread across too many files, too many people, too many moments in time. No single human held it all in mind at once.' This step distinguishes between a gap that expertise can close and one that is structurally impossible for any individual, which determines whether the solution is human development or systemic enforcement.

Step 3 — Ask whether AI can address that specific limit: Determine whether the principle can be articulated as a rule, whether the AI can access the context needed to evaluate against that rule, and whether it can check consistently at scale. If yes, this is a candidate for AI enforcement. If the task requires novel judgment, business context, or understanding things that aren't written down, it remains human work. This matters because the author draws a sharp structural line: AI has advantage specifically in 'holding more context and applying rules consistently' — security review, API consistency, accessibility, compliance, infrastructure drift — while novel design, business trade-offs, cross-system politics, and knowing when rules should be broken remain 'irreducibly human.' Skipping this test risks either automating tasks that require unarticulated judgment or leaving enforceable rules to human vigilance that the author has already shown will inevitably fail.

Step 4 — Design the handoff: Define what AI handles versus what humans handle, how humans can override AI when they have context the AI lacks, and how to prevent failure modes such as deskilling, ossification, and over-standardization. This matters because the author explicitly warns about failure modes — 'ossification, deskilling, gaming the system: what goes wrong when organizations automate enforcement without designing for it' — and the principle that every enforcement system needs a designed exception mechanism or engineers will create informal workarounds that defeat the purpose. This step prevents the common mistake of treating automation as a binary switch rather than a complementary system where enforcing the wrong rules at scale is worse than not enforcing them.

source_posts.title: My honest take on what AI is structurally better at than your best architects (and where it still falls short)

frameworks.example_application: A platform team's API designs keep violating their own published naming conventions, pagination standards, and error-response formats — not because engineers don't know the standards, but because no single person can hold 200+ existing endpoints in mind while designing a new one. That's a structural cognitive limit, not a skill gap. The rule is fully articulable ('all collection endpoints use cursor-based pagination'), the AI can access the full API surface to check against it, and it can run on every PR without fatigue. This is a clear enforcement candidate. However, the decision about whether a new endpoint should be RESTful or event-driven given the business context stays human — that requires cross-system judgment about downstream consumers that isn't written down anywhere. The handoff: AI blocks convention violations in CI with a one-click override that requires a brief rationale, preventing both drift and ossification.
do_not_use_when: Quality is slipping because the standard itself is contested or wrong, not because it's being inconsistently applied — the problem is what to enforce, not enforcement.
The team is small enough that a single experienced reviewer can realistically see all the work, so distributing attention across AI isn't the bottleneck.
Failures stem from misaligned incentives or deliberate shortcuts under deadline pressure — people know the rules and choose to skip them, which is a management problem not a context problem.
The user is evaluating whether to adopt AI tooling at all for a nascent process that has no established quality standard yet — there's nothing to systematize or hand off.
