frameworks.name: Agent Context Failure Catalog
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user's agent is degrading in production, costs are climbing unexpectedly, or a context window upgrade made things worse. Check their situation against the nine failure modes — append-everything trap, blind summarization, long-context delusion, cache destruction, tool schema bloat, and the rest. Push them to identify the specific signal before assuming the fix is more context or better prompting.
when_to_apply: An agent performs well in short demos but fails in production tasks lasting more than 20 minutes
We upgraded to a larger context window model and performance actually got worse
Our multi-agent system keeps hallucinating despite having clear role definitions for each agent
Agent costs are scaling way faster than task complexity and we can't figure out why
We added summarization to manage context length but the agent started dropping constraints it used to follow
principles: Append-everything trap: single growing transcript causes cost scaling and attention dilution predictably around the 20–30 minute mark
Blind summarization: compressing without a schema causes constraints and failures to be silently discarded (brevity bias / context collapse)
Long-context delusion: upgrading to a larger context window without fixing accumulation makes performance worse, not better
Observability as context: debug logs and stack traces in the same buffer as task instructions drown the model in noise
Tool schema bloat: too many overlapping tools consume attention budget and create ambiguity before the agent sees any task content
Anthropomorphic multi-agent: roleplay-style agent teams sharing a giant context produce hallucination, not coordination
Static configurations: no execution feedback loop means agents never improve and re-discover every failure
Over-structured harness: elaborate routing logic prevents more capable models from using their full capabilities
Cache destruction: unstable prefixes (timestamps, non-deterministic serialization) force full-cost recomputation on identical logical content

source_posts.title: Get the Cheat Code on Long-Running AI Agents—Here's What Manus, Google, and Anthropic Learned After Trial and Error + 12 Prompts to Help Build Long-Running Agents Yourself
My honest take on what AI is structurally better at than your best architects (and where it still falls short)

frameworks.example_application: The active failure mode is the append-everything trap. The agent's task completion rate drops sharply after 25 minutes, cost per run has tripled in the last sprint, and the team's attempted fix — blind summarization — silently discarded three safety constraints from the working context, introducing a second failure mode on top of the first. The tell was that the agent 'forgot' a file-write constraint it had acknowledged fifteen minutes earlier: that's attention dilution from unbounded accumulation, compounded by lossy compression that stripped the constraint during summarization.
do_not_use_when: The agent is a simple single-turn classifier that processes one request and terminates, so no context accumulation failure modes apply.
Performance degradation is caused by a third-party API returning stale or incorrect data, not by how the agent manages its context buffer.
The user is asking how to design agent roles and responsibilities from scratch before any system is built, so there are no failures to diagnose yet.
Cost scaling is driven by increased user volume and per-request token pricing, not by context growth within individual long-running agent sessions.
frameworks.description_original: Nine enumerated failure modes in agent context engineering, each with a recognizable signal and root cause, enabling diagnosis of why a long-running agent breaks down.

frameworks.name: Engineering Manager Identity Shift
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user's shipping velocity problem stems from how they're allocating attention, not from technical gaps. Shift their framing from 'engineer who writes code' to 'engineering manager responsible for team throughput' by challenging the assumption that hands-on coding is where their value lives. Push them to reorient around direction-setting, output review, and throughput optimization — letting go of the contributor identity is leverage, not loss.
when_to_apply: I'm using Copilot and Claude heavily but my actual shipping velocity hasn't meaningfully increased
I find myself rewriting most of what the AI produces and wondering what the point is
I'm trying to run multiple AI agents in parallel but feel cognitively overwhelmed keeping track of everything
I know AI can do more but I can't stop myself from hands-on-keyboard coding instead of delegating
The bottleneck in my workflow shifted from 'can I write this code' to 'can I coordinate all these outputs' and I don't know how to operate differently
principles: An engineering manager's job is to ensure their team produces valuable output, not to write code themselves
Agents are stateless, tireless, and prone to confident incorrectness — managing them requires different discipline than managing humans
Your value no longer lives in the code you produce; it lives in direction-setting, output review, and throughput optimization
Letting go of the 'engineer who writes elegant code' identity is leverage, not loss
Attention allocation changes fundamentally when you adopt a manager rather than contributor identity

source_posts.title: The identity shift that unlocked real throughput and how to make it stick (plus an in-depth builders guide for 2026)

frameworks.example_application: The conventional read is that this developer needs better prompts or a more capable model — they're reviewing every line of AI-generated code and feeling slower than before. That's wrong. The bottleneck isn't the AI's output quality; it's the developer's identity. They're still operating as an individual contributor who happens to have a tool, so they treat every AI output as their code that must meet their standards. The moment they reframe themselves as an engineering manager running a team of tireless but unreliable junior devs, everything shifts: attention moves from writing and polishing code to setting clear direction, triaging which outputs need deep review vs. spot-checks, and maximizing the number of parallel workstreams. The identity of 'elegant coder' was the bottleneck — not the AI.
do_not_use_when: The user is a solo developer on a personal project with no deadline pressure, where throughput optimization is irrelevant and craft satisfaction is the actual goal.
The user is a junior engineer whose velocity problem stems from not yet understanding the codebase well enough to review AI output, making delegation premature and harmful.
The user manages an actual human engineering team and is asking how AI tools should change their existing management practices, not their individual contributor identity.
The user's slow shipping velocity is caused by external blockers like unclear requirements or waiting on approvals, not by how they allocate coding effort.
frameworks.description_original: Reframes the AI-augmented developer's role from 'engineer who uses AI' to 'engineering manager responsible for team throughput,' changing how attention and effort are allocated.

frameworks.name: Strategic Altitude Shifting
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is struggling to calibrate how closely they review AI-generated code. The common blind spot is framing this as a binary choice — trust AI or don't. Push them to see that experiential debt is the real cost, then challenge them to identify their critical paths (authentication, data handling, core logic) and prove their mental model actually matches what was built there.
when_to_apply: I've been vibe coding for weeks and realize I couldn't explain how my own auth system works
I'm spending hours reviewing every line of AI-generated code and my throughput has cratered
I need to debug a production issue in AI-generated code and I have no mental model of how it works
I want a practical rhythm for when to trust AI output and when to read it carefully
My codebase has grown significantly through AI generation and I need to decide which parts I actually need to understand deeply
principles: Neither staying permanently high (pure vibe coding) nor permanently low (reviewing every line) is optimal
Drop altitude deliberately at critical paths: authentication, data handling, core business logic
Verify that your mental model matches reality at key checkpoints, then climb back out
Experiential debt (gap between built and understood) is distinct from technical debt and equally costly
The skill is knowing when to change altitude, not staying at one level
steps: Delegate initial implementation to agents at high altitude. This matters because raw ability to build is no longer the limitation — as the source material states, the bottleneck has moved from capability to cognitive architecture, so starting at high altitude conserves the scarce resource (concurrent thinking capacity) for where it actually counts.

Identify critical paths where verification matters most (authentication, data handling, core logic). This matters because without deliberate identification, experiential debt accumulates silently and uniformly — distinguishing critical from non-critical paths is what prevents the binary trap of either reviewing everything (staying permanently low) or trusting everything (pure vibe coding), concentrating your limited cognitive attention where failure is catastrophic.

Drop altitude deliberately to examine those specific areas and verify mental model against reality. This matters because experiential debt — the gap between what was built and what you understand — is distinct from technical debt and equally costly; this step is the only point where you close that gap at the places that matter, revealing whether what the agent actually built matches what you think it built.

Test edge cases that matter in the verified areas. This matters because verifying your mental model alone isn't sufficient — agents operate in a constrained environment with immediate feedback, so exercising edge cases at critical paths is what converts a conceptual match into proven correctness before you lose the context by climbing back out (inferred).

Climb back out to high altitude and continue directing. This matters because staying permanently low destroys the throughput gains that make coding agents transformative — the source material's core insight is that the constraint is how much you can concurrently think sensibly about, so returning to high altitude after verification is what lets you keep multiple workstreams fed, like Yegge running parallel agent instances where the bottleneck is keeping them supplied with work.

source_posts.title: The identity shift that unlocked real throughput and how to make it stick (plus an in-depth builders guide for 2026)

frameworks.example_application: The authentication module and payment processing flow are critical paths — those warrant dropping altitude to read every line, trace the token flow, and verify the mental model matches what the agent actually built. The UI layout components and boilerplate CRUD endpoints are not critical paths — those stay at high altitude, accepted on trust with a quick smoke test. After verifying the auth module and confirming the session handling matches expectations, altitude climbs back up and the next three features get delegated without line-by-line review. The experiential debt is now concentrated only in non-critical areas where it's tolerable.
do_not_use_when: The user is a non-technical founder who will never read code and needs to decide whether to hire an engineer, not manage AI output personally.
The user is asking about reviewing AI-generated marketing copy or business documents, where 'altitude' metaphors around code comprehension don't apply.
The user's codebase is a small throwaway prototype with no production users, where permanent high-altitude vibe coding is actually the correct approach.
The user is a team lead setting review policies for multiple engineers, requiring a governance framework rather than a personal altitude-shifting rhythm.
frameworks.description_original: A framework for deliberately moving between high-level delegation and low-level verification when working with AI agents, avoiding the twin failure modes of permanent high-altitude vibe coding and permanent low-altitude line-by-line review.
steps_original: Delegate initial implementation to agents at high altitude
Identify critical paths where verification matters most (authentication, data handling, core logic)
Drop altitude deliberately to examine those specific areas and verify mental model against reality
Test edge cases that matter in the verified areas
Climb back out to high altitude and continue directing

frameworks.name: Temporal Separation (Build/Reflect Rhythm)
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is shipping fast with AI but not compounding their improvements over time. Challenge their assumption that reflection can happen inside an active building session — the core blind spot is treating strategic review as overhead rather than a separate cognitive mode. Push them to prove they're actually creating reviewable artifacts (transcripts, logs, error reports) during building, because without instrumentation, their future reflecting self has nothing to analyze.
when_to_apply: I'm shipping a lot with AI but keep hitting the same problems week after week
I feel like I can't think strategically about my workflow while I'm in the middle of an active building session with agents
I want to build a feedback loop on my AI-augmented development process but don't know when or how to do the analysis
My AI-assisted work feels like plate-spinning — high throughput but no compounding improvement
I have tons of session transcripts and monitoring data but never actually review them to find patterns
principles: The generative/flow state and the evaluative/strategic state require different brain chemistry
Reflection sessions feel like overhead but are the difference between getting faster and getting better
Create artifacts during building (transcripts, monitoring data) that your future reflecting self can analyze
Strategic questions (what worked, what failed, what patterns emerged) can only be answered with temporal distance
Write drunk, edit sober — adapted for AI-augmented work
steps: During building sessions, focus on throughput — delegate, review outputs, redirect agents. This matters because the bottleneck has moved from capability to cognitive architecture, and building sessions demand a generative/flow state where strategic evaluation is neurologically incompatible — trying to reflect mid-build splits attention in a world where the constraint is 'how much you can concurrently think sensibly about.'

Instrument your work to create reviewable artifacts (session transcripts, monitoring logs, error reports). This matters because without instrumentation, your future reflecting self has nothing to analyze — as the example shows, the pattern that 60% of agent failures traced to a single missing context was invisible from inside the flow state and only surfaced when concrete artifacts existed to review with temporal distance.

Schedule separate reflection sessions with temporal distance from building (e.g., build Tuesday, reflect Friday). This matters because the generative/flow state and the evaluative/strategic state require different brain chemistry — 'write drunk, edit sober' adapted for AI-augmented work — and strategic questions like what worked, what failed, and what patterns emerged can only be answered with temporal distance, not inside the session that produced them.

In reflection sessions, analyze patterns: which prompts worked, where agents got stuck, what architectural decisions are causing pain. This matters because without pattern recognition across sessions, the same failure modes repeat indefinitely — the example developer shipped features daily for three weeks but noticed the same agent hallucination and prompt correction patterns recurring, a cycle that only breaks when you move between altitudes from implementation to strategic evaluation.

Use reflection insights to update your approach for the next building cycle. This matters because this is the difference between getting faster and getting better — reflection without closing the loop is overhead, but reflection that becomes a concrete artifact (like the 20-minute rules file update in the example) compounds improvements across cycles, which is how you update your cognitive operating system rather than just accumulating throughput.

source_posts.title: The identity shift that unlocked real throughput and how to make it stick (plus an in-depth builders guide for 2026)

frameworks.example_application: A developer has been running AI-assisted building sessions for three weeks straight, shipping features daily but noticing the same failure patterns repeating — agents hallucinating config values, prompts that need manual correction every time, architectural decisions made under time pressure that now create drag. The building sessions are high-throughput but the process never improves because there's no temporal distance for pattern recognition. Scheduling a Friday reflection session with the week's session transcripts and error logs reveals that 60% of agent failures trace to a single missing context pattern — a fix that takes 20 minutes but was invisible from inside the flow state. The next building cycle runs measurably cleaner because the reflection artifact became a rules file update.
do_not_use_when: The user is a solo developer who has been shipping with AI for only a few days and lacks sufficient session history to reflect on meaningful patterns.
The user's repeated problems stem from a broken external dependency or infrastructure issue, not from workflow habits that reflection could improve.
The user wants strategic thinking during an active session because a live client is waiting on an immediate architectural decision, not because of a general workflow habit.
The user is asking how to structure a one-time project retrospective for a completed engagement, not how to build an ongoing rhythm across recurring work cycles.
frameworks.description_original: A cognitive architecture practice that separates the generative building state from the evaluative reflection state across different time periods to enable both high-throughput shipping and strategic improvement.
steps_original: During building sessions, focus on throughput — delegate, review outputs, redirect agents
Instrument your work to create reviewable artifacts (session transcripts, monitoring logs, error reports)
Schedule separate reflection sessions with temporal distance from building (e.g., build Tuesday, reflect Friday)
In reflection sessions, analyze patterns: which prompts worked, where agents got stuck, what architectural decisions are causing pain
Use reflection insights to update your approach for the next building cycle

frameworks.name: Two Kinds of Architecture
frameworks.description: Use this framework when a user senses their AI-assisted project is technically sound but feels incoherent or directionless. Help them see the difference between civil engineering architecture — conventions and standards tractable enough to delegate — and scaling taste, the coherence and vision that remains human work. Ask what they're trying to hand off, then sort it: if it's codifiable, push it to agents; if it requires judgment about what feels right, redirect their attention there.
when_to_apply: My AI-generated code follows all conventions perfectly but the product still feels incoherent and directionless
I'm writing an AGENTS.md file and trying to figure out what belongs in it versus what I need to keep in my own head
I'm spending my time reviewing AI-written code for style consistency when I should be doing something else — but I'm not sure what that something else is
I want to delegate more architectural decisions to agents but I'm worried about losing the coherent vision of the system
My AI-assisted project is technically sound but lacks the 'soul' that makes it feel like one person designed it
principles: Civil engineering patterns (conventions, standards, consistency) are tractable — write them down and agents can follow them
Taste, coherence, and vision ('the quality without a name') remain human work and cannot yet be delegated
Agents excel at consistent application of best practices; humans must own judgment about what feels right
Conflating these two architectures leads to misplaced expectations about what AI can produce
When dealing with civil engineering architecture, lean hard on agents; when dealing with taste, that's where your attention must go

source_posts.title: The identity shift that unlocked real throughput and how to make it stick (plus an in-depth builders guide for 2026)
Executive Briefing: What Cursor's $57K CMS Deletion Reveals About Where Agent Value Actually Lives

frameworks.example_application: The codebase is immaculate — consistent naming, proper error handling, well-structured modules — because the agent followed every convention in AGENTS.md perfectly. But the product feels like a committee designed it: five different interaction patterns for similar tasks, a settings page that implies a mental model no user actually holds, and an API surface that's technically clean but tells no coherent story. That's the tell. The civil engineering architecture is fully delegated and working. The taste architecture — the 'why does this feature exist and how does it connect to everything else' — has no owner. The builder's attention needs to shift entirely from code consistency (the agent has that) to product coherence (only they can hold that).
do_not_use_when: The user's product feels incoherent because of misaligned stakeholder requirements, not because of how AI contributions were integrated.
The user is asking which specific linting rules or formatting conventions to include in their AGENTS.md, a purely technical scoping question.
The user is evaluating whether to adopt AI coding tools at all and needs a cost-benefit analysis, not a framework for dividing responsibilities once adopted.
The user's codebase lacks coherence because multiple human engineers have conflicting styles, and AI agents are not yet involved in the project.
frameworks.description_original: Distinguishes between codifiable technical patterns (delegatable to AI agents) and 'scaling taste' — the coherence and vision quality that remains a human responsibility and cannot yet be outsourced.

frameworks.name: Experiential Debt
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user's confusion about their codebase or product direction may stem from moving faster than their understanding could follow. Help them see the difference between technical debt (fixable with refactoring) and experiential debt (the gap between what's built and their embodied operator's knowledge of it) by asking what they actually discovered — or skipped discovering — during the build. Push them to recognize that skipping the messy middle isn't just a process shortcut; it's where the vision corrections happen.
when_to_apply: I vibe-coded a working prototype but now I feel like a tourist in my own codebase
My team shipped fast with AI but our debugging time has exploded and nobody understands the architecture deeply
I'm wondering whether AI-assisted speed is actually costing me something I can't easily name
I built what I thought I wanted quickly, but now realize I never discovered what I actually needed because I skipped the messy middle
Someone on my team can demo the product but can't explain why it's built the way it is
principles: Operator's knowledge — knowing where the nooks and crannies are — cannot be built at the same speed AI builds systems
The vision for a product is often fundamentally wrong; stepwise building reveals what you actually want
Skipping intermediate phases means skipping the discoveries that reveal what you actually want to build
You can build fast and still accumulate experiential knowledge, but it requires intentionality and actually using what you ship
Experiential debt manifests as debugging time, architectural confusion, and building the wrong thing faster

source_posts.title: The identity shift that unlocked real throughput and how to make it stick (plus an in-depth builders guide for 2026)

frameworks.example_application: This team's velocity problem isn't technical debt — it's experiential debt. They used AI to scaffold an entire event-processing pipeline in two days, but nobody on the team has ever manually handled a malformed event. Now every bug takes 4x longer to diagnose because they're reverse-engineering their own system. The tell: they can describe what the system does from the README, but they can't predict what will break when inputs change. The fix isn't to slow down — it's to actually use what they shipped, run edge cases by hand, and build the operator's intuition that the AI-assisted sprint skipped over.
do_not_use_when: The user inherited a poorly documented legacy codebase they didn't build and has no experiential gap to close — only an information gap.
The user is asking about a throwaway prototype explicitly never intended for production, where accumulating architectural understanding has no value.
The confusion stems from a team member's poor documentation practices, not AI-accelerated development — a communication or process failure, not experiential debt.
The user is a non-technical executive asking why their engineering team seems slow, where the relevant lens is team dynamics or resourcing, not personal experiential knowledge.
frameworks.description_original: Distinguishes experiential debt (the gap between what you've built and your embodied understanding of it) from technical debt, identifying it as a separate and underappreciated risk of AI-accelerated development.

frameworks.name: Colleague-Shaped vs. Tool-Shaped AI Selection Framework
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user needs to choose between iterative, collaborative AI and autonomous, execution-focused AI. Help them see the difference between colleague-shaped and tool-shaped AI by testing two axes: how precisely they can specify intent upfront, and how cheaply they can verify outputs afterward. Challenge the assumption that autonomous agents are simply more advanced — push them to prove their specification quality and verification cost actually support that choice.
when_to_apply: My AI agent keeps producing output that looks great but has fundamental errors I only catch later
I'm trying to decide whether to use ChatGPT-style back-and-forth or a fire-and-forget autonomous agent for a project
Junior team members are getting worse results from the same AI tools that work well for senior staff
I'm designing an AI workflow and need to decide how much human-in-the-loop interaction to build in
Someone on my team wants to switch to fully autonomous AI agents but I'm not sure they can specify tasks precisely enough
principles: The core axis is specification quality × verification cost: tool-shaped AI wins when the spec is crisp and verification is cheap; colleague-shaped AI wins when the spec is discoverable only through iteration or verification is expensive

Senior/expert practitioners benefit from tool-shaped AI because they can write precise specifications and verify outputs quickly; junior/developing practitioners benefit from colleague-shaped AI because the dialogue catches errors early and teaches simultaneously
Most people overestimate their ability to specify precise intent — the feedback loop that makes iterative AI feel slower is the same mechanism that catches errors before they compound
High-grade intent (the ability to produce complete, unambiguous specifications upfront) is a learnable skill and a prerequisite for effective use of autonomous AI
The same tool characteristic (e.g., yielding control frequently) is a bug in one context and a feature in another — context determines fit, not absolute capability
Organizations likely need both patterns simultaneously: autonomous delegation for domain experts and iterative collaboration for developing contributors

source_posts.title: The Specification Gap: Why Your AI Produces Impressive-Looking Output With Fundamental Problems + The Prompt Kit To Help You Fix It

frameworks.example_application: This team is using an autonomous coding agent but getting plausible-looking output with subtle architectural errors. The tell is specification clarity × verification cost: the junior developers can't write precise enough specs to get good autonomous output, and they lack the expertise to cheaply verify the results. They're in the colleague-shaped quadrant — iterative dialogue would catch these errors mid-stream instead of letting them compound into a finished artifact that looks right but isn't. The senior architect, by contrast, can specify exactly what she wants and spot problems in seconds — for her, the autonomous mode is correct and the iteration overhead is pure friction.
do_not_use_when: The user is choosing between two specific AI vendor products where both are tool-shaped and the decision hinges on pricing, API limits, or integration compatibility.
The user's AI outputs are unreliable due to a known model hallucination or technical bug, not a mismatch between task specification and interaction style.
The user is asking how to train or upskill their team on AI tools generally, not trying to match a specific task type to an AI interaction pattern.
The organization has already committed to a specific AI platform and needs implementation guidance, making the colleague-vs-tool selection question moot.
frameworks.description_original: A decision framework for choosing between iterative/collaborative AI (colleague-shaped) and autonomous/execution-focused AI (tool-shaped) based on two axes: specification clarity and verification cost.

frameworks.name: Two Kinds of Disposable Software
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user conflates personal throwaway software with disposable features inside enterprise products. Classify their situation into one of the two categories using the key differentiators: who bears the cost of change, and what their tolerance level is. Surface the hidden risks around trust, stability, and maintenance burden that the enterprise category carries — risks that "ship fast, kill fast" culture typically obscures.
when_to_apply: We're adopting a 'ship fast, kill fast' approach to features and I need to figure out where that's safe versus dangerous
Someone on the team is pointing to Cursor's success with rapid iteration as a model for our enterprise product
We're using AI to generate lots of small tools and features quickly, and I need to decide which ones need reliability investment versus which can stay throwaway
Our product strategy treats AI-generated features as experiments, but customers keep complaining when we deprecate things
I'm trying to figure out whether vibe-coded tools are appropriate for internal use versus customer-facing use
principles: Personal/throwaway software (one-off dashboards, personal tools, weekend projects) is unambiguously beneficial and represents genuine democratization
Disposable features inside enterprise products carry hidden risks around trust, stability, and maintenance burden
The two categories share a name but have fundamentally different cost structures and customer tolerance levels
Simple interfaces (e.g., terminal-based) better absorb constant change than complex GUIs, making disposability more viable

source_posts.title: Disposable software works for Cursor, but probably won't work for you. + The reliability playbook for everyone else

frameworks.example_application: The team wants to ship AI-generated features rapidly and deprecate them if they don't stick — a 'disposable software' philosophy. But this is an enterprise SaaS product with paying customers, not a weekend project. That makes it Category 2: disposable features inside a product people rely on. The cost structure is completely different — customers build workflows around features, and removing them erodes trust even if usage was low. The same rapid-churn approach that's unambiguously good for personal tools and one-off dashboards becomes a liability here. A terminal-based developer tool like Cursor can absorb constant churn because its interface is simple and its users expect instability; a complex enterprise GUI with onboarding flows and integrations cannot.
do_not_use_when: The user is asking about deprecating a mature, stable product line—not iterating on new features—so lifecycle strategy, not disposability taxonomy, applies.
The user's 'throwaway tools' are internal data pipelines with compliance and audit requirements, where reliability investment is mandatory regardless of intended permanence.
The user is evaluating whether to adopt a rapid-iteration culture organizationally, making this a change management question rather than a feature classification problem.
The user is building a prototype purely to secure investor funding with no customers yet, so customer trust dynamics the framework centers on are irrelevant.
frameworks.description_original: Classifies disposable software into two distinct categories with different risk profiles and strategic implications.

frameworks.name: Code Cost vs. Attention Cost Distinction
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user conflates cheap code generation with cheap software ownership. Help them see the difference between the collapsed cost of generating code and the unchanged cost of directing skilled human attention toward a goal by exposing what their ROI logic omits: maintenance burden, security remediation, and the opportunity cost of pulling senior builders off core mission work. The constraint was always attention, not software cost.
when_to_apply: My team says we should build it in-house because AI makes software basically free now
We're debating whether to pull engineers off the core product to vibe-code internal tools
Leadership is excited about replacing SaaS subscriptions with AI-generated internal software
Someone calculated ROI on AI-assisted development but only counted the coding time saved
We keep generating new internal tools with AI but our senior engineers are drowning in maintenance and security fixes
principles: The cost of generating code has collapsed to near zero; the cost of human attention directed at a goal has not
Opportunity cost of diverting senior builders from core mission is incalculable regardless of how cheap the software is to generate
Maintenance burden does not disappear with cheap initial generation — it shifts from upfront engineering to ongoing remediation
AI-generated code introduces security vulnerabilities that require skilled human review, adding back hidden costs
The constraint was always attention, not software cost

source_posts.title: Disposable software works for Cursor, but probably won't work for you. + The reliability playbook for everyone else

frameworks.example_application: The team wants to vibe-code an internal billing dashboard instead of paying $2K/month for a SaaS tool, arguing that Cursor makes it nearly free. That's code cost thinking. The real cost is three weeks of a senior engineer's attention — someone currently architecting the core product's payment integration. The code generation takes hours; the specification, security review, edge-case handling, and ongoing maintenance consume the same skilled attention they always did. The $2K/month SaaS is buying back the most constrained resource the company has: directed senior attention on the core mission.
do_not_use_when: The team is evaluating AI coding tools to speed up core product development, not to build internal tools or replace SaaS.
The user is a solo founder with no senior engineers whose attention cost is the bottleneck being asked about.
Leadership wants to sunset an existing internally-built tool and migrate to a SaaS vendor, making build-vs-buy moot.
The question is about AI-generated code quality and security practices specifically, not whether to build versus buy.
frameworks.description_original: Separates the collapsed cost of generating code from the unchanged cost of directing skilled human attention toward a goal, exposing the flaw in 'software is now free' reasoning.

frameworks.name: Developer Customers vs. CIO Customers Chasm
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user's product strategy tension stems from mismatched buyer archetypes. Classify their customer base as developer customers or CIO customers using the core distinction: developers can fix things when they break; CIO customers call their account manager. Then sort their specific complaints — feature velocity, SLA pressure, support escalations — against whichever archetype they actually serve, not the one their product philosophy assumes.
when_to_apply: We're shipping features fast and breaking things, but our enterprise customers keep escalating to their account managers
Debating whether our AI startup can displace an incumbent like ServiceNow or Workday by iterating faster
Our product team wants to adopt a disposable-software philosophy but we sell to Fortune 500 procurement teams
Trying to figure out why the same product strategy that works for developer tools is failing in our enterprise segment
Designing our support model and SLA tiers and unsure how much instability our customer base will tolerate
principles: Developer customers can fix things when they break; CIO customers call their account manager
Developers chose bleeding-edge tools knowing they would change; CIOs chose vendors with SLAs specifically to avoid thinking about the software
The gap between these customer types is not a temporary gap that closes as AI improves — it is a fundamental difference in what is being purchased
Enterprise customers are buying reliability and peace of mind, not features
CIO customers need a 'single ringable neck' — someone accountable when things fail

source_posts.title: Disposable software works for Cursor, but probably won't work for you. + The reliability playbook for everyone else

frameworks.example_application: This SaaS startup wants to ship weekly model updates and deprecate old API endpoints on a 30-day cycle, Cursor-style. But their buyers are mid-market operations teams whose CIOs selected this vendor after a six-month procurement process specifically for stability guarantees. These are CIO customers, not developer customers — they don't have engineers who can patch around breaking changes at 2am. The rapid-iteration playbook that works for developer-tool companies will generate support tickets, churn, and contract non-renewals here. The product philosophy needs to be proactive reliability with a 'single ringable neck,' not move-fast-and-ship.
do_not_use_when: The user sells to mid-market SMBs who lack dedicated IT procurement but behave like CIOs, where the real issue is pricing model mismatch, not buyer archetype.
The user is debating internal developer tooling adoption inside an enterprise, where all end-users are technical and the CIO dynamic is irrelevant.
The user's instability complaints stem from a single buggy integration or bad release, not a systemic product philosophy mismatch requiring archetype reclassification.
The user is a consumer SaaS product experiencing churn from power users versus casual users, which is a segmentation problem unrelated to enterprise procurement archetypes.
frameworks.description_original: Classifies enterprise software buyers into two archetypes with fundamentally different tolerances and expectations, determining which product philosophy is viable.

frameworks.name: Proactively Reliable AI: The Two-Step Enterprise Strategy
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when an enterprise software company is sequencing AI capabilities and weighing reliability against automation ambition. Challenge the user's assumption that shipping proactive AI is a prioritization question — it's a precondition question. Push them to prove Step 1 is genuinely complete before discussing Step 2; the common blind spot is mistaking customer demand for proactive AI as proof that trust is already earned.
when_to_apply: Our enterprise customers keep asking for AI features but we still have reliability issues they complain about
We're building an AI agent that takes actions on behalf of users and need to figure out how aggressively to automate
An AI-native competitor is winning developer mindshare but we have the enterprise trust — how do we sequence our AI roadmap?
Product leadership wants to ship proactive AI capabilities but our NPS scores show customers don't fully trust the platform yet
We're debating whether our AI should suggest actions or take them autonomously for enterprise customers
principles: Reliability is table stakes — without it, proactive AI creates anxiety rather than value
You cannot skip step one: attempting proactivity before proving reliability will terrify customers
Reactive AI (chatbots) waits to be asked and is no longer a differentiator; proactive AI creates value customers didn't know they were missing
Trust is earned incrementally — start with low-stakes autonomous actions and build a track record of correct decisions
Earned trust is the precondition for autonomous action on behalf of users
steps: Step 1 — Establish reliability: Prove your product works consistently, data is secure, SLAs are met, and customers have a human to call when something goes wrong. This must come before any autonomous AI capability. This matters because the author argues that the opportunity for enterprise software 'isn't shipping faster—it's earning the right to act autonomously on behalf of users,' and that right is earned only through proven reliability; without it, proactive AI creates anxiety rather than value, and CIOs—unlike developers—will not tolerate systems that make autonomous decisions on an unproven foundation.

Step 2 — Layer in proactive AI: Once reliability is proven and trust is earned, deploy agents that take autonomous action on behalf of users without being asked — surfacing insights, updating records, drafting responses, alerting stakeholders — creating value customers didn't know they were missing. This matters because the author distinguishes reactive AI (chatbots that wait to be asked) as no longer a differentiator from proactive AI that acts autonomously, and frames this proactive capability as 'what proactive AI actually requires'—but only after trust is earned incrementally through low-stakes actions, revealing that skipping the precondition doesn't just risk failure, it terrifies the very customers you're trying to serve.

source_posts.title: Disposable software works for Cursor, but probably won't work for you. + The reliability playbook for everyone else

frameworks.example_application: The product team wants to ship an AI agent that auto-reassigns support tickets based on urgency signals. But customers still file escalations about data sync delays twice a month, and there's no dedicated support line — just a chatbot. Deploying autonomous reassignment now will feel like the system is making decisions customers can't trust or override. The right move is to close the reliability gap first: hit the SLA consistently, give customers a human escalation path, then earn the right to auto-reassign by starting with low-stakes suggestions ('we would have reassigned this — approve?') before graduating to full autonomy.
do_not_use_when: The company is a small startup with no existing customers, so there is no earned trust or reliability track record to build upon.
The user is asking about AI features for a consumer app, where trust dynamics and enterprise procurement concerns don't apply.
Reliability issues are already resolved and customers are actively requesting more automation, making Step 1 redundant and Step 2 the only relevant question.
The product is an internal tooling decision for a single company's own AI infrastructure, not an enterprise software go-to-market sequencing problem.
frameworks.description_original: A sequential two-step framework for enterprise software companies to earn the right to deploy autonomous AI agents by first establishing reliability, then layering in proactive capability.
steps_original: Step 1 — Establish reliability: Prove your product works consistently, data is secure, SLAs are met, and customers have a human to call when something goes wrong. This must come before any autonomous AI capability.

Step 2 — Layer in proactive AI: Once reliability is proven and trust is earned, deploy agents that take autonomous action on behalf of users without being asked — surfacing insights, updating records, drafting responses, alerting stakeholders — creating value customers didn't know they were missing.

frameworks.name: Tool vs. Infrastructure Design Question
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user faces an architectural decision about how much extensibility to build in. Help them see the difference between building a tool that solves one problem and building infrastructure that creates leverage by enabling other systems to build on top of it. Test whether their situation calls for infrastructure thinking by asking how their data model, API exposure, and component modularity would change if three other systems needed to connect to it.
when_to_apply: I'm building a personal productivity system and wondering whether to add an API or keep it simple
I keep rebuilding the same components across different projects and wondering if I should create a shared foundation
Deciding whether my Notion/Obsidian setup should just work for me or serve as a hub that other automations connect to
I built a workflow that works great for one use case but now I want three other things to use its data
Trying to figure out how much modularity and extensibility to invest in upfront versus shipping something that just works
principles: A tool solves a problem; infrastructure enables other things to be built on top of it
Designing with infrastructure in mind creates leverage: one investment pays dividends across everything that connects to it
Infrastructure thinking changes data model choices, API exposure decisions, and how modular components are built
The same architectural patterns scale from simple personal tools to sophisticated multi-system infrastructure without breaking

source_posts.title: 50 people ignored my tool recommendations + here's why their systems still worked (Second Brain follow-up)

frameworks.example_application: This note-taking system is being designed as a tool — it captures and retrieves notes, full stop. But the user wants their task manager, writing workflow, and AI agents to all pull from the same data. That's infrastructure, not a tool. The data model needs to change: structured fields instead of free-text blobs, stable IDs that external systems can reference, and an API layer even if the only consumer today is one Zapier integration. The tell was 'I want my other systems to build on this' — that sentence means infrastructure, and the current flat-file design will break the moment a second system tries to consume it.
do_not_use_when: The user is deciding whether to buy an existing SaaS tool or build internally — a build-vs-buy question, not an architectural design question.
The user has a working system with real users and needs to prioritize which features to ship next — a roadmap prioritization problem, not an infrastructure design decision.
The user is asking whether to document their personal workflow so teammates can follow it — a knowledge-sharing problem where API and modularity thinking is irrelevant.

The user is evaluating whether their prototype is ready to show to customers — a validation and readiness question where infrastructure vs. tool framing would dangerously over-complicate an early-stage decision.
frameworks.description_original: Challenges builders to decide whether they are creating a standalone tool that solves one problem or infrastructure that other systems can build on top of, because the choice determines design decisions and long-term leverage.

frameworks.name: The Bidirectional Fit Assessment Interface
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user frames their job search problem as a presentation or visibility challenge. Shift their framing from credential assertion to capability demonstration by pushing them to build an interface that can be interrogated — not a document that makes claims. Challenge the assumption that better polish solves the problem; the real issue is whether evaluators can discover genuine depth, including honest gaps and explicit mismatches.
when_to_apply: I have deep expertise but keep getting rejected at the resume screen by people who can't evaluate what I actually do
I want to build a professional presence that works asynchronously — something that represents me when I'm not in the room
How do I stand out in a job market flooded with AI-polished resumes that all sound the same?
I'm tired of dumbing down my experience to fit a one-page resume format
I want employers to feel like they discovered my strengths rather than being pitched at
principles: Replace credential assertion with capability demonstration — an interactive interface that can be interrogated is harder to fake than a polished document
Make the fit assessment bidirectional — the tool should honestly tell employers when you are NOT a good match, not just pitch your strengths
Depth of response signals real expertise — multi-turn AI conversations about your work only hold up if genuine understanding underlies them
Publishing your gaps builds more trust than claiming universal competence
Honest rejection of bad fits signals market confidence and saves both parties time
The interface functions as proof of capability, not a claim of capability — evaluators feel they discovered the truth rather than being told it
The work required to build the interface (articulating expertise, identifying genuine strengths and gaps) improves the underlying substance it represents
steps: Choose one interface element to build first (AI-queryable summary, expanded achievement context, or fit assessment tool). This matters because the author explicitly provides an implementation spectrum 'from a 30-minute text document to a weekend build' — forcing a single starting point prevents the paralysis of trying to build everything at once and gets you out of the filtering pile faster, since any one element already shifts you from compressed bullet points to queryable depth.

Write a dense structured document of your real work organized for AI parsing, not human scanning — include specific projects, numbers, lessons, and honest gaps. This matters because the author argues that 'a resume compresses years of work into bullet points' and an ATS reduces you to keyword matches — structuring for AI parsing reverses that compression, and including honest gaps builds more trust than claiming universal competence, as demonstrated by the data engineer example where 'limited Spark Streaming experience' disclosed upfront paradoxically increased trust in every positive claim.

Write a system prompt governing how AI represents you: be specific, cite actual work, acknowledge limitations honestly, include explicit anti-sycophancy instructions and permission to reject mismatched roles. This matters because the author emphasizes 'the difference between asserting credentials and demonstrating capability' and that 'depth in an AI interface is almost impossible to fake' — anti-sycophancy instructions and explicit mismatch rejection make the bidirectional fit assessment real rather than performative, ensuring the tool tells employers NOT to hire you when the match is weak instead of just pitching strengths.

Build the simplest viable version (structured document + instructions for use, Custom GPT, or web interface depending on available time). This matters because the author specifically closed the gap between ambition and execution: 'Three years ago, building a custom interface required engineering skills or real money. That gap closed' — the implementation spectrum exists so that lack of engineering skill is no longer a valid reason to stay trapped optimizing for their broken system.

Publish it somewhere visible and distribute it through existing channels. This matters because the author's core argument is that 'the gates aren't the only path anymore' — if the interface isn't published, you're still a supplicant squeezing through filters; publishing creates 'the surface people encounter when they find you,' shifting you from competing for six-second attention spans to offering something people can 'query, explore, discover.'

Refine based on observed queries — add context where AI responses lack depth, cut material that never gets queried, improve prompts based on edge cases. This matters because the author argues that multi-turn AI conversations about your work 'only hold up if genuine understanding underlies them' — observing where the interface fails to answer with depth reveals where your own articulation of expertise is thin, and the work of fixing those gaps improves the underlying substance it represents, not just the presentation. (inferred)

source_posts.title: Why it's time to escape the application pile + the exact site I shipped (no code required!)

frameworks.example_application: A senior data engineer with 8 years of experience keeps getting filtered out by keyword-matching ATS systems because their resume compresses deep pipeline architecture work into generic bullet points. The conventional approach is to optimize the resume for more keywords. That's wrong here — optimization for keyword density compresses expertise further and makes them indistinguishable from junior candidates who've memorized the same terms. Instead, they build a queryable interface: a structured document of their actual projects (with real metrics, architectural decisions, and honest gaps like 'limited Spark Streaming experience') paired with a Custom GPT that can answer multi-turn technical questions about their work. When a hiring manager asks 'How did you handle schema evolution across 40 microservices?', the interface gives a detailed, cite-specific answer that no resume padding could survive. The interface also explicitly flags mismatches — 'This candidate has no production ML pipeline experience; if that's core to the role, this isn't a fit' — which paradoxically increases trust in every positive claim it makes.
do_not_use_when: The user is a recent graduate with minimal experience — no deep expertise exists yet to build a bidirectional interface around.
The user needs to apply to a government or regulated role where standardized application formats are legally mandated and unconventional interfaces would disqualify them.
The user is a consultant or freelancer seeking clients, not employment — the sales and trust dynamics require a different positioning framework entirely.
The user's rejection problem stems from a genuine skills gap, not an evaluation mismatch — reframing presentation won't fix a substance deficit.
frameworks.description_original: Reframes job-seeking from one-directional credential presentation to a mutual fit assessment where the candidate's interface actively evaluates and can reject mismatched opportunities.

frameworks.name: Asserting Credentials vs. Demonstrating Capability
frameworks.description: Help the user see the difference between asserting credentials and creating conditions for discovery by testing whether their current approach asks evaluators to accept conclusions or reach them independently. Push them to recognize that polish in a document proves only access to AI tools, while depth in an interactive interface proves genuine understanding. Design for evaluator discovery, not declaration — they architect the conditions; the evaluator feels they formed their own judgment.
when_to_apply: My resume looks the same as everyone else's because AI can generate polished bullets for anyone
I have deep expertise but evaluators keep treating me like every other applicant with similar-sounding credentials
I'm deciding whether to build a traditional portfolio or something interactive that lets people explore my work
Hiring managers in my field have become skeptical of polished application materials because they assume AI wrote everything
I want to stand out in a job search but I'm worried that more polish just looks like better prompting
principles: People believe conclusions they reach themselves more than conclusions they are told — design for discovery, not declaration
AI-mediated self-presentation makes depth almost impossible to fake because multi-turn interrogation surfaces what is actually there
Polish in a document proves only access to AI tools; depth in an interactive interface proves genuine understanding
Honest acknowledgment of gaps in an interface demonstrates self-awareness, which itself is a credibility signal
You architect the discovery conditions; the evaluator feels they formed their own judgment

source_posts.title: Why it's time to escape the application pile + the exact site I shipped (no code required!)

frameworks.example_application: This candidate's portfolio site is a static PDF with impressive bullet points — that's asserting credentials, not demonstrating capability. In a world where Claude can produce those same bullets for anyone, the signal value is zero. The candidate who built an interactive interface where the evaluator can ask follow-up questions, drill into edge cases, and probe reasoning depth is on the other side of the distinction — the evaluator discovers the expertise themselves and trusts it precisely because they feel they formed their own judgment rather than being told what to believe.
do_not_use_when: The user is a consultant pitching to enterprise clients who require standardized RFP submissions where interactive tools would be disqualified on procedural grounds.
The user is asking how to stand out in a field where evaluators are non-technical executives who interpret unconventional formats as signs of poor professional judgment.
The user already has a strong referral from an insider and needs advice on not undermining that advantage, not on reengineering how evaluators discover their capability.
The user is a recent graduate with no deep expertise to surface through interrogation, making the interactive-depth premise actively harmful compared to simpler differentiation advice.
frameworks.description_original: Distinguishes between telling evaluators what to believe about you (resume assertions) versus creating conditions for evaluators to discover your capability through their own exploration of an interactive interface.

frameworks.name: The Bottleneck Relocation Model
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user's chaos or paralysis stems from a capability upgrade, not a missing capability. Shift their framing from "we have an efficiency problem" to "our bottleneck relocated" by diagnosing which of the four new scarce resources — clarity, ambition, distribution, or relationships — is now the actual constraint. Then surface which of their existing habits and rituals were built to protect execution costs that no longer exist.
when_to_apply: Our team adopted AI tools and got faster at building, but somehow our output quality and impact went down
We have all these planning ceremonies and approval gates that used to feel essential but now feel like bureaucratic theater
I can build anything in a weekend now but I'm paralyzed about what to build — the hard part completely flipped
We're trying to figure out which organizational processes to kill versus keep after a major capability upgrade
My old workflow was optimized for a world where building was expensive, and it's not working anymore but I can't articulate why
principles: Every work system is implicitly organized around protecting whatever resource is most scarce
When a bottleneck is eliminated, it relocates downstream rather than disappearing
When execution gets cheap, the new scarce resources become clarity, ambition, distribution, and relationships
Habits and rituals designed to protect the old bottleneck become waste once the bottleneck moves
Judgment, taste, and knowing what's worth building become more valuable as the cost of building falls

source_posts.title: Grab the prompt kit I use when work feels inefficient but busy + specific experiments for each bottleneck

frameworks.example_application: The conventional read is that the team needs better project management because they're shipping lots of mediocre work. That's wrong here — the bottleneck relocated. Execution used to be scarce, so every ritual (sprint planning, PRDs, approval gates) was designed to protect execution capacity from waste. Now execution is cheap — AI handles most of the building — but the team never reorganized around what's actually scarce: clarity about what's worth building and distribution to get it in front of the right people. The sprint ceremonies aren't enabling work anymore; they're protecting a constraint that no longer exists, which means they're pure drag. The investment should shift to taste-setting rituals (what's worth building?) and distribution habits (who sees it and why?).
do_not_use_when: The team's slowdown is caused by a specific technical debt problem or infrastructure failure, not a capability upgrade shifting what's scarce.
The user is a solo creator asking which personal project to prioritize, with no organizational processes or team workflows involved.
The organization just downsized significantly and the chaos stems from missing headcount and skills, not from a bottleneck that relocated after an efficiency gain.
The user adopted AI tools recently but their core complaint is about output accuracy and hallucinations, not about paralysis over what to build or which processes to keep.
frameworks.description_original: Reframes workplace chaos and inefficiency as a predictable consequence of the bottleneck moving from execution to four new scarce resources (clarity, ambition, distribution, relationships), and diagnoses which old habits were built to protect the wrong constraint.

frameworks.name: Old-Ritual Failure Catalog
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user's team feels busy but slow, or when AI tools are available but process hasn't changed. Check their workflow against these eight failure modes — permission loops, polish as procrastination, meetings over prototypes, approval waiting, planning over building, decks over demos, consensus before action, hoarding until ready — and surface which specific ritual is eating velocity. Push them to name the last time a delay actually hedged a real risk.
when_to_apply: My team is busy all the time but our actual output velocity feels embarrassingly low
We have powerful AI tools available but our process still feels like it did two years ago
Someone on the team is spending more time preparing to do the work than actually doing it
I keep waiting for approvals or alignment meetings before I can make progress on something low-risk
Our workflow has a lot of steps that feel like they exist to manage risk but the risk they manage is tiny compared to the delay they cause
principles: Permission loops distribute accountability but cost more time than the risk they hedge when execution is cheap
Polish can be a form of procrastination and ego protection masquerading as diligence
Meetings surface opinions but rarely resolve questions as cleanly as a prototype does
Waiting for approvals or decisions now costs more than making provisional decisions and correcting course
Planning elaborates assumptions without generating learning; learning only happens when something is built
A deck describes a thing; a demo is the thing—the former invites abstract argument, the latter anchors discussion in reality
Consensus before action costs more than acting and reporting results, because people align around data more than proposals
Hoarding work until it feels ready delays feedback to the point where changing course is expensive

source_posts.title: Grab the prompt kit I use when work feels inefficient but busy + specific experiments for each bottleneck

frameworks.example_application: The team spent three days building a slide deck to get leadership alignment on a feature direction. That's the 'deck instead of demo' failure mode — the original logic was that building was expensive so you had to secure buy-in before committing resources, but now a working prototype takes less time than the deck does. The deck invited two rounds of abstract debate about hypotheticals that a clickable demo would have resolved in the first meeting. The substitute: build the simplest version, show it, let people react to reality instead of a description of reality.
do_not_use_when: The team's low output velocity stems from unclear strategy or conflicting priorities, not from ritual overhead slowing down well-directed work.
The approvals and review steps causing delays are legally or regulatorily mandated, so eliminating them would create compliance exposure, not efficiency.
The user is asking about a single personal productivity habit, not diagnosing a team-level workflow pattern across multiple people or handoffs.
The slowness is caused by technical debt or system instability requiring careful, high-risk changes where moving fast and correcting course is genuinely dangerous.
frameworks.description_original: Enumerates eight specific work habits that were rational under expensive-execution economics but now waste time or hide judgment, each with its original logic, its failure mode in the new environment, and a concrete substitute behavior.

frameworks.name: AI Usage vs. AI Leverage Distinction
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user conflates AI adoption metrics with genuine capability improvement. Help them see the difference between an activity claim ("I use AI") and a leverage claim ("my output is different now") by pressing them to name concrete, measurable changes in deliverables. Push back on usage statistics as evidence of progress — the real diagnostic question is whether workflows were restructured or tools were merely inserted into existing processes.
when_to_apply: My team all uses AI tools now but I can't point to any measurable improvement in our output
We're tracking how often employees use ChatGPT or Copilot and I'm not sure that metric tells us anything real
Someone on my team talks a lot about AI but their actual deliverables look the same as before
Our company mandated AI adoption and everyone complied, but nothing seems to have actually changed
I want to distinguish between employees who are genuinely transformed by AI and those who are just performing adoption
principles: 'I use AI' is an activity claim; 'my output is different now' is a leverage claim — only the latter has value
Performative productivity emerges when usage is measured instead of outcomes
AI leverage requires workflow restructuring, not just tool insertion into existing processes
The gap between usage and leverage is what separates companies with compounding AI advantage from those with the appearance of transformation

source_posts.title: Shopify's AI Memo Was a Filter, Not a Productivity Play. Grab the AI Leverage Audit I built after watching Duolingo fail and Shopify succeed.

frameworks.example_application: This team reports 92% AI adoption — every member uses Copilot daily — but their sprint velocity, code quality metrics, and feature throughput are statistically identical to six months ago. That's usage, not leverage. The tell: they inserted AI into existing workflows without restructuring any of them. The developer who actually has leverage is the one who eliminated the entire manual QA review step by building an AI-driven test generation pipeline — her output is structurally different, not just AI-assisted.
do_not_use_when: The user is asking how to select which AI tools to adopt in the first place, before any usage has begun — the distinction between usage and leverage is premature.
The user's team shows no output improvement because of a broken underlying process unrelated to AI, making AI leverage analysis a distraction from the real bottleneck.
The user wants to build an internal AI usage policy for compliance or legal reasons, where tracking adoption metrics is genuinely the goal rather than a misdiagnosis.
The user is a solo founder asking whether AI tools are worth learning at all, not diagnosing an organizational gap between adoption and outcomes.
frameworks.description_original: Separates the act of using AI tools (activity) from actually achieving different, measurable outputs through AI (leverage), preventing workers and organizations from confusing adoption metrics with genuine capability improvement.

frameworks.name: Two AI Economies Framework
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user needs to calibrate AI risk tolerance across different tasks. Classify their work into the production/abundance economy or the judgment/complexity economy, then match the appropriate tool philosophy to each: aggressive adoption where speed and volume dominate, adoption quality over speed where human expertise is what the AI amplifies. Push back on any single risk posture applied across all tasks — that misalignment is the primary failure mode this framework exists to correct.
when_to_apply: I'm trying to figure out whether it's okay to trust AI output without heavy review for this particular task
My team uses the same review process for every AI-assisted deliverable and it feels wrong — some things we over-check and others we under-check
I'm building a career strategy around AI and need to understand where human expertise still commands a premium versus where speed wins
We're debating whether to adopt AI aggressively across the board or take a cautious approach, and neither extreme feels right
I need to set different AI risk tolerances for different parts of our workflow but don't have a clear framework for which is which
principles: Tasks that produce outputs (content, drafts, media, creative exploration) belong to the production/abundance economy where speed and volume matter most
Tasks that exercise judgment (production code, legal analysis, medical decisions, high-stakes analysis) belong to the complexity/judgment economy where reliability and verifiability matter most
In the production economy, adopt aggressively—competitors will, and the market handles benefits automatically
In the judgment economy, prioritize adoption quality over adoption speed—preserve human judgment alongside AI assistance
The advantage in the production economy is knowing what to do with outputs, not just having the tools
The advantage in the judgment economy is the human expertise the AI amplifies, not the AI itself
Using the same risk posture for all tasks is the primary failure mode—generating freely when you should verify, or over-reviewing when speed matters

source_posts.title: Two founders, two safety theories, two products—and a framework for knowing which one matches your risk tolerance

frameworks.example_application: Writing marketing copy for A/B testing falls squarely in the production/abundance economy — errors are cheap, iteration is fast, and the competitive advantage goes to whoever generates and tests more variants. The team should use the fastest, most aggressive AI tools available and stop over-reviewing drafts. But the same team's contract review workflow belongs to the judgment/complexity economy: an undetected clause error creates real liability. There, the advantage comes from the lawyer's expertise being amplified by AI, not replaced by it, and adoption quality matters far more than adoption speed. The failure happening right now is that legal is reviewing AI-generated contracts with the same casual posture the marketing team rightly uses for ad copy.
do_not_use_when: The user is deciding whether to adopt a specific AI vendor or platform, where procurement, pricing, and integration concerns dominate rather than task-level risk calibration.
The user's organization is so early in AI adoption that no workflows use AI yet, making economy classification premature before basic tooling decisions are resolved.
The user is asking about AI governance policy for regulatory compliance, where legal mandates override internal risk-tolerance calibration entirely.
The user wants to evaluate the accuracy of a specific AI tool on a known benchmark, which is a technical assessment question not a workflow-categorization problem.
frameworks.description_original: A classification system that sorts work into two distinct AI economies—abundance/production and judgment/complexity—each with a matched tool philosophy and risk posture.

frameworks.name: AI as Multiplier (The Multiplier Insight)
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user attributes uneven AI results to tools, prompts, or workflows. Shift their framing from "what multiplier should I use" to "what am I multiplying" by surfacing the depth of context and expertise feeding their AI inputs. Challenge the assumption that prompt optimization is the highest-leverage investment — redirect them toward building compounding context as the real infrastructure question.
when_to_apply: I've tried multiple AI tools and workflows but my output quality hasn't meaningfully improved
Prioritizing between building domain knowledge vs. learning more AI techniques
Explaining to a team why two people using the same AI tools get wildly different results
Deciding whether to invest time in prompt engineering courses or in systematizing my professional knowledge
I feel like I'm getting faster but not smarter with AI
principles: AI is a multiplier, so its value is determined by what it multiplies, not by the multiplier itself
Shallow context multiplied produces faster shallow output; deep expertise multiplied produces qualitatively different output
The strategic question is 'what am I multiplying?' not 'which tools should I use?'
Building compounding context (captured knowledge, relationships, project history) is the highest-leverage AI investment
Infrastructure that lets AI amplify accumulated expertise outperforms any prompt optimization

source_posts.title: Why every system you've tried has failed + grab the 90-minute guide to one that won't

frameworks.example_application: Two consultants use the same Claude setup with similar prompts. One produces boilerplate strategy decks; the other produces insights clients call transformative. The difference isn't prompt skill — it's that the second consultant has 15 years of encoded pattern recognition, a personal knowledge base of 200+ engagements, and documented frameworks from every failure. AI is multiplying deep, structured expertise in one case and multiplying surface-level familiarity in the other. The highest-leverage move for the first consultant isn't a better prompt template — it's spending six months building the knowledge infrastructure that gives AI something worth amplifying.
do_not_use_when: The user is a beginner with no domain expertise yet, so there is no existing knowledge base for AI to multiply.
The user's output quality problem stems from broken data pipelines or hallucination errors, not shallow context inputs.
The user needs to choose between two specific AI vendor products on cost and integration criteria, not justify an investment philosophy.
The user's team uses identical AI outputs uniformly across a compliance checklist where expertise variation is deliberately suppressed.
frameworks.description_original: Reframes AI leverage not as a function of prompts or tools but as a function of the depth of context and expertise being multiplied, making knowledge infrastructure the primary investment.

frameworks.name: The Factory Curve
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user's question centers on compute access, infrastructure timing, or competitive speed — it reframes AI competition from model capability to supply chain position. Shift their framing from "who has the better model" to "who controls the integrated factory module" by surfacing upstream procurement signals (wafer-level memory, packaging slots, power agreements) as the real demand indicators. Challenge the assumption that falling behind can be corrected gradually — 'catch up later' means spot prices and queues, not a closing gap.
when_to_apply: Is the current AI infrastructure buildout a bubble, or is demand genuinely outrunning physical supply?
We're debating whether to lock in GPU/memory capacity now or wait for prices to drop — what's the real risk of waiting?
Our AI product roadmap assumes compute availability that our vendor hasn't actually guaranteed
Why is our competitor shipping faster when our model is technically better?
Trying to understand which companies in the AI stack have real structural advantages versus hype-driven valuations
principles: Bubbles don't pre-buy bottlenecks — upstream procurement behavior (wafer-level memory, packaging slots, power agreements) reveals whether demand is real
Supply ramps slowly due to physics and permitting; capital alone cannot accelerate it
Demand compounds with state — stateful/agentic workloads grow memory footprint faster than request count
'Catch up later' doesn't work — falling behind the curve means paying spot prices or queuing, not gradually closing the gap
The unit of competition is the integrated system (factory module), not the individual component or model

source_posts.title: Why CES 2026 marks a turning point + the constraint map behind the headlines (and yes, there are prompts)

frameworks.example_application: The conventional read is that Company A is behind because its benchmark scores trail the frontier by six months. That's wrong here. Company A pre-bought 18 months of HBM packaging capacity and locked 200MW of power in three regions. Company B has a better model on paper but is already queuing inference jobs and paying spot rates for memory allocation. The binding constraint isn't the model — it's the factory curve. Company A can serve stateful agentic workloads at scale next quarter; Company B cannot, regardless of research velocity. The tell that this isn't a bubble: upstream suppliers are reporting committed wafer-level memory purchases with 18-month lead times, not speculative option contracts.
do_not_use_when: The user is a startup evaluating whether to build on a public cloud API versus fine-tune their own model — a build-vs-buy decision, not a supply chain positioning problem.
The user is asking why a competitor is shipping faster when the real bottleneck is the competitor's superior go-to-market motion or sales cycle, not compute access.
The user is a policymaker assessing national AI competitiveness at a geopolitical level, where the relevant constraints are export controls and talent, not factory economics for a single firm.
The user is already capacity-constrained by software architecture or data pipeline issues, making physical supply chain analysis irrelevant to their actual bottleneck.
