frameworks.description_original: Reframes AI competition from model capability to supply chain position, arguing that the binding constraint has shifted from research milestones to physical factory economics (memory allocation, packaging capacity, power).

frameworks.name: Four-Lane Supply Strategy
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is evaluating the completeness of an AI infrastructure procurement strategy. Classify their current sourcing position across all four lanes — bridge capacity, second-source compute, custom silicon, and memory supply at wafer level. Push them to prove coverage beyond the most visible constraint, and surface whether Lane 4 exposure exists before it becomes unacquirable.
when_to_apply: We've secured GPU capacity but I'm worried we're missing other infrastructure bottlenecks that will surface in 12-18 months
Evaluating whether a competitor's AI infrastructure position is actually durable or just addresses the most visible constraint
Building a multi-vendor AI supply chain and need to identify which lanes we haven't covered
Our custom silicon program is on track but I'm not sure we've thought about upstream physical inputs like memory
Stress-testing an AI infrastructure procurement plan to find gaps before they become crises
principles: Each lane solves a distinct constraint — time, supply risk, unit economics, and physical input scarcity
A complete strategy requires coverage across all four lanes, not just the most visible one
Multi-vendor sourcing across lanes mirrors multi-cloud logic — diversification reduces chokepoint risk
Lane 4 (upstream physical inputs like memory at wafer level) is the most binding and hardest to acquire late
steps: Lane 1 — Bridge capacity: Solve the time constraint by securing rental-at-scale access while longer-term infrastructure comes online. This matters because the author warns that teams who didn't lock capacity early are 'now waiting in queues, paying spot prices, or discovering their vendor can't deliver what they promised' — bridge capacity closes the gap between having a strategy and having allocation before the longer-term lanes deliver.

Lane 2 — Second-source compute: Solve supply risk by establishing a second GPU ecosystem or specialized infrastructure outside primary vendors. This matters because the author frames the next era as one where 'allocation is the bottleneck' and you compete on supply position — a single-vendor compute dependency creates a chokepoint that mirrors the exact fragility multi-cloud logic was designed to prevent, and the example application shows that even an impressive-looking compute position is structurally fragile without it. (inferred)

Lane 3 — Custom silicon: Solve unit economics by pursuing purpose-built accelerators for predictable high-volume inference workloads. This matters because the author identifies the shift to 'factory economics' as the defining transition — when 10× cheaper inference unlocks ambient AI, purpose-built silicon is how you bend the cost curve on high-volume inference rather than perpetually renting general-purpose compute at prices that don't work at scale.

Lane 4 — Memory supply: Solve the binding physical constraint by engaging memory suppliers at the wafer level as a strategic input. This matters because the author warns that 'supply can't catch demand, and waiting doesn't work' — the example application reveals that wafer-level memory commitments get locked up 18 months before a team even recognizes the constraint, making Lane 4 the lane where late movers find the resource literally unacquirable and where custom silicon investments fail despite being sound in isolation.

source_posts.title: Why CES 2026 marks a turning point + the constraint map behind the headlines (and yes, there are prompts)

frameworks.example_application: This company has locked in massive GPU reservations with a hyperscaler (Lane 1 bridge capacity) and started a custom silicon program (Lane 3), but has zero second-source compute relationship outside NVIDIA (Lane 2 gap) and no direct engagement with HBM suppliers at the wafer level (Lane 4 gap). The custom silicon bet won't matter if they can't secure memory allocation — Lane 4 is the binding constraint, and by the time they realize it, wafer commitments will already be locked up by competitors who moved 18 months earlier. Two of four lanes are uncovered, which means this infrastructure position is structurally fragile despite looking impressive on the compute side.
do_not_use_when: The user is assessing AI infrastructure for a small startup using cloud APIs exclusively, where no physical procurement decisions exist.
The user wants to evaluate a competitor's AI strategy but the competitor is a software-only SaaS vendor with no hardware dependencies.
The user is stress-testing a procurement plan for non-AI manufacturing supply chains where GPU bottlenecks and silicon lanes are irrelevant.
The user is asking about internal GPU utilization efficiency and workload scheduling, not about sourcing or procurement gaps.
frameworks.description_original: A classification of four distinct supply chain lanes that map to different factory bottlenecks, used to evaluate whether an AI infrastructure strategy addresses all binding constraints.
steps_original: Lane 1 — Bridge capacity: Solve the time constraint by securing rental-at-scale access while longer-term infrastructure comes online
Lane 2 — Second-source compute: Solve supply risk by establishing a second GPU ecosystem or specialized infrastructure outside primary vendors
Lane 3 — Custom silicon: Solve unit economics by pursuing purpose-built accelerators for predictable high-volume inference workloads
Lane 4 — Memory supply: Solve the binding physical constraint by engaging memory suppliers at the wafer level as a strategic input

frameworks.name: Ambient Failure Cascade
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is diagnosing failure modes of a committed ambient AI system. Check their situation against the degradation → missed signal → harm → investigation → liability → pullback cascade. Push back on the assumption that uptime SLAs cover inference quality — these are distinct failure surfaces. Surface the shift from "bad answer" to "not there when needed" as the governing failure mode.
when_to_apply: We're moving from a request-based AI feature to an always-on ambient system and need to understand what new failure modes we're accepting
Our AI vendor's SLA covers uptime but I'm worried about silent quality degradation that nobody would catch
We had an incident where the AI system didn't flag something it should have — how do we think about the full downstream exposure?
Leadership wants to treat our continuous inference system with the same governance model we use for our chatbot
We're designing reliability and governance requirements for an AI system that runs without per-request human review
principles: Degradation → missed signal → harm → investigation → liability → pullback is the standard cascade sequence
The critical failure mode shifts from 'bad answer' to 'not there when needed'
Reliability becomes existential — failure modes tolerable in occasional-use systems become unacceptable in always-on systems
Governance becomes operational — compliance must be explainable in real time at scale, not checked at deployment
Downtime becomes political when people depend on inference being continuously available
SLAs covering uptime do not cover inference quality degradation — these are distinct failure surfaces

source_posts.title: Why CES 2026 marks a turning point + the constraint map behind the headlines (and yes, there are prompts)

frameworks.example_application: The ambient monitoring system didn't crash — it quietly degraded inference quality over three weeks, missing a pattern it would have flagged at full fidelity. The missed signal led to a patient safety incident, which triggered a regulatory investigation. The vendor's SLA covered uptime (99.9%) but said nothing about inference quality, so the liability landed entirely on the deploying organization. This is the standard cascade: degradation → missed signal → harm → investigation → liability → pullback. The failure mode was never 'bad answer' — it was 'not there when needed,' which is categorically harder to detect and categorically more dangerous.
do_not_use_when: The user is evaluating whether to adopt an ambient AI system at all, not diagnosing failure modes of one already committed to.
The system runs continuously but outputs are always reviewed by a human before any action is taken, negating the unreviewed-inference assumption.
The incident involved a one-time batch processing job misclassifying records, not a persistent inference system with ongoing exposure.
Leadership wants governance for a scheduled nightly report generated by AI, which has natural human checkpoints and lacks the always-available dependency dynamic.
frameworks.description_original: Enumerates how ambient (always-on) AI systems produce categorically different failure modes than request-based AI, following a predictable cascade from degradation through liability to system pullback.

frameworks.name: Constraints vs. Preferences vs. Proof vs. Confidence Distinction
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is struggling to define when an agent's output is "done" or which quality checks can be automated. Help them see the difference between constraints (objectively checkable gates), preferences (human-judgment calls), proof (a verifiable artifact), and confidence (a belief state that cannot close a loop). Push them to convert each quality standard into one of these four categories — anything that remains a preference must be evaluated by a human, not delegated.
when_to_apply: My agent loop keeps running in circles and never seems to converge on a final output
I'm writing acceptance criteria for a task I want to delegate to an AI agent and I'm not sure what counts as 'done'
Some of my quality standards are gut-feel things like 'professional tone' and I need to figure out which checks to automate vs. review myself
I can't tell whether the agent actually verified something or just expressed confidence that it's correct
I want to build an automated review layer but I'm struggling to formalize what 'good' looks like for every dimension
principles: Constraints are what must be true and are objectively checkable ('must include a recommendation', 'must not exceed one page')
Preferences are what you'd like but cannot be verified by a system ('should feel professional', 'should be compelling') — these require human evaluation
Proof is a checkable artifact: the source link exists, the number reconciles, the quote appears in the transcript
Confidence is a belief state ('I think this is correct') — it cannot be verified by a loop and requires human review at that stage
Repeatable standards (always true regardless of context) can be built into automated checks; situational standards (meaning varies by context) require human judgment each time
If you cannot convert a preference into a constraint, you must evaluate it yourself — it cannot be delegated to a loop

source_posts.title: My honest field notes on the verification gap no one's talking about, plus the complete guide + prompt kit that makes agent loops actually converge

frameworks.example_application: The brief says the output 'must include three sourced recommendations' and 'should feel strategic.' The first requirement is a constraint — an agent loop can check whether exactly three recommendations exist and whether each has a source link (proof). The second is a preference — 'feels strategic' is a belief about tone that no automated check can verify. The team was stuck because their eval loop kept rejecting drafts on vibes it couldn't measure. Splitting the spec into checkable constraints and human-reviewed preferences means the loop converges on structure while a human makes the final taste call on tone.
do_not_use_when: The user is asking how to prioritize which AI tasks to automate first, not how to define done-criteria for tasks already chosen for delegation.
The user's loop is stuck because of a technical bug or API failure, not because acceptance criteria are ambiguous or unverifiable.
The user wants to evaluate whether to trust an AI vendor's claims about accuracy benchmarks, not classify their own internal quality standards for delegation.
The user is designing a human approval workflow for regulated decisions where no automation is permitted, making constraint-versus-preference sorting irrelevant to their actual problem.
frameworks.description_original: A four-part vocabulary for classifying work requirements so that teams can separate machine-checkable gates from human-judgment calls, enabling reliable agent delegation.

frameworks.name: Problem Portfolio Assessment
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user needs to assess which parts of their current role are gaining or losing value. Challenge their instinct to list skills or job functions — push them to prove which problems would go unsolved without them. Surface the blind spot that time allocation rarely matches where the appreciating problems sit, which generic career advice never catches.
when_to_apply: I have a nagging sense that half of what I do every day could be done by AI in a year, but I'm not sure which half
I'm preparing for a career conversation and need to articulate my value beyond my job title or tech stack
I want to figure out which parts of my role to actively grow versus which to hand off or automate away
I'm considering a career pivot and need to know which of my capabilities are portable versus locked to my current employer
My performance review is coming up and I realize I can't clearly name the three problems that justify my compensation
principles: Define your portfolio by the three to five problems that would go unsolved if you disappeared — not your title or skill list
Scarcity of substitutes determines value: the shorter the list of people who can solve a problem without supervision, the more valuable it is
Consequence severity matters: high-downside problems command premium value for the skill to solve them correctly
Assess AI directionality per problem: some problems are being automated (depreciating), others become more judgment-intensive as output volume increases (appreciating)
Transferability multiplies value: skill that travels across companies and contexts is worth more than knowledge locked to one context
steps: List the three to five problems you are actually paid to solve — stated as what would go unsolved, not as job functions. This matters because the author identifies a predictable self-deception pattern: people describe their value in terms of titles, skills, or activities rather than unsolved problems, which lets them avoid confronting whether their work actually matters — the same way 'being patient' can disguise passivity in better language.

For each problem, answer: How many others could solve this without supervision? This matters because the author's principle that 'scarcity of substitutes determines value' is the core economic test — if many people can solve the problem unsupervised, your hold on that work is fragile regardless of how much time you spend on it, and skipping this step lets you maintain the comforting narrative that your experience is 'valuable and hard to replace' without evidence.

For each problem, answer: What breaks if it is solved poorly — money, trust, speed, or safety? This matters because the author argues that consequence severity commands premium value — as shown in the example where debugging production incidents matters precisely because wrong data cascades into billing errors, and without naming the specific downside you cannot distinguish high-stakes judgment work from work that merely feels important.

For each problem, answer: Does AI make this cheaper to do, or does it make mistakes more expensive to catch? This matters because the author insists on assessing AI directionality per problem rather than in aggregate — some problems depreciate as AI automates them (like migration scripts), while others appreciate because AI increases output volume and failure surface area, making human judgment more critical, not less; missing this distinction is the blind spot that generic career advice never catches.

For each problem, answer: Does this skill transfer across companies and contexts, or is it locked to your current situation? This matters because the author warns that people tell themselves their experience is 'valuable and hard to replace' while ignoring signals that their knowledge is context-dependent — a skill locked to one employer's systems gives you no leverage and no exit, which transferability testing reveals. (inferred)

Classify each problem as appreciating, depreciating, or neutral based on the four answers. This matters because the author's prompt system explicitly forces you to look at your own recorded answers before classifying — 'it's harder to fool yourself when you're looking at your own words' — and the classification prevents the narrative drift where you quietly reclassify depreciating work as still valuable without confronting the evidence.

Identify the gap between where you spend time and where the appreciating problems sit. This matters because the author's core insight is that time allocation rarely matches where appreciating problems sit — as in the example where 40% of time went to depreciating migration scripts and under 10% to the appreciating incident diagnosis work — and without surfacing this gap explicitly, the unreliable narrator in your head will insist your calendar already reflects your priorities.

source_posts.title: My honest field notes on being my own unreliable narrator + the governance mechanism I finally built to help

frameworks.example_application: A senior data engineer defines their real portfolio as: (1) designing data pipelines for novel integrations, (2) debugging production data quality incidents under time pressure, (3) writing migration scripts, (4) mentoring junior engineers, (5) vendor evaluation for data tools. Problem 3 — migration scripts — has few substitutes today but AI is rapidly closing that gap; it's depreciating. Problem 2 — debugging production incidents where wrong data could cascade into billing errors — has high consequence severity, few people who can do it unsupervised, and AI actually makes it harder because automated pipelines create more failure surface area; it's appreciating. The gap is clear: 40% of weekly time goes to migration scripts, less than 10% to building systematic incident diagnosis capability. The reallocation target writes itself.
do_not_use_when: The user is a recent graduate with no work history to assess — they lack an existing problem portfolio to evaluate.
The user is asking which technical skills to learn next, not which current capabilities to invest in or exit.
The user's role is entirely execution-based with no discretionary judgment, making consequence-severity and substitute-scarcity distinctions meaningless.
The user is evaluating an external job offer's compensation fairness, not diagnosing the value of problems they currently own.
frameworks.description_original: A four-question diagnostic applied to each problem you are paid to solve that classifies whether each skill is appreciating or depreciating in value, surfacing where to invest versus exit.
steps_original: List the three to five problems you are actually paid to solve — stated as what would go unsolved, not as job functions
For each problem, answer: How many others could solve this without supervision?
For each problem, answer: What breaks if it is solved poorly — money, trust, speed, or safety?
For each problem, answer: Does AI make this cheaper to do, or does it make mistakes more expensive to catch?
For each problem, answer: Does this skill transfer across companies and contexts, or is it locked to your current situation?
Classify each problem as appreciating, depreciating, or neutral based on the four answers
Identify the gap between where you spend time and where the appreciating problems sit

frameworks.name: Magnifying-Glass Company vs. Tiger-Team Company
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user's AI investment decisions or team performance concerns map onto the tension between visibility and execution. Help them see the difference between a magnifying-glass company and a tiger-team company by testing whether their AI tools follow work or dictate it — and whether measurement overhead is suppressing the autonomous execution that actually produces value.
when_to_apply: We're rolling out AI productivity scoring and our best people seem disengaged — is the tool the problem?
Our dashboards show improving metrics but actual product velocity feels slower than before we added all this visibility tooling
I'm deciding whether to invest our AI budget in management oversight tools or in giving small teams better execution capabilities
High-performing teams that used to operate autonomously are now spending significant time on reporting and legibility work
We have extensive AI-powered metrics but I suspect people are gaming the measurements rather than doing better work
principles: Legibility should follow work, not dictate it — AI should reconstruct what happened after the fact, not impose structure before
The magnifying-glass path selects for the feeling of control; the tiger-team path selects for the reality of output
Surveillance creates concealment: when measurement systems reward clean legibility, real messy work goes underground
When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure — AI accelerates this failure mode by making the measurement layer cheap and authoritative-looking
Small, high-trust teams with clear scope and autonomy are the primary production units of value
AI's role in a tiger-team company is as translator and historian, not bureaucrat or overseer

source_posts.title: Grab the 4 prompts I use to make messy work legible--without killing what made it valuable + the visibility trap most companies fall into (and how to avoid it)

frameworks.example_application: This organization is a magnifying-glass company. The tell: they just deployed AI-powered productivity dashboards across engineering, and their best engineers are now spending 30% of their time making work legible to the dashboard rather than doing the work. Sprint velocity looks great on the executive deck, but the three senior engineers who drove 60% of the team's real output are interviewing elsewhere. Meanwhile, the messy experimental work that produced last quarter's breakthrough feature has stopped entirely — nobody will touch ambiguous projects that score poorly on the visibility tools. The AI investment is selecting for the feeling of control while destroying the conditions that produce output.
do_not_use_when: The team's underperformance stems from unclear goals or missing skills, not from measurement overhead suppressing autonomous execution.
The organization operates in a regulated industry where audit trails and documented oversight are legally required, not optional cultural choices.
The user is asking about AI tooling for a single individual contributor's personal productivity, with no team-level or organizational design dimension.
Metrics are lagging because the product itself is architecturally broken, making org-design framing a distraction from a technical root cause.
frameworks.description_original: A strategic fork distinguishing organizations that use AI primarily for visibility and oversight from those that use AI to multiply execution power in small, high-trust teams.

frameworks.name: Legible vs. Illegible Work
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is trying to measure, protect, or formalize work that resists easy capture. Help them see the difference between legible work — tickets, OKRs, dashboards — and the illegible layer of favors, backchannels, and shared intuition that actually generates value. Push them to read their own emergencies: who people went to during the last crisis reveals the real org chart, not the formal one.
when_to_apply: Our top performer's contributions don't show up in any dashboard or OKR, and I'm worried they'll get passed over or managed out
We're rolling out AI productivity monitoring and I need to think about what it will actually capture versus what it will miss
During a crisis, the people who stepped up weren't the ones on the org chart — how do I protect that dynamic without formalizing it to death?
We're deciding which informal processes to formalize and I'm worried about killing the fast paths that actually keep us running
A team looks great on paper metrics but something feels off about their actual output and impact
principles: Illegible work — favors, backchannels, shared intuition, emergency response — is the actual engine of value, not a supplement to legible work
The legible layer is scaffolding: necessary and useful, but not where value gets created
The company tells the truth about itself in emergencies: who people actually go to reveals the real org chart
AI amplifies illegible work by giving small teams leverage, making the illegible layer more powerful and more at risk from surveillance
Tiger teams — ad hoc small groups that form organically to handle crises — are the clearest expression of illegible work in action

source_posts.title: Grab the 4 prompts I use to make messy work legible--without killing what made it valuable + the visibility trap most companies fall into (and how to avoid it)

frameworks.example_application: This team's dashboards show green across every OKR, but the product launch nearly failed until three people outside the formal project structure stepped in to unblock vendor negotiations and rewrite the integration spec over a weekend. That rescue operation — the tiger team that formed organically around the crisis — is the illegible layer doing the real work. The legible metrics can't see it, which means the next reorg might eliminate the exact people who saved the launch. The performance system is measuring scaffolding and calling it the building.
do_not_use_when: A top performer's work is invisible because they are hoarding information or blocking collaboration, not because their contributions are structurally hard to measure.
The user wants to redesign their OKR system itself and needs a goal-setting methodology, not a diagnosis of what OKRs fail to capture.
The informal processes the user wants to formalize are undocumented compliance or safety procedures, where legibility is legally required and the illegibility is a liability.
A small team's unmeasured impact is low because they are underperforming, and the user needs a performance management approach rather than a framework that might rationalize invisibility as depth.
frameworks.description_original: A classification that separates work that fits neatly into organizational systems (tickets, OKRs, dashboards) from the informal, trust-based, backchannel work that actually keeps companies running.

frameworks.name: The Potemkin Organization Diagnostic
frameworks.description: Use this framework when a user suspects their AI reporting layer is producing confident noise instead of genuine organizational understanding. Challenge their assumption that green dashboards mean things are actually fine — the danger here is not blindness but overconfidence in a precise map that has drifted from the territory. Push them to prove the metric measures what they think it measures, and to surface whether teams have learned to write toward the signals rather than report reality.
when_to_apply: Our AI dashboards all show green but something still feels off — teams are struggling and customers are unhappy despite the metrics
I suspect my team is writing status updates to trigger the right signals in our AI reporting tool rather than describing what's actually happening
We deployed an AI-powered management visibility layer and I want to check whether it's actually improving decisions or just generating confident noise
An IC is pushing back on our metrics saying they don't capture what their work actually produces, and I'm not sure they're wrong
Leadership is making decisions based on AI-generated reports and I need to audit whether those reports reflect reality or a Potemkin version of it
principles: Confidence and accuracy are not the same thing — authoritative-looking outputs can be precisely wrong
Ask what a metric actually measures, then trace whether that maps to an outcome anyone cares about
Check whether teams have learned to game the inputs — writing updates to trigger desired signals rather than report reality
The danger is not blindness but overconfidence in the wrong map: a detailed, precise map that has drifted from the territory
AI drops the cost of generating the appearance of understanding toward zero, making fake visibility cheaper and more dangerous than ever
steps: Identify a dashboard, metric, or AI-generated report that feels authoritative. This matters because AI has dropped the cost of generating the appearance of understanding toward zero — authoritative-looking outputs are now trivially cheap to produce, which means the feeling of 'finally seeing what's happening' is exactly where overconfidence takes root.

Ask what the metric literally measures — not what it claims to measure, but the actual data inputs. This matters because the author argues that cheap legibility produces fake visibility: AI generates the appearance of understanding faster than organizations can distinguish appearance from reality, so you must close the gap between what a metric claims to represent and what data actually feeds it.

Trace whether that literal measurement maps to the outcome leadership actually cares about. This matters because the author identifies a specific failure mode — a detailed, precise map that has drifted from the territory — and skipping this step means you never test whether the metric connects to real outcomes or just produces a clean dashboard that leadership mistakes for understanding.

Check whether teams know how the system scores them and have changed behavior to hit those scores. This matters because the author warns that surveillance creates concealment: when people know how they're being measured, they respond rationally by optimizing for the signal rather than the reality, and the organization starts contorting itself to feed the appearance rather than fix the underlying work.

Determine whether the report is helping leadership understand reality or generating a confident map the organization is bending itself toward. This matters because this is the fork the author says most leaders don't realize they're facing — the difference between legibility that follows work and legibility that dictates it, and getting it wrong means the company looks more organized while the root system that actually produces value quietly dies.

source_posts.title: Grab the 4 prompts I use to make messy work legible--without killing what made it valuable + the visibility trap most companies fall into (and how to avoid it)

frameworks.example_application: The AI-generated sprint health dashboard shows 94% on-time delivery and green across all teams — but the metric literally measures 'stories marked done by sprint end.' Teams learned this six months ago and started splitting work into trivially small stories and marking them complete with known defects. Leadership sees a picture of execution excellence; the actual product ships late every quarter. The dashboard isn't producing understanding — it's producing the appearance of understanding, and the organization is contorting itself to feed the appearance rather than fix the reality.
do_not_use_when: The metrics are genuinely broken due to a data pipeline bug, not organizational gaming — this is an engineering fix, not a trust-layer audit.
A single IC is disputing their personal performance score because they dislike the evaluation criteria — this is a performance management conversation, not a systemic visibility failure.
The organization hasn't yet deployed AI reporting and is asking whether they should — the framework diagnoses an existing system, not whether to build one.
Leadership dashboards are accurate but the underlying business model is failing — the map reflects reality correctly; reality is just bad.
frameworks.description_original: A structured check for whether AI-generated dashboards and reports are producing genuine organizational understanding or a confident-looking map that has drifted from reality.
steps_original: Identify a dashboard, metric, or AI-generated report that feels authoritative
Ask what the metric literally measures — not what it claims to measure, but the actual data inputs
Trace whether that literal measurement maps to the outcome leadership actually cares about
Check whether teams know how the system scores them and have changed behavior to hit those scores
Determine whether the report is helping leadership understand reality or generating a confident map the organization is bending itself toward

frameworks.name: The Weekend-Hack Test
frameworks.description: Use this diagnostic to test whether a user's planning and measurement systems select for legibility over value. Pose the weekend-hack question directly: if an engineer showed up Monday with something built off-roadmap, would their systems flag it as a problem or recognize it as value? Push them to distinguish the magnifying-glass company from the tiger-team company — and challenge the assumption that a tighter process is the same thing as a better one.
when_to_apply: We're implementing AI-powered productivity metrics and I'm worried they'll punish our best people
Our sprint process feels airtight but our best engineers say the most important work happens despite the process, not because of it
I want a quick gut-check on whether our OKR and planning system is crowding out emergent innovation
We're designing a performance review process and need to make sure it doesn't optimize for visibility over actual impact
Someone on my team just built something amazing that wasn't on any roadmap and I'm not sure our systems can even recognize it
principles: Ask: if an engineer showed up Monday with something built over the weekend — no ticket, no sprint, no OKR — would our systems flag it as a problem or recognize it as value?
The magnifying-glass company measures unplanned work out of existence; the tiger-team company protects the conditions that made it possible
The most valuable work is often the work that cannot be planned in advance because it solves problems the process cannot acknowledge
A leader's job when unplanned valuable work surfaces is not to squish it but to recognize its alignment and pull it in without killing the conditions that produced it

source_posts.title: Grab the 4 prompts I use to make messy work legible--without killing what made it valuable + the visibility trap most companies fall into (and how to avoid it)

frameworks.example_application: Last quarter, an engineer built a migration tool over a weekend that eliminated a recurring production incident — no ticket, no OKR, no sprint story. The sprint review flagged it as unplanned work, the velocity chart treated it as noise, and the performance review couldn't account for it because it didn't map to any committed objective. That's the diagnostic verdict: this organization's measurement stack is selecting for legibility over value. The most impactful work of the quarter was structurally invisible to every system that decides what counts.
do_not_use_when: The user is in a regulated industry (finance, healthcare, aviation) where unplanned work bypassing process creates genuine compliance or safety liability, not just legibility problems.
The user's concern is that low performers are hiding poor output behind claims of doing invisible high-value work, making recognition of unplanned work the wrong lever entirely.
The user is asking how to evaluate a specific candidate's past contributions during hiring, not diagnosing whether their organizational systems reward the right behaviors.
The team is early-stage with no formal planning process yet, so the framework's contrast between planned and unplanned work has no existing system to diagnose against.
frameworks.description_original: A single-question test for whether an organization's measurement and planning systems are selecting for legibility or for value, by asking whether unplanned, off-roadmap work could survive and be recognized.

frameworks.name: Three Failure Patterns of Agent Intent Misalignment
frameworks.description: Use this framework when a user reports an agent failure that feels wrong but resists easy explanation. Check their situation against the three failure modes — ambiguity, wrong-optimization, and social boundary — by looking for characteristic signals of each. Classify the root cause, then surface the common thread: the model committed before the misread could be caught.
when_to_apply: My AI agent completed a task correctly by one measure but the result feels obviously wrong in a way I can't articulate
An agent picked a valid interpretation of my request but it wasn't the one I meant, and I need to understand why
I'm doing a post-mortem on an agent action that caused real-world damage and need to classify the root cause
My agentic workflow keeps producing subtle failures and I want to know if they share a common pattern
An AI assistant did something socially inappropriate that any human colleague would have known to avoid
principles: Most agent failures fall into one of three predictable buckets, not random edge cases
Ambiguity failures occur when a model silently picks one of multiple valid interpretations without surfacing the choice
Wrong-optimization failures occur when the model improves a measurable proxy while degrading the real outcome
Social boundary failures occur when implicit human context (relationships, timing, exclusions) is missing from the instruction
The common root cause across all three is the model committing before the misread can be caught

source_posts.title: Why capable AI is a liability when intent is off + my template that makes interpretation visible before action

frameworks.example_application: The agent scheduled a client dinner and invited the founder's ex-cofounder — technically a 'key stakeholder' per the CRM data, but anyone with organizational context would know that relationship is toxic. This is a social boundary failure, not an ambiguity or optimization problem. The instruction 'invite key stakeholders' was unambiguous and the optimization target was correct — the failure is that implicit human context (who should be excluded, why, and the relational history) was never part of the agent's information set. The fix isn't better prompting; it's adding an exclusion layer or requiring human confirmation on attendee lists where relationship dynamics matter.
do_not_use_when: The agent failure was caused by a data pipeline feeding it stale or corrupted inputs, making this an infrastructure problem rather than an intent-interpretation problem.
The user wants to choose between two AI architectures before building anything, so no actual agent failure has occurred to classify.
The agent behaved incorrectly because it lacked access to a required tool or permission, not because it misread what the user wanted.
The user is frustrated that the agent's output was factually wrong on a knowledge question, which is a capability gap rather than an intent misalignment.
frameworks.description_original: Classifies the three primary ways AI agents misread user intent into distinct failure modes, each with characteristic signals and corresponding fixes.

frameworks.name: Builder-Engineer Composability Diagnostic
frameworks.description: Apply this diagnostic when a user is questioning whether their builders and engineers are set up to collaborate effectively in an AI-assisted development environment. Challenge the user's assumption that filing tickets or slow prototyping is a workflow problem — push them to prove their builders can show work, not describe it, and that their engineers can bound what AI can and cannot touch. What generic advice misses is the composability ratio signal: all implementation and zero composability engineers means the team is staffed for a prior era.
when_to_apply: Our designers and PMs keep filing tickets for things they could probably prototype themselves if they had the right skills — are they actually blocked or just not trying?
We're about to let AI generate parts of our front end and I need to know if our architecture can handle that safely
Our engineering team is 100% implementation and 0% platform/composability — is that a problem?
I want to understand whether our product team and engineering team are actually ready to collaborate differently in a world of AI-assisted UI generation
We're restructuring our front-end team and need to figure out who should be building what
principles: Builders should be able to show a working prototype, not just describe a feature — inability to do so signals a collaboration gap
Engineers should be able to articulate in one page what can vary, what cannot, and where AI can and cannot touch the UI
A composability ratio of all implementation engineers and zero composability engineers signals staffing for a prior era
The correct answer to 'what can your system generate safely' is specific and bounded — not 'nothing' or 'everything'
steps: For builders: Ask when you last built something (not specced or described it — actually built it). This matters because the bottleneck between 'I can see it' and 'it exists' is gone — tools like Lovable let non-engineers build working prototypes in two hours, so a builder who hasn't built anything recently is failing to walk through a door that is already open.

For builders: Ask whether you could show your next feature idea rather than describe it. This matters because for twenty years builders had to describe what they wanted to someone who could code — expensive, slow, and 'the thing that came back never quite matched what you imagined' — so the ability to show rather than describe is the specific collaboration shift that distinguishes the new era from the old one.

For builders: Ask whether you understand why your last three engineering requests were scoped the way they were. This matters because builders and engineers need shared vocabulary to make organizations faster, and a builder who can't explain scoping decisions reveals a collaboration gap where the builder is still just describing wishes rather than engaging with the composability constraints engineers are defining. (inferred)

For engineers: Count the ratio of implementation engineers to composability engineers. This matters because implementation work — taking Figma files, wiring up components, pushing pixels — is collapsing into something cheap and fast that AI handles, while someone still needs to define what can vary and what can't; a team with all implementation engineers and zero composability engineers is staffed for a prior era.

For engineers: Ask what your system can generate safely and whether the answer is specific. This matters because when anyone can build — PMs prototyping in Lovable, AI generating dashboards — someone must ensure the result 'feels like your product and not fourteen different apps wearing the same logo'; a vague answer like 'we'd have to think about that' reveals that no one owns generation guardrails, one of the four composability capabilities the author identifies.

For engineers: Ask whether you can articulate your UI generation constraints — what can vary, what can't, where AI can touch — in one page. This matters because front-end composability means defining the boundaries that make safe composition possible for builders and AI agents alike; if an engineer cannot articulate these constraints concisely, the systems that make Lovable-style building reliable inside the product simply don't exist yet.

source_posts.title: The Composability Era: What Happens When Anyone Can Build a UI (+ 4 Prompts to navigate the front-end revolution)

frameworks.example_application: The product team has five builders and twelve engineers, but zero engineers focused on composability infrastructure — the entire engineering team is writing implementation code. When asked 'what can your system generate safely?', the tech lead says 'we'd have to think about that.' Meanwhile, the lead PM last built something herself eight months ago and can't explain why her last three engineering requests were scoped the way they were. This team is staffed and skilled for a pre-composability era: builders who can only describe, engineers who can only implement, and no one owning the surface area where AI or non-engineers could safely generate UI.
do_not_use_when: The team is a solo founder with no engineers yet, so there is no org structure to diagnose — the bottleneck is hiring, not composability readiness.
The front-end is a legacy monolith with a scheduled full rewrite, making composability gap analysis irrelevant until the new architecture is chosen.
The question is whether to outsource the entire product team, not how existing builders and engineers should collaborate — a make-vs-buy lens is needed instead.
The designers filing tickets are blocked by legal and compliance review cycles, not skill gaps or architecture limits, so composability diagnostics will not surface the real constraint.
frameworks.description_original: A set of structured questions for builders and engineers to assess their readiness for the composability era — revealing gaps in prototyping capability for builders and systemic composability gaps for engineers.
steps_original: For builders: Ask when you last built something (not specced or described it — actually built it)
For builders: Ask whether you could show your next feature idea rather than describe it
For builders: Ask whether you understand why your last three engineering requests were scoped the way they were
For engineers: Count the ratio of implementation engineers to composability engineers
For engineers: Ask what your system can generate safely and whether the answer is specific
For engineers: Ask whether you can articulate your UI generation constraints — what can vary, what can't, where AI can touch — in one page

frameworks.name: The Front-End Fork
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a front-end engineer or their manager needs to choose a career or team direction under AI compression. Classify the user's situation into the composability lane or the handcrafted specialist lane. Surface the blind spot that drifting between paths defaults to obsolescence, and use their existing craft knowledge as evidence that composability work isn't a departure — it's context they already have.
when_to_apply: I'm a front-end developer and AI tools are handling more and more of what I used to do — where should I invest my time?
We're restructuring our front-end team and need to figure out which roles are about building design systems versus which are about pixel-level craft
I love the craft of building beautiful UI, but I'm worried it's becoming a niche — should I pivot or lean in?
As a manager, how do I create career ladders for front-end engineers when AI is compressing implementation work?
I'm a senior front-end engineer and I can't tell if my skills are becoming more valuable or less — the signals are contradictory
principles: Path 1 (Composability): Accept less direct making in exchange for more leverage over how making happens at scale
Path 2 (Handcrafted): Remain in implementation craft, which is becoming a specialist niche rather than the default path — choose it deliberately
Existing craft knowledge is essential context for composability work, not obsolete — knowing which decisions need locking requires having seen what happens when they aren't
Choosing neither path deliberately means drifting into obsolescence by default

source_posts.title: The Composability Era: What Happens When Anyone Can Build a UI (+ 4 Prompts to navigate the front-end revolution)

frameworks.example_application: This engineer has spent eight years perfecting CSS animations and accessible component APIs — that's Path 2, handcrafted specialist work. The critical question is whether they're choosing it deliberately. Right now their team is adopting AI-generated components for 70% of new surfaces, which means their craft is migrating from 'default expectation' to 'specialist niche.' If they stay, they need to own the quality ceiling — the work AI can't reach — and price accordingly. If they'd rather have leverage over the whole system, they shift to Path 1: building the design tokens, component constraints, and composability guardrails that make AI-generated UI consistently good. Their existing craft knowledge isn't wasted in that move — it's the exact context needed to know which decisions must be locked down versus left flexible. What they cannot do is stand still and assume the default path still exists.
do_not_use_when: The user is a back-end or full-stack engineer asking about AI's impact on their career — the fork's two paths assume front-end craft context that doesn't transfer.
The user is asking whether to leave engineering entirely for product management or design — the framework assumes staying in engineering is already decided.

The user is a hiring manager at a startup with no existing front-end team, needing to decide what roles to hire first — the framework addresses existing engineers choosing paths, not greenfield team composition.
The user is a front-end engineer at an agency whose concern is client acquisition and pricing strategy under AI commoditization — a business model problem, not a career trajectory one.
frameworks.description_original: A two-path classification for front-end engineers choosing their career trajectory as AI compresses implementation work — composability work versus the handcrafted specialist lane.

frameworks.name: Delegation Spec Drill
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user suspects their delegation failures stem from vague instructions rather than model limitations. Score their spec against five binary criteria: stranger-executability, binary success criteria, explicit constraints, approvals at reversibility boundaries, and specified failure handling. Push them to prove each point is explicit rather than implied — the common blind spot is writing specs that only make sense to someone who already knows the context.
when_to_apply: I keep getting back work from my AI agent that misses the point, and I suspect the problem is my instructions, not the model
I want to start delegating recurring tasks but I'm not sure which ones I can actually hand off versus which ones live in my head
I wrote a prompt or brief for someone and it generated more clarifying questions than actual output
I'm trying to build a weekly habit of getting better at specification writing for AI-assisted work
A task I delegated created more cleanup work than if I'd just done it myself
principles: A spec is only good if a stranger can execute it without questions
Success criteria must be binary, not subjective
Constraints must be explicit rather than implied
Approvals must be placed at reversibility boundaries — moments where actions become hard to undo
Failure handling must be specified for each step
Score 3 or below means the spec would create more work than it saves; 4 or 5 means it's delegation-ready
steps: Pick one task from the past week that took more than 30 minutes. This matters because the author's core argument is that delegation has never been worth the overhead for the forty-minute tasks that fill most of your week — selecting a task of real duration ensures the delegation math can actually flip in your favor, rather than creating more coordination cost than execution cost.

Write the specification you would have needed to delegate it to someone who knows nothing about your context. This matters because the author identifies that most knowledge workers operate on improvisation and make 'a thousand implicit decisions without noticing' — writing for a stranger forces those invisible decisions into the open, exposing the gap between what you know and what you've actually communicated.

Define Inputs: What information or access is required to start? This matters because the author notes that real agent infrastructure now includes 'permission systems and audit trails' and persistent connections to calendars, email, and files — specifying inputs explicitly maps what access and information the agent needs before execution begins, preventing the back-and-forth that makes delegation overhead exceed execution time.

Define Steps: What sequence of actions produces the output? This matters because the author describes how most people 'figure it out as you go' and hold everything in their heads — as the example application shows, vague steps like 'look at their websites' are what make a spec score 2/5 and generate more coordination than they save.

Define Constraints: What must be true about the output, and what must not happen? This matters because constraints are the most common blind spot — as the example demonstrates, entirely implied constraints (which competitors, what dimensions, what format) are invisible to the person who wrote them but fatal to anyone else executing, and the author warns that coping mechanisms built on implicit decisions 'don't transfer and certainly don't delegate.'

Define Approvals: Where would you need to sign off? Place these at reversibility boundaries. This matters because the author traces the evolution of agent failure modes from 'it said the wrong thing' to 'it did the wrong thing' — placing approvals specifically at moments where actions become hard to undo prevents the most costly class of delegation failure, where an agent takes an irreversible action you never sanctioned.

Define Failure Handling: What happens if something goes wrong at each step? This matters because without explicit failure handling, the agent either stops silently or improvises — and the author's central point is that improvisation is a coping mechanism that doesn't transfer; specifying failure paths is what prevents a delegated task from bouncing back to you as more work than it would have been to do yourself.

Score the spec on five points: (1) Can a stranger execute it without questions? (2) Are success criteria binary? (3) Are constraints explicit rather than implied? (4) Are approvals at reversibility boundaries? (5) Is failure handling specified? This matters because the author frames specification as a skill that must be deliberately built — the binary scoring forces an honest assessment of whether your spec is delegation-ready (4-5) or would create more overhead than it saves (3 or below), directly addressing the author's core claim that delegation fails not because of model limitations but because 'the bottleneck moves to our ability to say what we want in a way that something else can execute.'

source_posts.title: Grab the Delegation Kit I Use to Turn AI into my Chief of Staff + the 8 Prompts That Turn Ramblings into Executable Tasks

frameworks.example_application: The task was 'research competitors and summarize findings' — took 90 minutes last Tuesday. The draft spec scored 2/5: steps were vague ('look at their websites'), success criteria were subjective ('a good summary'), constraints were entirely implied (didn't specify which competitors, what dimensions to compare, or output format), and failure handling was nonexistent. The spec would have generated more back-and-forth than it saved. Rewriting with binary success criteria ('table comparing 5 named competitors on pricing, integrations, and target segment, with source URLs for each cell') and explicit constraints ('no competitors under $1M ARR, no blog posts as sources') brought it to 4/5 — delegation-ready for an agent or junior analyst.
do_not_use_when: The user wants to delegate a one-time creative task where the value comes from collaborative iteration, not upfront specification.
The user's AI output quality problems stem from a known model capability gap, not ambiguous instructions.
The user is asking which AI tool to adopt for delegation, not how to write better specs for an existing tool.
The user needs to decide whether to hire a human employee versus automate, making workforce strategy the relevant lens.
frameworks.description_original: A weekly practice for building the skill of translating implicit work intentions into explicit, executable specifications that can be delegated to an agent or human.
steps_original: Pick one task from the past week that took more than 30 minutes
Write the specification you would have needed to delegate it to someone who knows nothing about your context
Define Inputs: What information or access is required to start?
Define Steps: What sequence of actions produces the output?
Define Constraints: What must be true about the output, and what must not happen?
Define Approvals: Where would you need to sign off? Place these at reversibility boundaries.
Define Failure Handling: What happens if something goes wrong at each step?

Score the spec on five points: (1) Can a stranger execute it without questions? (2) Are success criteria binary? (3) Are constraints explicit rather than implied? (4) Are approvals at reversibility boundaries? (5) Is failure handling specified?

frameworks.name: The 30-Minute Delegation Rule
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is unsure whether a task is worth delegating at all. Challenge their assumption that delegation is inherently productive — push them to prove the task clears at least one condition: recurrence, duration beyond overhead, or batchability. What generic advice misses is that delegation overhead is a real cost, and this framework surfaces whether the math actually works before any spec gets written.
when_to_apply: I keep delegating small tasks to my AI assistant and spending more time reviewing the output than it would take to just do it
I'm building a list of tasks to automate or delegate and need to filter out the ones that aren't worth the setup cost
A task feels like it should be delegated but it's a one-time thing and I'm not sure the overhead is justified
I want a quick litmus test before writing a detailed delegation spec or prompt for an AI agent
My weekly review keeps surfacing tasks that could theoretically be delegated but I'm not sure which ones actually should be
principles: If you're doing a task once, don't delegate it — just do it
Delegation only pays off when the task recurs (instructions will be reused), takes longer than the delegation overhead, or can be batched with similar items
The goal is not to delegate everything, but to delegate the right things — systematic, repeatable, verifiable work that doesn't require your judgment
steps: Ask: Does this task recur? If no, do it yourself. This matters because recurrence is what makes the specification cost amortizable — as the author argues, delegation overhead (specifying, reviewing, correcting) is a real time cost, and if the instructions will never be reused, you've paid that cost for a single execution, which is almost never worth it.

Ask: Does this task take longer than the delegation overhead (specification + review + correction)? If no, do it yourself. This matters because the author identifies this as the core arithmetic most people ignore: 'By the time you've specified what you want, checked on progress, reviewed the output, and fixed what's wrong, you've spent more time coordinating than you would have spent just doing the thing.' This step forces you to compare actual execution time against the full coordination cost, not just the handoff.

Ask: Can this task be batched with similar items? If none of the three conditions are met, do it yourself. This matters because batching is the escape hatch for tasks that fail the first two conditions individually — a task that doesn't recur and is short on its own might still clear the overhead threshold when grouped with similar items, as shown in the example where the weekly metrics summary gets batched with three other weekly reporting tasks to justify a single delegation spec (inferred).

If one or more conditions are met, proceed to write a delegation spec. This matters because the author frames specification as a skill most knowledge workers have never developed — 'the bottleneck moves to our ability to say what we want in a way that something else can execute' — so this gate ensures you only invest in building that costly specification skill for tasks where the delegation math actually works, rather than burning effort on specs for tasks you should just do yourself.

source_posts.title: Grab the Delegation Kit I Use to Turn AI into my Chief of Staff + the 8 Prompts That Turn Ramblings into Executable Tasks

frameworks.example_application: Formatting a one-off investor report fails all three conditions: it won't recur (this is a custom request), it takes 20 minutes (less than writing the spec, reviewing, and correcting), and there's nothing to batch it with. Do it yourself. But the weekly metrics summary passes two conditions — it recurs every Monday and can be batched with the other three weekly reporting tasks. That's worth a delegation spec.
do_not_use_when: The user is deciding whether to hire a human assistant or contractor, where relationship fit and trust matter more than task recurrence math.
The user already knows the task recurs and clearly justifies delegation — they need help writing the delegation spec, not a filter on whether to delegate.
The user is a founder deciding which entire functional areas to delegate to new hires, where org design and role scope apply, not per-task overhead logic.
The user is asking whether to automate a task that carries legal, financial, or safety risk, where compliance and accountability outweigh efficiency calculations.
frameworks.description_original: A three-condition filter for determining whether a task is worth delegating at all, based on recurrence, duration, and batchability.
steps_original: Ask: Does this task recur? If no, do it yourself.
Ask: Does this task take longer than the delegation overhead (specification + review + correction)? If no, do it yourself.
Ask: Can this task be batched with similar items? If none of the three conditions are met, do it yourself.
If one or more conditions are met, proceed to write a delegation spec.

frameworks.name: Delegation Scope Expansion Model
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is structuring AI delegation or diagnosing why a delegation approach broke down. Classify their situation into the appropriate horizon — five, ten, twenty, or forty hours — then surface the principle they're likely missing: that each horizon represents a qualitatively different kind of work, not a scaled-up version of the last. Push back on any assumption that skills transfer automatically across horizons.
when_to_apply: I'm trying to figure out which parts of a large project I can delegate to AI versus which I need to do myself
My team is jumping straight to complex agent workflows without mastering simpler AI delegation first
I need to plan what AI delegation skills to invest in now versus what I can learn later as capabilities improve
I delegated a multi-phase project to an AI agent and it fell apart — I'm trying to understand why the same approach that works for simple tasks failed here
I'm designing oversight and review processes for AI-generated work and need to calibrate how much supervision different types of work require
principles: A five-hour delegatable task is not a scaled-down forty-hour task — each horizon represents a qualitatively different kind of work
Each horizon expansion opens entirely new categories of work, not just more of the same
Skills to delegate effectively at each level build on prior levels — practitioners who skip levels start from scratch
The distinction between delegating work and delegating judgment starts to blur at the forty-hour horizon
steps: Five-hour horizon: delegate discrete tasks with clear boundaries, single-session work, verifiable against explicit success criteria. This matters because five hours is where the current 50% success horizon sits according to METR benchmarks — this is the frontier of what's reliably delegatable right now, and building the skill of specifying and verifying work at this level is the foundation without which all larger delegations fail catastrophically.

Ten-hour horizon: delegate projects requiring planning, multiple phases, and synthesis — agent must make sequencing decisions and maintain coherence. This matters because the doubling trajectory projects the 50% horizon reaching ten hours by spring, and this isn't just twice as much five-hour work — it opens entirely new categories of delegatable work requiring multi-phase planning, which the author identifies as a qualitative shift the scope expansion creates as horizons grow.

Twenty-hour horizon: delegate initiatives spanning multiple work sessions — requires agent judgment about prioritization, not just execution. This matters because the trajectory projects this horizon arriving by summer, and as the example application shows, a twenty-hour competitive landscape scan demands the agent decide which dimensions matter and how to weight conflicting signals — prioritization judgment that is qualitatively different from execution, and practitioners who haven't built oversight muscles at lower horizons will miss the distinction entirely.

Forty-hour horizon: delegate judgment-laden work (business plans, audits, book-length drafts) where dependencies and decision points blur the line between work and judgment. This matters because this horizon approaches a full work week — projected by fall if the super-exponential pace holds — and the author warns this is where the distinction between delegating work and delegating judgment starts to blur, meaning the question shifts from 'can the AI do the task' to 'what happens to work, and to the people who do it, when the kinds of things that become delegatable keep expanding at this pace.'

source_posts.title: My honest field notes on the super-exponential + why "I'll catch up later" is now the riskiest bet

frameworks.example_application: A team lead wants to delegate a competitive analysis. At the five-hour horizon, the AI can research a single competitor and produce a structured summary — discrete, verifiable, bounded. At the twenty-hour horizon, the AI could run the full competitive landscape scan across twelve players, deciding which dimensions matter most and how to weight conflicting signals — that's an initiative requiring prioritization judgment, not just execution. The team lead who hasn't built the skill of specifying and verifying five-hour tasks will fail catastrophically at the twenty-hour delegation because the specification and oversight muscles are qualitatively different, not just scaled up.
do_not_use_when: The user wants to delegate to a human employee, not an AI system, and is asking about task breakdown and oversight for their team.
The user is evaluating which AI vendor or tool to purchase, not how to structure delegation across capability horizons.
The user's AI deployment is fully automated with no human-in-the-loop design intended, making supervision calibration irrelevant.
The user is troubleshooting a specific technical failure in an AI pipeline, not diagnosing a structural mismatch in delegation approach.
frameworks.description_original: A classification system that maps how the nature of delegatable work fundamentally changes at each order-of-magnitude expansion of AI time-horizon capability (tasks → projects → initiatives → judgment).
steps_original: Five-hour horizon: delegate discrete tasks with clear boundaries, single-session work, verifiable against explicit success criteria
Ten-hour horizon: delegate projects requiring planning, multiple phases, and synthesis — agent must make sequencing decisions and maintain coherence
Twenty-hour horizon: delegate initiatives spanning multiple work sessions — requires agent judgment about prioritization, not just execution
Forty-hour horizon: delegate judgment-laden work (business plans, audits, book-length drafts) where dependencies and decision points blur the line between work and judgment

frameworks.name: The Reversibility Gap
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is troubleshooting agent failures in production or planning deployment infrastructure. Shift their framing from "the agent isn't smart enough" to "the environment wasn't designed to make mistakes survivable" by diagnosing which workflows lack reversibility infrastructure. Challenge the assumption that waiting for better models solves the problem — the limiting factor is reversibility, not intelligence.
when_to_apply: My agent works great in demos but keeps causing problems in production that require manual cleanup
We're debating whether to wait for a better model before deploying agents, or ship now with the current one
I need to figure out why agents work well in software engineering but keep failing in our operations/finance/HR workflows
We're planning what infrastructure to build before giving our agents more autonomy
Leadership is asking why our agent made an irreversible mistake and I need to explain what went wrong structurally
principles: The limiting factor for agent deployment is reversibility of mistakes, not agent intelligence
Environments designed for safe failure (like software engineering) enable agent autonomy; environments that weren't designed that way resist it
The path to agent autonomy runs through reversibility infrastructure, not model capability improvements
Humans have been providing an informal safety throttle that disappears when agents replace them — this must be explicitly replaced
Boring, predictable, bounded, recoverable agent operations are the goal, not sophisticated ones

source_posts.title: Executive Briefing: Five Primitives That Make Agent Operations Safe

frameworks.example_application: The conventional read is that the customer service agent fails because it hallucinates refund policies — it needs a better model. That's wrong here. The real problem is that when the agent issues a refund incorrectly, there's no automated clawback, no staged approval, no transaction hold. A human agent making the same mistake would have caught it mid-process or a supervisor would have reversed it within the hour — that informal safety net was never formalized. The fix isn't GPT-5; it's a 15-minute refund hold with automatic review triggers. The environment needs reversibility infrastructure, not more intelligence.
do_not_use_when: The agent is failing in demos too, not just production — the core problem is model capability or prompt quality, not environment design.
The user is asking about a narrow, single-step automation with no downstream dependencies where mistakes are already trivially reversible by default.
Leadership is asking about an agent mistake that caused reputational or legal harm where reversibility infrastructure would not have changed the outcome.
The user is evaluating whether to build agents at all for a use case, not how to deploy ones they've already decided to build.
frameworks.description_original: Reframes AI agent deployment failures as a reversibility problem rather than an intelligence problem — agents fail in production not because they aren't smart enough, but because most business environments weren't designed to make mistakes survivable.

frameworks.name: The Jagged Frontier Framework
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user can't explain why AI works brilliantly on some tasks and fails on adjacent ones. Classify their tasks into the three zones — AI reliably better, AI reliably worse, high variance — and sort their claims using the jagged frontier lens. Push them to see that inconsistent results aren't random: they're evidence of deployment outside the frontier, and redesigning around that boundary is what separates 30% gains from 300%.
when_to_apply: AI works great for some tasks in my workflow but produces garbage for seemingly similar ones, and I can't figure out the pattern
We're getting inconsistent results from an AI deployment and need to figure out which pieces to keep vs. pull back to humans
Some people on my team get massive productivity gains from AI while others doing similar work see almost nothing — what explains the gap?
I need to decide which parts of a process to automate with AI vs. keep human-led, and 'try it and see' isn't a strategy
Our AI pilot showed impressive demos but real-world performance is disappointing and we need to diagnose why
principles: AI capability surfaces are jagged, not smooth — peaks and valleys coexist on adjacent tasks
Misuse outside the frontier doesn't just fail to help — it actively degrades outcomes
The 30% gains crowd treats AI as a power tool (more output, same shape of work); the 300% gains crowd treats AI as a routing layer (redesigned workflows matching AI's structural advantages)
Fluency means navigating jaggedness intentionally, not just generating more AI output
Each deployment surface has its own failure modes — a failure in one context doesn't predict failure in another
Map tasks into three zones: AI reliably better, AI reliably worse, and high variance
steps: Inventory your tasks and map each into one of three zones: AI reliably better, AI reliably worse, high variance. This matters because AI capability surfaces are jagged, not smooth—peaks and valleys coexist on adjacent tasks—so treating a category of work as one block (like the legal team treating 'contract review' as monolithic) hides the boundary between where AI wins and where it actively degrades outcomes.

Identify which tasks sit inside vs. outside the AI frontier for your specific context. This matters because you don't need to smooth the whole AI capability surface to unlock massive value—you need to find the right gaps; inconsistent results aren't random, they're evidence of deployment outside the frontier, and locating that boundary precisely is what turns confusion into a usable map.

Redesign workflows so AI handles tasks in the 'reliably better' zone and humans cover edge cases and failure modes. This matters because the 30% gains crowd treats AI as a power tool (more output, same shape of work) while the 300% gains crowd treats AI as a routing layer with redesigned workflows matching AI's structural advantages—skipping this step means you're just generating more AI output without exploiting the peaks or routing around the valleys.

Build evaluation harnesses and 'known failure mode' checklists per workflow to catch regressions. This matters because each deployment surface has its own failure modes—a failure in one context doesn't predict failure in another—so you need context-specific QA (like catching typography drift, semantic labeling errors, and translation instability in visual generation) with gates that prevent broken outputs from shipping.

Continuously update the map as capability thresholds shift. This matters because a single gap closure can spawn three generations of new value in thirty days—the frontier is moving so fast that yesterday's 'AI reliably worse' zone can become tomorrow's 'reliably better' zone, and missing that shift means missing the next cascade of unlocks.

source_posts.title: NEW: One Google Update Spawned 3 Startup Generations in 30 Days—Here's the Pattern + 4 Prompts to Position Before the Next Cascade

frameworks.example_application: A legal team getting 'mixed results' from AI contract review has been treating all contract tasks as one block. Mapping the jagged frontier reveals: extracting standard clause language and flagging missing sections sit inside the frontier (AI reliably better — faster, more consistent). But evaluating whether a non-standard indemnification clause is commercially acceptable in this deal's context sits firmly outside it (AI reliably worse — it generates confident but wrong risk assessments). The team redesigned: AI handles extraction and completeness checks, humans handle commercial judgment calls, and the high-variance zone — summarizing negotiation history — gets AI drafts with mandatory human review. That routing shift moved them from marginal gains to transformative ones, not by using AI more, but by using it only where the frontier map says it wins.
do_not_use_when: The team has already mapped AI task performance and needs vendor selection criteria, not capability diagnosis.
Inconsistent AI results stem from bad training data or model drift, requiring MLOps fixes rather than workflow redesign.
A solo founder asking which of two specific AI tools to buy for a single, well-defined task needs a product comparison, not a capability-mapping taxonomy.
The organization lacks basic AI access or budget and the real decision is whether to adopt AI at all, not how to route tasks within an existing deployment.
frameworks.description_original: A classification system for mapping AI capability peaks and valleys across tasks, then routing work to match AI's structural advantages while humans cover failure modes.

Identify which tasks sit inside vs. outside the AI frontier for your specific context
