Build evaluation harnesses and 'known failure mode' checklists per workflow to catch regressions
Continuously update the map as capability thresholds shift

frameworks.name: Cascade Scanner / Gap-Close Pattern
frameworks.description: Use this framework when a user is trying to predict whether an AI capability gap is about to close and what business cascade will follow. Challenge their assumption that broad capability progress matters — push them to identify the single specific blocker, not the general frontier. Reveal what generic analysis misses: whether distribution infrastructure is already in place to propagate a breakthrough the moment the gap closes.
when_to_apply: A new foundation model just dropped and I'm trying to figure out if it's incremental or if it crosses a threshold that unlocks entire product categories
I can see that 90% of the building blocks for a capability exist but deployment is still stuck — what's the actual blocker and when does it break?
I want to place bets on where to build before the next wave of AI startups becomes obvious to everyone
I'm scanning adjacent AI capability areas to decide which gap-close would create the most downstream opportunity for my company
Multiple AI capabilities seem close to usable but none have broken through to mass adoption yet — which one tips first?
principles: You don't need to improve the entire AI capability surface — you only need to fill in the right gap
Look for areas where almost all building blocks exist but one specific component is missing
A gap closes faster when distribution infrastructure is already in place (pipes already laid)
The question for each area is: what exists now, what's missing, and what would a real breakthrough look like?
When a capability crosses the usability threshold plus hits broad distribution simultaneously, the cascade happens in weeks not years
Three lineages tend to light up at once when a shared missing piece is filled: consumer creation, knowledge-work collateral, and professional tooling
steps: Identify a capability area where progress is happening but deployment is still blocked. This matters because the author emphasizes that 'you don't need to smooth the whole AI capability surface to unlock massive value — you need to fill in the right gap'; this step forces you to distinguish areas of genuine near-threshold progress from areas of broad but diffuse improvement, which is where the 30% gains crowd gets stuck instead of finding the 300% gains.

Enumerate what building blocks already exist (models, infrastructure, distribution surfaces). This matters because the author shows that before Nano Banana Pro, every previous model could generate gorgeous visuals and the infrastructure was already in place — the breakthrough only mattered because nearly everything else was ready; skipping this step blinds you to whether a gap closure will actually compound or just sit inert.

Identify the single specific gap that is acting as the hard blocker. This matters because the author's core insight is that text rendering inside images was the one gap blocking entire categories of business collateral — not image quality, not distribution, not cost — and fixing that single gap unlocked three generations of startups in thirty days; generic frontier-watching misses this precision.

Assess whether distribution infrastructure is already in place to propagate a breakthrough. This matters because the author notes that when a capability crosses the usability threshold and hits broad distribution simultaneously, the cascade happens in weeks not years; if pipes aren't already laid (e.g., billions of camera-equipped devices, mobile OS integrations), even a real breakthrough stalls instead of compounding.

Predict the downstream cascade: which product categories unlock the moment the gap closes. This matters because the author tracks three generations of businesses stacked in thirty days — startups using tools built on tools built on the release — revealing that a single unlock doesn't create one opportunity but ignites three lineages at once (consumer creation, knowledge-work collateral, professional tooling), and mapping these in advance is the only way to see the full value surface.

Position or build before the threshold is crossed, not after the cascade is visible. This matters because the author explicitly frames this as what separates builders from spectators: once three layers of startups are already stacked, positioning is too late; the entire article is structured around the question 'how many opportunities are you going to miss watching from the sidelines,' making pre-threshold action the decisive competitive move.

source_posts.title: NEW: One Google Update Spawned 3 Startup Generations in 30 Days—Here's the Pattern + 4 Prompts to Position Before the Next Cascade

frameworks.example_application: Real-time video understanding already has strong models (GPT-4V, Gemini), cloud infrastructure, and billions of camera-equipped devices as distribution surfaces. The single missing piece is sub-second multimodal inference at consumer-grade cost. The moment that threshold is crossed — likely within one model generation — three lineages ignite simultaneously: consumer apps (real-time AR translation, cooking coaches), knowledge-work collateral (auto-generated meeting summaries with visual context), and professional tooling (quality inspection, surgical assist). The distribution pipes are already laid through existing mobile OS integrations, so adoption will cascade in weeks. Building the harness layer now — before the unlock is visible — is the only way to capture position.

The user's bottleneck is internal change management or budget approval, not an external AI capability gap waiting to close.

frameworks.name: Model + Y + X Framework (The Harnessing Layer)
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user believes their domain expertise or proprietary data should be producing better AI outputs than they're seeing. Shift their framing from Model + X to Model + Y + X by naming Y — the harnessing layer of validation logic, routing, constraint enforcement, and failure instrumentation — as the missing multiplier. Challenge the assumption that better experts or more data is the bottleneck; push them to examine whether Y is actually built.
when_to_apply: We have better domain experts than our competitors but our AI product still underperforms theirs
Our AI demos are impressive but we can't get the system to work reliably at scale in production
We're debating whether to invest in model fine-tuning vs. building validation and error-handling infrastructure
Leadership keeps saying 'we have proprietary data' as our moat but our actual outputs aren't better than competitors using the same base model
Our team has deep expertise but can't figure out why the AI system doesn't reflect that knowledge in its outputs
principles: Domain expertise (X) alone is insufficient—it stays theoretical without a harnessing layer
Y (the harnessing layer) is the multiplier that unlocks X
The harnessing layer includes validation logic, routing, constraint enforcement, repair steps, and failure instrumentation
Teams that ship are the ones who built Y, not the ones with the best models or most resources
The messy middle integration layer is underbuilt and represents the primary opportunity

source_posts.title: 9 bets I'm making on AI in 2026 + the audit I use to spot real systems

frameworks.example_application: The conventional read is that Company A wins because they have deeper clinical expertise and fine-tuned models. That's wrong here — Company B ships reliable results with a generic model because they built the harnessing layer: validation logic that catches hallucinated drug interactions, routing that escalates ambiguous cases, constraint enforcement that blocks outputs violating formulary rules, and repair steps that auto-correct common failure patterns. Company A's domain expertise is theoretical — it lives in their team's heads, not in executable system logic. The multiplier is zero without Y, so Model × 0 × X = 0 no matter how good X is.
do_not_use_when: The team lacks domain expertise entirely and is hoping system design can compensate — Y cannot multiply X when X is near zero.
The AI underperformance stems from a known base model capability gap that no validation layer can route around or repair.
The user is evaluating whether to build AI products at all, not how to improve an existing one — this is a go/no-go decision, not an integration design problem.
The reliability issues are caused by upstream data pipeline failures or infrastructure outages, not by missing validation or constraint logic in the AI layer.
frameworks.description_original: Reframes the conventional wisdom that AI competitive advantage = Model + Domain Expertise, by inserting a critical middle variable 'Y' (the harnessing layer of system design, validation, and constraint enforcement) that determines whether domain expertise actually gets leveraged.

frameworks.name: The Devil's Game (Friction Trade-off)
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user treats consumer-enterprise AI tension as a solvable UX or governance problem. Shift their framing from "how do we fix the friction" to "which game are we actually playing" — because the product decisions that win consumer distribution (speed, simplicity, no visible cost) actively teach the wrong mental model for delegation legibility. Make the structural irreconcilability explicit: these are not tunable trade-offs.
when_to_apply: Our employees love ChatGPT personally but our enterprise AI deployment keeps failing on governance and accountability
We're debating whether to wait for our AI vendor to add enterprise features or build internal governance tooling ourselves
Why does adding verification and oversight to our AI workflows always tank user adoption?
Our AI vendor keeps promising enterprise capabilities but the product keeps optimizing for consumer speed and simplicity
We're trying to understand whether consumer AI adoption is helping or hurting our enterprise AI strategy
principles: Making delegation legible requires friction (work orders, verification, visible cost, slower execution)
Consumer distribution punishes friction — speed and simplicity drive retention at scale
These two optimization targets are not just in tension; product decisions that win one game actively teach the wrong mental model for the other
The same product walks into the enterprise through consumer adoption, embedding the wrong mental model before enterprise tooling can correct it

source_posts.title: Executive Briefing: The Bubble Test for OpenAI (Unit Economics, Capacity, Proof—Three Signals to Watch in 2026)

frameworks.example_application: The conventional read is that ChatGPT's consumer simplicity is a stepping stone to enterprise readiness — just add admin controls and audit logs. That's wrong here because the core product teaches users that AI interaction is instant, frictionless, and requires no specification of intent. Every employee who adopts the consumer product internalizes that mental model before IT can deploy enterprise governance. The friction required for delegatable AI — work orders, verification steps, visible cost signals, slower execution with audit trails — isn't a feature gap to close; it's a design direction that directly contradicts what made the consumer product successful. The company isn't failing to serve enterprise; it's structurally incapable of optimizing for both without forking the product.
do_not_use_when: The user's AI adoption problem stems from poor change management or training gaps, not a structural consumer-vs-enterprise product design conflict.
The user is evaluating a purpose-built enterprise AI tool with no consumer distribution history, so the consumer-model-contamination assumption doesn't apply.
The user is asking about a specific UX friction point that has a known technical fix, not a structurally irreconcilable governance trade-off.
The user's organization has already achieved governance compliance and is now asking how to improve adoption speed within those existing constraints.
frameworks.description_original: Reframes AI product design tensions not as solvable UX problems but as structurally irreconcilable trade-offs, where the design choices that win consumer adoption actively undermine enterprise delegation capability.

frameworks.name: Work Primitives
frameworks.description: Use this framework when a user suspects their AI adoption is underperforming or wants to deploy agents on existing workflows. Evaluate their work structure against the four primitives as necessary preconditions for delegation — not nice-to-haves. Score each dimension and surface where work is locked in human heads or opaque admin panels, since that structural illegibility is what generic adoption advice misses.
when_to_apply: We bought Copilot licenses for the whole team but adoption is flat and nobody can explain why
I want to deploy AI agents on our workflows but I'm not sure which processes are actually ready
Our AI tools give good advice but nothing actually gets done automatically — there's always a human copy-pasting
We're a non-technical team wondering what we'd need to change about how we work before AI agents could help
Why does our competitor seem to get 10x from AI while we're stuck at 1.2x despite using the same models?
principles: Agent leverage requires work to be structured in materials that agents can read and act on — not locked in human heads or opaque admin panels
The four primitives are necessary preconditions for delegation, whether to humans or agents
Organizations that lack these primitives will be limited to an advisory layer with capable models but limited actual impact
These are not coding skills — they are structural properties of how work is organized
Rollback capability is what makes high throughput safe, not just fast

source_posts.title: Inside OpenAI's Codex Team: Always-On AI Feedback, Everyone Commits Code, No One Cares About Titles—A Look at the Future of Work + 6 Prompts to Make it Real in Your Business

frameworks.example_application: This team scores poorly on all four primitives. Tasks live in Slack threads and verbal handoffs (no machine-readable task definitions), artifacts are created in admin panels with no API (no programmatic access), there's no version control on their core deliverables (no rollback capability), and completion criteria are 'the manager looks at it and says it's done' (no verifiable done state). The model they deployed is GPT-4-class — plenty capable — but it's reduced to a chat assistant because there's nothing structured for it to operate on. Restructuring the work primitives is the prerequisite; upgrading the model is irrelevant until then.
do_not_use_when: The team has clear, documented workflows but AI adoption is low because employees distrust the technology — a change management problem, not a structural legibility problem.
The organization wants to automate a single, already-digitized transactional process like invoice matching — scoped implementation advice beats a full four-dimension audit.
The leader is asking which AI vendor or model to purchase, not whether their work structure is ready to support agents — this is a procurement decision, not a readiness assessment.
The company is a two-person startup with no formal processes yet — the framework assumes existing organizational work structures to evaluate, which don't yet exist.
frameworks.description_original: A four-dimension assessment of whether an organization's work structure is legible enough for AI agents to operate on, determining whether agent leverage can actually be captured.

frameworks.name: Moving Goalposts Failure Pattern
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user's AI project feels broken but no one can point to a specific model failure. Look for signals of silent correctness redefinition — each stakeholder layer adding undocumented requirements without reconciling prior ones. Challenge the user's assumption that the AI degraded; push them to prove human standards didn't shift instead.
when_to_apply: Our AI outputs used to be fine but now everyone's unhappy and nobody can explain what changed
Different stakeholders keep rejecting the same AI output for completely different reasons
Engineering says they met the spec but the business side says the product is broken
We keep adding 'small tweaks' to what the AI should produce and each sprint feels like starting over
My personal AI workflow that used to feel great now feels inadequate even though I haven't changed the prompts
principles: Correctness redefinition happens silently — each change feels like a minor adjustment but the aggregate shift is a new product
The AI is not becoming less reliable; human standards are shifting without acknowledgment
Each stakeholder layer adds requirements without removing or reconciling prior ones
The failure is upstream in human specification, not in model performance
Catching this pattern requires naming what you want, noticing when it changes, and updating specifications explicitly

source_posts.title: I've reviewed 20+ enterprise AI builds this year—they all skip this conversation + 7 prompts that force it before anyone writes code

frameworks.example_application: The team says the model's summarization quality has 'degraded' over three sprints, but no model changes were made. The real timeline: Sprint 1, the PM defined 'correct' as factually accurate summaries. Sprint 2, Legal added a requirement that summaries must flag liability language — never written down, communicated verbally in a review meeting. Sprint 3, the CFO rejected outputs that didn't include financial impact estimates, which no one had ever specified. The team is now building three products — a summarizer, a legal risk scanner, and a financial impact estimator — under the label of one. The model isn't failing; it's being evaluated against a specification that doesn't exist yet.
do_not_use_when: The AI system's outputs degraded because the underlying model was updated or retrained, making this a technical drift issue rather than a human specification problem.
Stakeholders reject outputs for the same core reason expressed differently, indicating a single unmet requirement rather than layered undocumented redefinitions.
The team is explicitly aware their requirements changed and wants help writing a new spec, not diagnosing why the old one failed.
A solo user's personal workflow feels inadequate because their skill level has grown and they now recognize genuine output quality limits they previously lacked context to notice.
frameworks.description_original: Enumerates the progressive, unacknowledged redefinition of 'correct' that occurs in AI projects, where each stakeholder layer adds undocumented requirements until the team is effectively building multiple different products without realizing it.

frameworks.name: Work Delegation Bucket Classification
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user needs to prioritize or calibrate AI delegation across multiple task types. Classify each task into one of three buckets — new work, high-value existing work, or tedious recurring work — then match the appropriate trust and verification posture to each. Push users past the common blind spot of applying uniform scrutiny: spot-checking tedious recurring work reveals model quality fast, while high-value existing work demands a baseline comparison before relying on output.
when_to_apply: I have a dozen tasks I could try with AI but I don't know which ones to start with
I'm worried about AI making mistakes on important work but I also don't want to over-verify everything
Some of my work is brand new exploration and some is repetitive drudgery — should I treat them the same when delegating to AI?
I want to build an AI delegation habit but need a way to calibrate how much I trust the output for different task types
My team is adopting AI tools and we need a simple framework for which tasks get full autonomy versus careful review
principles: New work (tasks never completed before) has low downside risk — any progress is a win, so it is safe to experiment freely
High-value existing work requires careful baseline comparison — verify that AI output improves on what you'd produce yourself before trusting it
Tedious recurring work is the safest and most immediately valuable target — spot-checking quickly reveals model quality with low stakes
steps: Classify the task: Is this new work that has never been done? High-value existing work with a known baseline? Or tedious recurring work? This matters because the author argues that "delegation craft" — knowing how to define and delegate meaningful blocks of work — is the skill that separates people who get genuine leverage from those who end up redoing generic output; without classifying first, you apply uniform scrutiny and miss that each bucket demands a fundamentally different trust and verification posture.

For new work: gather available data and delegate freely — any output is net-positive progress. This matters because the author frames models like GPT-5.2 as capable of sustaining attention across large, messy artifacts and returning coherent deliverables; when no baseline exists, any structured output is a win worth experimenting with, and over-vetting work that has never been done before wastes the exact leverage the model provides.

For high-value existing work: delegate with careful data preparation, then compare output to your baseline to assess quality before relying on it. This matters because the author warns about the trap of long feedback loops — when a model chews on work for 20-40 minutes and you discover the output is wrong, you've wasted an afternoon; running AI output side-by-side against your vetted baseline is the checkpoint that catches problems before that cost compounds.

For tedious recurring work: delegate and spot-check — quality is easy to assess and the leverage is immediate. This matters because the author emphasizes that the transformative value of these models is handling genuine work assignments, not just quick exchanges; recurring tasks with known structure and known outputs let you verify model quality fast with minimal risk, giving you the fastest proof of whether delegation is working before you scale trust to harder tasks.

source_posts.title: NEW: ChatGPT 5.2 Complete Teardown—I tested Excel, PowerPoint, and 10,000-row datasets—Here's My Take, Comparison vs. Opus 4.5 and Gemini 3 + 15 Prompts to Power Up GPT 5.2

frameworks.example_application: This weekly client report is tedious recurring work — same structure, same data sources, same format every Friday. That makes it the highest-leverage delegation target: hand it to the model, spot-check two or three outputs against last week's reports, and if quality holds, it's automated. The strategic competitor analysis the CEO requested, on the other hand, is new work that's never been done before — there's no baseline to beat, so any structured output is a net win worth experimenting with freely. But rewriting the pricing model — that's high-value existing work where the team already has a vetted spreadsheet. Delegating that requires running the AI output side-by-side against the current model and verifying every formula before trusting it.
do_not_use_when: The user needs to decide whether to adopt AI tooling at all, not how to classify tasks once adoption is underway.
The user is evaluating a single high-stakes task and needs a risk assessment framework, not a multi-bucket sorting taxonomy.
The user's 'tedious recurring work' involves regulated outputs like financial filings where spot-checking assumptions understate compliance risk.
The user is a solo worker with only two or three total tasks, making a three-bucket classification system an unnecessary overhead.
frameworks.description_original: A three-category classification of work types for deciding how to approach AI delegation, based on whether the work is new, high-value existing, or tedious recurring.
steps_original: Classify the task: Is this new work that has never been done? High-value existing work with a known baseline? Or tedious recurring work?
For new work: gather available data and delegate freely — any output is net-positive progress
For high-value existing work: delegate with careful data preparation, then compare output to your baseline to assess quality before relying on it
For tedious recurring work: delegate and spot-check — quality is easy to assess and the leverage is immediate

frameworks.name: Five Core Knowledge Work Skills (Plus One to Argue Against)
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user needs to evaluate knowledge worker effectiveness, design promotion criteria, or diagnose why team output is mediocre. Classify their situation using the five skills — Judgment, Orchestration, Coordination, Taste, and Updating — by identifying which artifact surfaces and characteristic failure modes appear in their team's actual written output. When prompting or AI training comes up, redirect toward orchestration and specification literacy as the deeper skills worth building.
when_to_apply: Designing a rubric for evaluating knowledge worker output beyond surface-level writing quality
My team keeps producing mediocre documents and I can't pinpoint whether it's a skills gap or a process gap
We're debating whether to invest in prompt engineering training or something more fundamental
Building promotion criteria or job descriptions that reflect what actually makes someone effective, not just their title
Deciding which skills to target in a deliberate practice program for knowledge workers
principles: Skills live in artifacts — the documents you leave behind — not in job titles or LinkedIn taglines
Each skill has a characteristic failure mode that is observable in written output
Orchestration and specification literacy are the deeper skills that make prompting work — train those instead
Updating is visible in how positions evolve over time, not in how they are defended
Taste requires being able to articulate what 'good' looks like, not just recognize it

source_posts.title: Grab the 9 prompts I use to turn docs into practice reps + a 90-day pilot you can steal

frameworks.example_application: This team's quarterly planning docs keep getting sent back for revision, and the instinct is to blame 'communication skills.' But the artifacts tell a different story. The plans show strong coordination (stakeholders are mapped, dependencies noted) and decent taste (the format and structure are clean). The failure is in judgment — every plan treats three competing priorities as equally important, never making the hard call about what to cut. That's not a writing problem; it's a judgment deficit that shows up in writing. The development investment should target judgment practice reps, not another 'better business writing' course. And the request to add 'prompt engineering' training is a distraction — what these people actually lack is specification literacy and orchestration skill, which are the deeper capabilities that make any tool (including AI) produce better output.
do_not_use_when: The team's underperformance is traced to unclear role ownership or competing priorities, not to individual skill deficits that artifacts can reveal.
The user needs to evaluate manual, physical, or procedural workers whose effectiveness doesn't surface in written documents or reasoning artifacts.
The user is asking whether to hire a single specialist for a narrow technical role, not designing a broad rubric for knowledge worker effectiveness.
The organization lacks basic documentation practices entirely, making artifact-based skill diagnosis premature until output hygiene is established.
frameworks.description_original: A classification of the five recurring skills that determine knowledge worker effectiveness — Judgment, Orchestration, Coordination, Taste, and Updating — each defined by its artifact surface and characteristic failure mode, plus an argument against treating 'prompting' as a top-level skill.

frameworks.name: Two Memory Problems Distinction
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user reports agent memory or confusion issues to distinguish between two failure modes: cross-session amnesia (domain memory) and within-session degradation (context engineering). Help the user see the difference by testing whether confusion resets at session boundaries or compounds mid-task. Challenge the assumption that adding persistent memory files solves everything — without context engineering, mid-session degradation continues regardless.
when_to_apply: An agent loses progress between conversation sessions but works fine within a single session
An agent starts sharp but becomes confused or repetitive deep into a long task
We added persistent memory files but the agent still degrades mid-task — what are we missing?
Evaluating whether an agent vendor's 'memory' feature solves cross-session continuity, within-session coherence, or both
Trying to figure out whether confused agent behavior is a storage problem or a context window management problem
principles: Domain memory (cross-session): the agent has no persistent record of where things stand; each session starts fresh; solved by structured external records (task lists, progress logs, validation criteria)
Context engineering (within-session): the agent accumulates too much in the context window mid-task, burying critical signal under noise; solved by computed views and active state management
Both problems are necessary to solve; external records without context engineering still produces mid-session degradation
Context engineering without domain memory means every session starts without continuity even if the session itself stays coherent
The two failure modes look similar (confused, forgetting things) but have completely different root causes and fixes

source_posts.title: Get the Cheat Code on Long-Running AI Agents—Here's What Manus, Google, and Anthropic Learned After Trial and Error + 12 Prompts to Help Build Long-Running Agents Yourself

frameworks.example_application: This team added a task log and progress file between sessions, but the agent still goes off the rails 40 minutes into complex multi-step work. That's not a domain memory problem — the agent starts each session knowing exactly where it left off. The failure is context engineering: mid-session, the context window fills with raw tool outputs, prior reasoning traces, and accumulated conversation history until the critical constraints get buried. The fix isn't better external records — it's computed views that surface only the active task state, validation criteria, and relevant constraints instead of dumping the full session history into the window.
do_not_use_when: The agent is forgetting things mid-session because the underlying LLM has a known bug or API instability, not a context management problem.
The user is asking whether a specific vendor's memory product is worth purchasing, requiring a product evaluation lens rather than an architectural diagnosis.
The agent confusion stems from ambiguous or contradictory instructions in the system prompt, not from session boundaries or context window overload.
The user has a single-session, single-turn agent that never runs long tasks and never needs continuity, making both failure modes structurally irrelevant.
frameworks.description_original: Separates two commonly conflated agent memory failure modes—cross-session amnesia (domain memory) and within-session degradation (context engineering)—clarifying that they have different causes and require different architectural solutions.

frameworks.name: λ/Δ/θ Focus Capacity Model
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user treats low output as a willpower or time-management failure. Challenge their assumption that more hours or better habits will fix the problem — push them to prove whether deep work is even statistically possible given their current λ, Δ, and θ. What this reveals that generic advice misses: if θ exceeds available block sizes, no amount of discipline produces meaningful work.
when_to_apply: I feel like I'm busy all day but can't point to a single meaningful thing I accomplished
I'm trying to decide whether to accept another recurring meeting and want to know the real cost to my deep work
My team complains they never have time for real work despite having 'open' calendars
I had a terrible productivity day and want to pinpoint whether it was interruptions, slow recovery, or too-small time blocks
I'm redesigning my team's Slack and meeting norms and need a quantitative model for how changes affect focus capacity
principles: Focus capacity is a function of measurable environmental variables, not willpower or character
Interruption rate (λ), recovery time (Δ), and minimum block size (θ) together determine whether deep work is statistically possible on a given day
Count real work units by asking how many θ-sized chunks fit into each focus block, rounding down — the rounding is harsh but honest
Small changes to any single variable can produce disproportionately large improvements in total capacity
Roughly half of interruptions are self-inflicted, making personal habit change as important as environmental design
If θ exceeds available block sizes, the result is constant thrashing regardless of total time spent working
steps: Establish your baseline λ: count how many times per hour your attention is pulled away (Slack, email, questions, pop-ups). This matters because research shows many knowledge workers get interrupted every few minutes, and until you have an actual count, you can't see that 'no amount of willpower fixes arithmetic' — you'll keep misattributing a math problem to a character flaw.

Establish your baseline Δ: estimate how many minutes it takes to mentally re-engage with deep work after each interruption. This matters because the author emphasizes that if your brain needs ten or fifteen minutes to reload after each interruption, 'the numbers don't work out' — Δ is the hidden multiplier that turns even modest interruption rates into total schedule destruction.

Establish your baseline θ: identify the minimum uninterrupted block length before you feel you've made meaningful progress on real work. This matters because θ is the threshold that determines whether deep work is even statistically possible on a given day; if θ exceeds your available block sizes, the result is constant thrashing regardless of total hours spent, which is the core insight the framework exists to reveal.

Audit your calendar to identify your actual focus blocks — the stretches between scheduled interruptions. This matters because the author's model shows that your day's capacity is shaped 'before it even starts' by structural conditions — this step forces you to see what your schedule actually allows rather than what you assume it allows, closing the gap between nominal work time and real availability.

For each focus block, calculate how many θ-sized chunks fit inside it (rounding down), then sum across blocks to get your daily capacity. This matters because the rounding down is 'harsh but honest' — a 70-minute block yields only one 45-minute deep work unit, not 1.5 — and this arithmetic is what converts vague feelings of unproductivity into a concrete number that proves the problem isn't motivation, it's math.

Identify which variable (λ, Δ, or θ) is the binding constraint on your current capacity. This matters because as the example application shows, the senior engineer's binding constraint was specifically λ, not calendar structure or recovery time — misidentifying the constraint means applying interventions that won't move the needle, while correctly identifying it reveals where 'small changes to those parameters can produce surprisingly large effects.'

Apply targeted interventions: reduce λ via triage and async defaults, reduce Δ via context-capture habits, reduce θ via work decomposition. This matters because the author uses AI not as a generic productivity boost but as 'a way to nudge those variables' — each intervention maps to a specific parameter, and roughly half of interruptions are self-inflicted, meaning personal habit change on the right variable can produce disproportionate gains without requiring organizational permission.

frameworks.example_application: A senior engineer has 8 hours of nominal work time but gets interrupted roughly 4 times per hour (λ=4), takes about 15 minutes to re-engage each time (Δ=15), and needs at least 45-minute blocks to make meaningful progress on architecture work (θ=45). After mapping scheduled meetings and calculating interruption-fragmented gaps, only 2 blocks per day exceed 45 minutes — yielding exactly 2 deep work units. That's not a motivation problem; it's arithmetic. The binding constraint is λ: cutting interruptions from 4/hour to 2/hour by batching Slack into 30-minute check windows would nearly double usable capacity without touching the calendar at all.
do_not_use_when: The user's low output stems from unclear priorities or wrong strategic bets, not from fragmented time — optimizing focus blocks won't produce meaningful work if the work itself is misdirected.
The user is a manager whose primary job IS coordination and responsiveness, making high interruption rate a feature of the role rather than a capacity defect to diagnose.

The user's team has ample deep work time but is blocked by dependencies, approvals, or missing information from other teams — a scheduling model misattributes an organizational bottleneck as a focus problem.

The user wants to know whether to hire a dedicated focus-time enforcer or adopt a new productivity tool — this is a resourcing or tooling decision, not a diagnostic moment where quantifying λ/Δ/θ adds value.
frameworks.description_original: A three-variable model that quantifies deep work capacity by measuring interruption rate (λ), recovery time (Δ), and minimum viable work block size (θ), then calculating how many meaningful work units fit into a given day.

frameworks.name: Task Decomposition Framework
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is struggling with a complex workflow they've been forcing through a single model or prompt. Challenge their assumption that better prompting will fix mediocre outputs — the real problem is usually that distinct cognitive operations (extraction, synthesis, analysis, generation, validation) are being collapsed into one task. Push them to map what a skilled human actually does step-by-step before touching model selection.
when_to_apply: I'm trying to automate a complex knowledge work process and my single-prompt approach keeps producing mediocre results that need heavy editing
My team uses one AI model for everything and I suspect we're overpaying for simple tasks while underserving complex ones
I need to design an AI workflow but the process involves very different types of thinking — some parts need precision, others need creativity
We want to move from ad-hoc AI usage to a repeatable, teachable methodology our whole team can follow
I'm building a multi-step AI pipeline and need to figure out which model to assign to which step
principles: Map what humans actually do step-by-step before designing any AI workflow
Identify each distinct cognitive operation as a separate task, not as part of a single prompt
Match each task to the cognitive type category it belongs to (extraction, synthesis, analysis, generation, validation)
Assign models based on the cognitive type and the specific requirements of that task
Treat the cost question as a math problem: measure time saved versus cost of additional tools
Intuition for which model fits which task can only be built through deliberate, tracked experimentation — not documentation
Professional-looking output is not a signal of correctness; validate outputs against the actual requirements of each task type
steps: Map the workflow by documenting every distinct step a skilled human performs, not the high-level description of the deliverable. This matters because most workflows contain five or six tasks pretending to be one — 'Generate a PRD' sounds like one thing but is actually customer synthesis, UI analysis, feature design, roadmap alignment, and document construction, and planning at one level of abstraction while executing at another is the deeper gap behind failed implementations.

Identify the cognitive type for each step (extraction, synthesis, analysis, generation, or validation). This matters because each cognitive type requires different capabilities, and when you collapse them into a single prompt you're asking a specialist to be a generalist — which produces output that looks professional but falls apart under scrutiny.

Note the specific requirements of each task — precision needs, context volume, style consistency, rule complexity. This matters because extraction and validation demand precision while synthesis and generation require nuance and style consistency — without identifying these specific requirements, you cannot distinguish which tasks need a frontier model from which tasks a smaller, cheaper model handles more reliably.

Match each task to a model suited to that cognitive type and those specific requirements. This matters because AI doesn't fail at the workflow level, it fails at the task level — assigning models based on the actual cognitive demands of each task prevents the expensive pattern of throwing entire workflows at one model, getting disappointing outputs, blaming the model, and upgrading to something more expensive.

Run deliberate experiments routing the same tasks to different models and tracking quality outcomes. This matters because intuition for which model fits which task can only be built through deliberate, tracked experimentation — not documentation or benchmarks — and the author explicitly distinguishes patterns from dozens of implementations over theoretical benchmarks as the basis for model-task matching.

Build the multi-model pipeline with each task routed to its matched model. This matters because a single-model approach can actually perform worse on specific task types — for example, a frontier model over-elaborates on extraction instead of returning clean structured data — so routing each task to its matched model improves quality while reducing cost.

Calculate actual cost versus time saved to validate the approach economically. This matters because multi-model setups quietly beat 'one model for everything' once you do the math — the author found running all tasks through a single frontier model costs 4x what a multi-model pipeline costs, and without treating cost as a concrete math problem teams burn through multiple enterprise contracts chasing better outputs.

frameworks.example_application: A consulting firm's report-writing process actually decomposes into five distinct cognitive operations: extracting key metrics from client data (extraction), identifying patterns across quarters (analysis), synthesizing findings into a narrative (synthesis), generating client-facing prose (generation), and checking claims against source data (validation). Extraction and validation demand precision — a smaller, cheaper model with structured output handles these reliably. Synthesis and generation require nuance and style consistency — that's frontier model territory. Analysis sits in between and needs experimentation to route correctly. Running all five through GPT-4 costs 4x what the multi-model pipeline costs, and the single-model approach actually performs worse on extraction because the model over-elaborates instead of returning clean structured data.
do_not_use_when: The user wants to automate a single, well-defined task like invoice parsing — decomposition adds orchestration overhead with no quality benefit.
The workflow bottleneck is poor source data quality, not model selection — routing tasks better won't fix outputs built on unreliable inputs.
The user is evaluating whether to adopt AI at all, not how to structure it — decomposition assumes the build decision is already made.
The process requires real-time human judgment at every step for regulatory compliance, making autonomous AI task routing inappropriate regardless of decomposition quality.
frameworks.description_original: A structured method for breaking any workflow into atomic, AI-ready tasks by identifying cognitive type, matching model capabilities, and routing each sub-task to the most appropriate tool rather than applying one model to the entire workflow.

frameworks.name: Accuracy vs. Intelligence Failure Distinction
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user's AI output looks professional but fails expert review, or when they're deciding whether to fix their prompt, switch models, or redesign their task. Help them see the difference between an accuracy failure (incorrect rule application, fixable with better model selection or task isolation) and an intelligence failure (absent contextual judgment, requiring task redesign) by asking them to test whether the output is statistically correct but interpretively blind — a model can count without being able to see.
when_to_apply: My AI draft has all the right data but an expert would say it completely misses the point
I'm trying to decide whether to fix my prompt, switch models, or redesign how I've broken down the task
Two different AI workflows are both producing useless output and I need to figure out if they're failing for the same reason
The AI's analysis is technically correct but reads like it was written by someone who has never worked in this domain
My outputs only reveal their problems when a subject matter expert reviews them — they pass surface-level checks fine
principles: Both failure modes produce the same symptom: professional-looking output that misses the point
Accuracy failures occur when a model applies rules or calculations incorrectly — a precision problem fixable by better model selection or task isolation
Intelligence failures occur when a model lacks the contextual judgment to interpret what correct data means — a reasoning problem requiring different task design
Diagnosing the correct failure type before redesigning a workflow prevents solving the wrong problem
A model can count without being able to see — statistical correctness and interpretive insight are separate capabilities

frameworks.example_application: The financial summary the model produced has correct revenue figures and accurate growth percentages, but it completely missed that the growth is coming from a single customer who represents 60% of revenue — a concentration risk any analyst would flag immediately. This is an intelligence failure, not an accuracy failure. The numbers are right; the interpretation is absent. Switching to a better model won't fix this — the task needs to be restructured so that interpretive questions ('what does this data pattern mean for risk?') are separated from data extraction, and domain-specific judgment criteria are injected into the prompt as explicit evaluation lenses.
do_not_use_when: The AI output is useless because the underlying training data is outdated, not because of how the model reasons or applies rules.
The user needs to choose between two AI vendors for a procurement decision, not diagnose why a specific workflow is failing.
The output quality problem disappears when the user simply provides more complete input data, making failure-mode diagnosis irrelevant.
The user's workflow is failing due to API rate limits or infrastructure errors producing truncated responses, not a reasoning or precision issue.
frameworks.description_original: A diagnostic distinction between two fundamentally different AI failure modes — precision errors in rule application versus absence of contextual judgment — that produce identical symptoms (professional-looking but useless output) but require different fixes.

frameworks.name: Edge-First Automation Framework
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is sequencing AI automation against a workflow that has a high-judgment core surrounded by manual tedium. Shift their framing from "automate the valuable part first" to "automate the edges until the core earns it." Challenge the assumption that stalled projects failed technically — push them to see that automation is an organizational trust exercise, and that touching the core before inputs are clean, exceptions are visible, and operators trust the system is what locks away the tribal knowledge they need.
when_to_apply: We tried to automate a complex workflow end-to-end and the project stalled or people lost confidence in it
My team wants to use AI agents but we're not sure which part of the process to target first
Stakeholders are skeptical about AI automation because a previous attempt broke something that worked fine before
We have a high-judgment workflow surrounded by tedious manual steps and I need to figure out the sequencing
Our AI automation project keeps expanding in scope and we need a principled way to constrain it
principles: Start with the edges (data prep, QA, synthesis, packaging, coordination) before touching the core
Core workflows contain hidden complexity, tribal knowledge, and judgment that current models reliably underestimate
Automation is an organizational trust exercise, not just a technical project — losing trust locks away the tribal knowledge you need
Early wins should be fast (one to two weeks), semi-manual, and designed to capture 70-80% of cases while routing exceptions to humans
Automate around human expertise, not through it — protect the craft by eliminating the tedium surrounding it
Each edge automated builds the infrastructure, exception maps, and trust needed to eventually approach the core
Do not attempt core automation until inputs are clean, edge-to-core boundaries are clear, exceptions are visible, operators trust the system, and edge automations run stably
steps: Pick a workflow you touch every week that matters to you or your team. This matters because the author observes that teams stall when they pick ambitious, distant workflows instead of ones they personally experience — weekly contact ensures you have real friction data and genuine motivation to iterate, rather than theorizing about someone else's process (inferred).

Map the five edge categories: data preparation, QA, synthesis, packaging, and coordination. This matters because the author identifies these five categories as the 'mechanical stuff that surrounds the valuable work' — without explicitly naming them, teams default to seeing the workflow as a monolith and fixate on the high-judgment core, which is exactly the trap that causes automation projects to stall.

Identify where time and energy disappear in the pre- and post-core phases. This matters because the author's core insight is that the real pain usually isn't in the judgment-heavy decision itself — as in the underwriting example, the pain is the 6 hours spent gathering documents, normalizing formats, and chasing missing fields. Skipping this step means you misdiagnose the bottleneck and target the wrong thing.

Select the simplest edge — not the most impressive, but the one with the fastest, clearest lift. This matters because the author explicitly warns that 'the edges feel like the boring parts' and teams are drawn to impressive-looking core automation instead. The framework insists early wins must be fast — one to two weeks — because speed of visible results is what builds the organizational trust needed for everything that follows.

Build a semi-manual version-0 that automates the predictable 70-80% and flags the rest for human review. This matters because the author describes this as the antidote to 'the agent moonshot trap' — teams that try to build fully autonomous systems burn months on edge cases, while the 70-80% approach ships in days, routes exceptions to humans, and avoids the loss of trust that comes from a system silently mishandling cases it doesn't understand.

Ship, observe real usage, and iterate based on what exceptions surface. This matters because the author argues that each edge automated builds 'exception maps' critical for eventually approaching the core — the underwriting example shows that real usage surfaces patterns like incomplete appraisals and non-standard property types that any future core automation would need to handle. You cannot discover these exceptions from a design document.

Stack multiple successful edge automations before assessing readiness to approach the core. This matters because the author observes that compounding edge wins do three things simultaneously: they deliver immediate ROI (the team 'down the hall' freed 30% of their week from three 'boring' tasks), they build the infrastructure and exception visibility the core needs, and they earn the organizational trust without which operators will lock away the tribal knowledge required for core automation.

Run a readiness check on five dimensions before moving inward: clean inputs, clear edge-core boundary, visible exceptions, operator trust, and stable edge automations. This matters because the author's central diagnosis of failed projects is that teams attempted core automation before earning the right — 'touching the core before inputs are clean, exceptions are visible, and operators trust the system is what locks away the tribal knowledge you need.' This gate prevents the exact failure mode the entire framework exists to avoid.

frameworks.example_application: The conventional instinct is to automate the core underwriting decision — that's where the most labor-intensive judgment sits, so it looks like the biggest win. That's wrong here because the underwriting team's real pain isn't the decision itself; it's the 6 hours per case spent gathering documents, normalizing data formats, and chasing brokers for missing fields. Those are edges — data prep and coordination — where 80% of cases follow a predictable pattern. Automating those first delivers immediate time savings, builds the team's trust that AI handles their inputs reliably, and surfaces the exception patterns (incomplete appraisals, non-standard property types) that any future core automation would need to handle anyway.
do_not_use_when: The workflow has no meaningful 'core' — it is already entirely mechanical and rule-based, so edge-first sequencing adds no value over direct full automation.
The user needs to decide whether to automate at all, not how to sequence it — the framework presupposes a go decision that hasn't been made yet.
The automation target is a greenfield process with no existing operators, tribal knowledge, or trust to protect, so the organizational trust logic doesn't apply.
Stakeholder skepticism stems from budget or job-loss fears, not from a prior technical failure — resequencing automation won't address the actual objection.

frameworks.name: Five Edge Categories
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user needs to systematically identify automatable work surrounding a high-judgment core workflow. Classify their peripheral tasks across five categories — data preparation, QA, synthesis, packaging, and coordination — then sort their claims using the shared profile: low-judgment, well-defined outputs, inputs already ready. Surface any edge work they've overlooked, especially coordination and synthesis, which users routinely miss when cataloging the obvious prep and QA tasks.
when_to_apply: I can see that our team spends most of their time on stuff around the actual work, not the work itself, and I want to systematically catalog what's automatable
We're starting an automation initiative and need to prioritize which peripheral tasks to tackle first across a complex workflow
I keep hearing 'automate the edges' but I need a concrete taxonomy to make sure I'm identifying all the edge work, not just the obvious stuff
Our knowledge workers are drowning in prep work, QA, and formatting — I need to classify these tasks to build a sequenced automation roadmap
I want to audit a workflow to find where current LLM capabilities can actually deliver value without requiring deep domain judgment
principles: Data preparation: collecting, cleaning, normalizing, and reconciling inputs before the core work begins
QA: verifying completeness, consistency, and absence of obvious errors — automatable without understanding the full workflow
Synthesis: summarizing, consolidating, or translating information from sprawling sources into actionable formats
Packaging: transforming finished work into the required deliverable format for the next stage
Coordination: moving context between systems or people, eliminating the human translation layer in handoffs
All five categories share the profile of low-judgment, well-defined outputs, and inputs that are already ready — making them suitable for automation even with imperfect models

frameworks.example_application: A legal team's contract review process has five distinct edge categories consuming human hours. Data preparation — pulling clause libraries and prior agreements from three different systems — takes 40% of paralegal time. Synthesis — consolidating redline comments from four stakeholders into a single change summary — takes another 25%. Both are low-judgment, well-defined-output tasks with inputs already available. Packaging (reformatting final agreements into client-specific templates) and coordination (emailing status updates between internal counsel and outside firms) round out the automation surface. QA on formatting consistency is trivially automatable. The core judgment — whether a clause creates unacceptable risk — stays human. Starting with data preparation yields the highest time savings with the lowest verification burden.
do_not_use_when: The user wants to automate the core judgment work itself (e.g., underwriting decisions, clinical diagnoses), not the peripheral tasks surrounding it.
The user is asking which automation vendor or tooling to purchase, not how to classify or sequence what to automate.
The workflow has no stable, repeatable structure — it's bespoke each time — so 'edges' cannot be consistently identified or separated from the core.
The user already has a completed task inventory and needs a prioritization scoring model, not a classification taxonomy to discover tasks.
frameworks.description_original: A classification system for the five types of automatable peripheral work that surround any high-judgment core workflow, used to systematically identify where to start an automation initiative.

frameworks.name: Core Automation Readiness Check
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is weighing whether to extend automation into the high-judgment core of a workflow. Challenge their assumption that technical capability or early wins have earned them the right to go deeper — readiness is earned, not assumed. Push them to prove all five dimensions are satisfied, because partial readiness is not readiness, and rushing the core before preconditions are met costs more time than waiting.
when_to_apply: We've had some wins automating the simpler parts of our workflow and leadership wants us to automate the high-judgment center next
Our last attempt to automate the core decision-making step of a process failed and we're trying to understand why
The team is debating whether to start an automation project at the most valuable step or work inward from the periphery
Edge automations are running but I'm not sure the preconditions are actually met to go deeper
Operators who do the core work are skeptical of expanding automation scope and I need to assess whether their concerns are legitimate
principles: Rushing the core before preconditions are met costs more time than waiting
All five dimensions must be satisfied — partial readiness is not readiness
Readiness is earned through successful edge automation, not assumed from technical capability
steps: Assess whether inputs to the core are now clean and reliable (from edge automation of data prep). This matters because the author identifies data preparation as a key "edge" category that must be automated first — if the mechanical work surrounding the core still produces dirty or unreliable inputs, any core automation will inherit those errors and collapse under real conditions, not because the core logic failed but because it was fed garbage.

Assess whether the boundary between edge work and core work is clearly defined. This matters because the author warns that teams fail when they can't distinguish "the part that requires deep expertise and judgment" from "the mechanical stuff that surrounds the valuable work" — without a clear boundary, you risk automating core judgment work while thinking you're still on the edges, or leaving edge work unautomated because you mistakenly classified it as core.

Assess whether exceptions that were previously invisible are now visible and mapped. This matters because the author's example shows that an incomplete exception taxonomy ("three new edge cases surfaced last week that nobody had mapped") is a disqualifying condition — edge automation is supposed to surface the hidden complexity that was previously buried in human workarounds, and if that map is still incomplete, core automation will "collapse under real exception load."

Assess whether the operators who do the core work trust the automation system you have built. This matters because the author frames AI automation as "an organizational trust exercise, not a technical project" and argues that attacking edges first "earns you the right to eventually touch the core" — the example shows operators who "have been burned by silent failures twice" represent a failed trust dimension, and without their trust, a technically functional system will be resisted or abandoned.

Assess whether your edge automations run stably without constant human intervention. This matters because the author contrasts teams that "automated three boring tasks and freed up 30% of their week" with teams that stalled — if edge automations still require constant human babysitting, they haven't actually freed capacity or demonstrated reliability, meaning you haven't earned readiness through successful edge automation, you've only created the appearance of it (inferred).

If all five are yes, proceed to core automation; if any are no, continue building edges until they are. This matters because the author's central principle is that "partial readiness is not readiness" and "rushing the core before preconditions are met costs more time than waiting" — the example demonstrates that two failing dimensions out of five means the right move is to keep running edges, not to proceed with caveats, because the result would be "a system that looks functional in demos but collapses under real exception load."

Reliability drift is an evaluation problem, not a drafting problem
Production failures may live in orchestration or deployment layers, not in the prompt text itself
steps: Ask: Is the goal unclear or under-specified? → Stage 1 problem; define objectives, constraints, and output format before rewording. This matters because the author identifies intent formation as the missing stage in how we talk about prompting — 'There is almost nothing at all out there for ideation and intent formation in prompting. In fact, we don't even talk about it.' Without diagnosing this first, teams skip straight to wordsmithing a prompt whose purpose was never properly defined, which no amount of redrafting can fix.

Ask: Is the wording messy or ambiguous despite clear intent? → Stage 2 problem; use drafting tools or optimizers. This matters because the author treats authoring and drafting as a distinct stage ('getting the words right') that only makes sense after intent is locked down; conflating wording problems with goal problems is exactly the kind of muddle that occurs 'when we can't talk about it as distinct stages' and 'we mostly just muddle through.'

Ask: Is output reliability drifting across runs? → Stage 4 problem; build test cases and run evaluations. This matters because the author explicitly separates evaluation and testing from drafting as its own lifecycle stage, and as the example application shows, a team can rewrite a prompt twelve times when the real fix is building regression test cases — misidentifying drift as a wording problem wastes effort on the wrong stage entirely.

Ask: Is the prompt failing in production context? → Stage 5 or 6 problem; check orchestration logic, monitoring, and deployment configuration. This matters because the author's lifecycle includes workflow construction, automation, deployment, and integration as separate downstream stages with their own specialized tools — failures here live in engineering layers the prompt author may never see, and diagnosing them as prompt-text problems leads to endless rewrites that can never address orchestration or infrastructure root causes. (inferred)

source_posts.title: Prompting is Too Hard: Check Out My Easy Prompt Lifecycle Guide + 19 Prompting Tools + a Custom Prompt to Analyze your Prompting Strengths & Weaknesses

frameworks.example_application: The team has rewritten their summarization prompt twelve times, but outputs still vary wildly between runs. The wording is actually fine — the task specification is clear, the format is defined, and a single run produces good results. The real problem is Stage 4: there are no evaluation test cases, so they have no way to detect or measure the drift. They need a regression suite, not another prompt rewrite. The fix is to build five canonical input-output pairs and run automated checks, not to add more instructions to the system prompt.

The user's 'degrading output quality' is caused by a confirmed upstream data pipeline failure already identified by their engineering team.
The user is asking why a specific prompt technique like chain-of-thought works conceptually, not troubleshooting a broken workflow.
The user is a researcher evaluating benchmark performance across models, not diagnosing a deployed production system.

frameworks.name: AI-Native Job Transformation Roadmap
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user wants to move from AI experimentation to shipping a workflow their team actually depends on. Challenge their assumption that accumulating more tool familiarity is the bottleneck — the blind spot is usually that they haven't mapped their workflows like a systems designer before touching AI. Push them to prove they can articulate one workflow's trigger, inputs, decision points, and exception handling before jumping to prompting or governance conversations.
when_to_apply: I use AI tools at work but it still feels like toy demos — I want to ship something real that my team actually depends on
Our org is rolling out AI tooling and I want to be the person who shapes how it lands in my function, not the person it happens to
I'm a senior IC who needs to demonstrate AI workflow design credibility for my next performance cycle or job search
My manager asked me to figure out where AI fits in our team's workflows and I need a structured approach
I want to build a relationship with our AI governance team but I don't have anything concrete to show them yet
principles: Design the AI-native version of your job before someone else does it for you
AI augments structured, repetitive, verifiable work—not judgment-heavy or politically nuanced work
Work within approved organizational tools and security guardrails, not around them
Ship one real workflow that others rely on rather than accumulating toy demos
Pair business-side workflow knowledge with governance vocabulary to become a cross-functional bridge
The goal is to shift your value from executing work to supervising and designing workflows
steps: Step 1 — Map your work like a systems designer: Identify 3–5 recurring workflows you own and for each document the trigger, inputs, steps, decision points, outputs, verification checks, and exception handling. This matters because the author argues most people have never been asked to think about their work this way — they say 'I do marketing' instead of decomposing their role into explicit, repeatable workflows, and without that decomposition you cannot identify which bits are 'AI workflow-able' versus which stay human, meaning someone else will decompose and automate your work without your input.

Step 2 — Learn to express those workflows to your existing approved AI tools: Give AI structured, scoped instructions; feed clean formatted inputs; request directly usable outputs; iterate until you have a stable, repeatable prompt recipe for each workflow. This matters because the author emphasizes working inside the tools your company already has (ChatGPT Enterprise, Copilot, Gemini, or internal bots) — the stack is finally stable enough for non-specialists to do meaningful work, so the real bottleneck isn't tool familiarity but your ability to translate mapped workflows into structured instructions AI can execute reliably and repeatably.

Step 3 — Ship an MVP of one meaningful AI-augmented workflow: Pick a high-frequency, painful, low-blast-radius workflow; automate 60–80% of the steps while keeping yourself in the loop for approval and exceptions; measure time saved, error rate, and throughput; document it as a one-pager with numbers. This matters because the author distinguishes between people who accumulate toy demos and the person who can say 'here's what we automate, here's what stays human, here's how we keep it safe' — shipping one real workflow with measured results is what converts you from someone who uses AI sometimes into someone managers ask for input rather than surprise with a new process.

Step 4 — Build a relationship with whoever owns AI and platform governance in your org: Show your experiment as a responsible insider, ask what patterns they are standardizing, surface where they are nervous about AI in your function, and align your work to their highest-priority modernization targets. This matters because the author says people leaders are actively looking for someone within existing roles who can bridge business-side workflow knowledge with governance and security concerns — by plugging into the platform and security people you become the cross-functional person who defines what gets automated and what stays human, which is where durable career value lives rather than in isolated experimentation.

The campaign brief workflow had the highest frequency, lowest blast radius, and clearest verification criteria (does the brief match the intake form plus historical performance data?). Automating 70% of brief generation with a stable prompt recipe inside the approved enterprise ChatGPT instance saved 6 hours per week across the team. Documenting that result as a one-pager with time-saved and error-rate numbers, then presenting it to the platform governance team, converted the manager from 'person who uses AI sometimes' into the go-to bridge between marketing and the AI modernization initiative — which is where durable career value lives.

frameworks.name: Workflow Decomposition API
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user's AI outputs feel generic or they're struggling to specify what an AI tool should do for their role. The core blind spot to challenge: they likely cannot describe their own work explicitly enough for any model to help with it. Push them to prove this wrong by walking through the seven components — what they uncover about their own implicit knowledge is the real output, not just a prompt template.
when_to_apply: I keep asking AI to help with my job but the outputs are generic and miss the nuances of what I actually do
I need to onboard a new hire or document my role and I'm realizing how much of my process lives only in my head
My company is rolling out an AI initiative and I need to figure out which parts of my workflow are automatable vs. judgment-heavy
I want to build a custom GPT or AI assistant for my role but I don't know how to specify what it should do
I'm trying to figure out why AI tools work well for some of my tasks but completely fail on others
principles: Most knowledge workers have never made their own work explicit—doing so is itself a competitive advantage
If you cannot describe the work clearly enough to write it down, an AI model has no chance of helping with it
Making work explicit is the prerequisite to improving it, whether or not AI is involved
Every recurring job function can be decomposed into trigger, inputs, steps, decisions, outputs, verification, and exception handling
steps: Identify the trigger: what event or condition starts this workflow? This matters because most people describe their work as a vague blob ('I do marketing') rather than explicit, repeatable workflows — identifying the trigger forces you to pinpoint where a workflow actually begins, which is the first move in turning 'I do [role]' into something an AI can act on.

List the inputs: what information or resources do you need before you can begin? This matters because without surfacing inputs explicitly, you cannot identify which parts of the work are synthesis-heavy (strong AI candidates) versus judgment-heavy — as the PRD example shows, knowing the inputs (customer research, capacity estimates, strategic goals) is what reveals that input synthesis is automatable while scoping decisions are not.

Document the steps: what do you actually do, in order? This matters because the author argues most knowledge workers have never made their own work explicit, and documenting steps is where your implicit knowledge becomes visible — skipping this means your work gets 'decomposed and partially automated without your input' by someone else in the organization.

Mark the decision points: where do you make judgment calls and what criteria do you use? This matters because this is the step that distinguishes what stays human from what gets automated — the author's core framing is that you need to be the person who can say 'here's what we automate, here's what stays human,' and decision points are precisely where that line gets drawn.

Define the outputs: what do you produce at the end? This matters because without a defined output, you cannot specify what 'good' looks like to an AI tool — the PRD example shows that defining the output (a PRD with acceptance criteria) is what transforms a vague request ('write a PRD') into something that produces non-generic results.

Specify verification: how do you check that the output is correct? This matters because verification is how you 'keep it safe' — the author explicitly frames the AI-native worker as someone who can articulate 'here's how we keep it safe,' and without a verification step, you have no guardrail distinguishing AI-assisted output from AI-hallucinated output.

Define exception handling: what do you do when something goes wrong or an edge case appears? This matters because exception handling reveals the parts of your work that require adaptive human judgment — as the PRD example shows, cases like mid-sprint dependency invalidation are where AI integration breaks down, and surfacing these prevents you from automating a workflow that fails silently at the edges (inferred).

source_posts.title: Grab the AI Native Job Prompt—A Custom Guide to Make YOUR Role AI Native in 2026

frameworks.example_application: A product manager says 'I want AI to help me write PRDs.' Running the decomposition reveals: the trigger is a prioritization decision from the roadmap review, the inputs are customer research summaries, engineering capacity estimates, and strategic goals, the steps include synthesizing competing signals into a single problem statement, the key decision point is scoping — choosing what to cut — using criteria like engineering cost, revenue impact, and strategic alignment, the output is a PRD with acceptance criteria, verification is a stakeholder review meeting where engineering confirms feasibility, and exception handling covers cases where dependencies on other teams invalidate assumptions mid-sprint. Now the actual AI integration points are visible: synthesis of inputs and first-draft generation are strong candidates, but the scoping decision and exception handling require human judgment. Without this decomposition, the PM would have asked AI to 'write a PRD' and gotten generic output that misses the real work.
do_not_use_when: The user's role is non-recurring and project-based, so decomposing repeatable workflows is irrelevant to their actual work structure.
The user wants to evaluate which AI vendor or platform to adopt company-wide, not document individual workflows for integration.
The user's AI outputs are generic because they're using the wrong tool for the task, not because their prompts lack workflow context.
The user is a one-time consultant documenting a client's process for handoff, not making their own implicit knowledge explicit.
frameworks.description_original: A structured method for making implicit job work explicit by breaking any recurring workflow into seven defined components, creating a 'mental API' for your own role that enables AI integration and process improvement.

frameworks.name: Vercel's 'Build It Now' Filter
frameworks.description: Apply this filter when a user needs to decide which workflows are ready for an AI agent deployment now versus later. Score each candidate workflow against the five criteria: verifiability, step-wise and bounded structure, recurring toil, known inputs and outputs, and human-in-the-loop approval. Push back on any workflow the user describes as "strategic" or "judgment-based" — those signal open-ended work that fails the bounded criterion before evaluation begins.
when_to_apply: We have a list of ten workflows and need to decide which ones get an AI agent first
My team wants to automate a process with an agent but I'm not sure it's the right kind of work for current AI capabilities
I need a quick go/no-go filter before we invest engineering time building an agent for a specific task
We're scoping an AI agent pilot and need to avoid picking a use case that will fail and kill organizational momentum
Someone proposed automating a workflow that feels too open-ended or hard to verify — I need a structured way to say why
principles: The work must be verifiable — checking whether the agent performed correctly requires no heroics
The workflow must be step-wise and bounded — completable in a defined sequence, not open-ended strategy work
The task must be recurring and painful — people describe it as toil, not as valued work
Inputs and outputs must be known — you understand exactly what enters the system and what constitutes good output
A human must remain in the loop — the agent prepares work, a person approves, edits, or rejects it
