frameworks.name: Buy vs. Build Strategic Importance Matrix
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is weighing whether to build a custom AI agent or license a ready-made platform. Classify their initiative using the two axes — strategic importance and differentiation potential — to place it in the correct quadrant. Then pressure-test their assumptions: most organizations overestimate their need for custom development, so push them to prove high differentiation potential before endorsing a build decision.
when_to_apply: We're debating whether to build a custom AI agent or buy a platform, and the engineering team is pushing hard for custom
Our vendor quoted us $150K for an AI agent platform and leadership thinks we could build it cheaper in-house
We have three AI agent initiatives on the roadmap and limited budget — which ones should we build vs. buy?
The timeline to launch our AI capability keeps slipping and we're wondering if we should just license something
We need to justify to the board why we're spending $800K on custom AI development instead of buying an off-the-shelf solution
principles: High strategic importance + high differentiation potential = build custom
High strategic importance + low differentiation potential = buy ready-made
Low strategic importance = buy ready-made regardless of differentiation potential
Ready-made licensing is only 30-50% of total first-year costs; implementation services add 50-100% of licensing
Custom development provides strategic flexibility but ranges from $100K to $1.5M+ and 32-64 weeks
Most organizations overestimate their need for custom development

source_posts.title: The Definitive Guide to AI Agents in 2025: Technical Implementation, Strategic Decisions, and Market Reality

frameworks.example_application: This customer support agent falls in the high-strategic-importance but low-differentiation quadrant — every competitor needs the same ticket-routing and escalation logic, and three commercial platforms already handle it well. The instinct to build custom is driven by the engineering team's enthusiasm, not by any actual competitive wedge. Licensing at $80K/year plus $120K implementation gets this live in 12 weeks; a custom build would run $600K+ and 40 weeks to reach the same capability. The strategic energy should go toward the proprietary underwriting model where differentiation is real, not toward reinventing support automation.
do_not_use_when: The organization has already signed a contract with a vendor and is asking how to maximize value from the purchased platform, not whether to buy or build.
The user is deciding between two competing off-the-shelf vendors, not evaluating whether to build internally at all.
The question is about whether to build a data pipeline or analytics infrastructure, not an AI agent with strategic differentiation implications.
A startup with no engineering team is exploring AI options, making custom development a non-viable option that eliminates the need for comparative analysis.
frameworks.description_original: A two-axis classification matrix that maps strategic importance against differentiation potential to determine whether an organization should buy a ready-made agent solution or build a custom one.

frameworks.name: Compression vs. Expansion Distinction
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user's AI workflow feels productive but shallow, or when they're deciding how to deploy AI on a high-stakes problem. Help them see the difference between compression (optimizing for brain time saved) and expansion (optimizing for brain time on subject) by testing whether their current workflow is cleaning up existing thought or generating thinking that didn't exist before. Push back on the assumption that faster output signals better AI use.
when_to_apply: We automated a bunch of knowledge work with AI and our output is faster but somehow feels thinner
I'm trying to figure out whether to use AI to clean up my draft or to challenge and expand my thinking before I even draft
Our AI adoption strategy is mostly about summarization, extraction, and formatting — and I'm wondering if we're missing the bigger opportunity
I have a genuinely novel problem and the AI keeps giving me generic structured outputs instead of helping me discover something new
My team treats AI as a productivity tool but I suspect the real value is in using it as a thinking partner for ambiguous decisions
principles: Compression removes the tangents, contradictions, and recursion that are the actual mechanisms of breakthrough thinking
Expansion uses AI to access cognitive modes and ideas that would not emerge through individual or traditionally organized thinking
The same AI tools can be used for either mode; the distinction lies in the intent and workflow design
Compression has legitimate value for routine communication tasks; expansion is appropriate for high-stakes, ambiguous, or creative intellectual work
Optimizing for brain time on subject (expansion) yields greater long-term returns than optimizing for brain time saved (compression)

source_posts.title: We're Using AI Backwards—Here's How to Max Your Brain on AI (I call it Cognitive Choreography)

frameworks.example_application: This is compression, not expansion. The team built an AI pipeline that takes meeting transcripts, extracts action items, and produces clean summaries — and they're calling it their 'AI-augmented strategy process.' But the actual strategic thinking happened in the meeting; the AI is just a secretary. The real opportunity is using AI to pressure-test the reasoning that emerged in that meeting — surface contradictions between stated priorities and resource allocation, generate adversarial scenarios the team didn't consider, or explore analogies from adjacent domains. The clean summary feels productive but produces zero new insight. The messy, recursive, AI-challenged version of the same meeting content is where durable strategic advantage lives.
do_not_use_when: The user needs AI to process high-volume compliance documentation where accuracy and speed matter more than generating novel insight.
The user's 'thin output' problem stems from poor data quality or wrong AI tools, not a compression-vs-expansion workflow choice.
The user is asking whether to adopt AI at all, not how to use it—a buy-vs-build or change management question, not a cognition mode question.
The team's AI use feels shallow because they lack domain expertise to evaluate outputs, not because they're compressing instead of expanding.
frameworks.description_original: Distinguishes between two fundamentally different modes of AI use—compression (summarizing, organizing, and cleaning up existing thought) and expansion (using AI to discover, explore, and generate thinking that didn't exist before)—arguing that only the latter enables breakthrough cognition.

frameworks.name: The Agency Stack
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is trying to evaluate, demonstrate, or develop high-agency capability — in themselves, a hire, or a team member. Challenge the assumption that shipping output proves ownership; push them to map the full cycle from problem recognition to learning integration. What this reveals that generic advice misses: most people stall at execution and never close the loop by teaching the pattern to others.
when_to_apply: I'm building a portfolio to show employers I can work with AI tools, but I'm not sure what these projects are actually supposed to prove
We're designing interview questions to filter for people who can own problems end-to-end versus people who just execute tasks handed to them
Someone on my team ships good work when directed but never surfaces problems or improves processes on their own — I need to diagnose what's missing
I want to evaluate whether my side project demonstrates real career-relevant skill or is just a wrapper around a tutorial
I'm advising a junior person on what capabilities to develop so they stay valuable as AI automates more execution work
principles: Agency is demonstrated through the full cycle from problem recognition to learning integration, not just execution
Shipping code or output is not the point — navigating from a broken state to a better state is
The ability to teach others the pattern (Learning Integration) is what distinguishes agency from one-off competence
Resource marshaling includes tools, knowledge, and people — not just technical tools
Employers test for this stack whether or not they consciously articulate it
steps: Problem Recognition: See issues others ignore before they are named as problems. This matters because without evidence of genuine problem recognition, even polished output becomes what the author calls 'competence theater' — like the candidate who built a dashboard from a tutorial dataset but never identified a real problem, indistinguishable from the sea of vibe-coded apps where 'nobody can find signal.'

Solution Design: Imagine a better state and articulate what it looks like. This matters because the author distinguishes navigating from a broken state to a better state as the actual point — skipping this step means you're executing someone else's predefined pattern rather than demonstrating you can envision and articulate what 'better' looks like, which is the difference between showing you do work and having the actual job skills that matter. (inferred)

Resource Marshaling: Gather what is needed — tools, knowledge, and people — without waiting for permission. This matters because the author explicitly includes tools, knowledge, and people — not just technical tools — and the example candidate pulled in a DevOps friend and three unfamiliar tools; skipping this step or narrowing it to technical execution misses the proactive, permission-free resourcefulness that employers test for whether or not they consciously articulate it.

Execution: Navigate from the current broken state to the better state, handling what breaks along the way. This matters because the author argues 'shipping code or output is not the point' and warns that 'just ship something to GitHub' is turtles-all-the-way-down thinking — if everyone ships vibe-coded apps, we're drowning in noise; what distinguishes real execution is handling the things that break along the way, not producing a clean artifact.

Learning Integration: Update your models based on what worked and what failed, then teach others the pattern. This matters because this is where the author says most people stall — they stop at execution and never close the loop; the example candidate wrote up what they learned and onboarded two teammates, and the author explicitly states this step is what distinguishes agency from one-off competence, turning individual problem-solving into a teachable, repeatable pattern.

source_posts.title: The Kids Will be Ok: How To Skip the Jobs AI Doom Spiral and Actually Prepare for the Age of AI: A Tech Career Manifesto

frameworks.example_application: This portfolio project fails at Stage 1. The candidate built a polished dashboard, but there's no evidence they identified a real problem — they picked a tutorial dataset and executed a known pattern. Compare that to the candidate who noticed their team was losing hours to a broken deploy pipeline, sketched what a fix would look like, pulled in a DevOps friend and three tools they'd never used, shipped the fix while handling two things that broke along the way, then wrote up what they learned and onboarded two teammates. The second candidate demonstrated the full stack — problem recognition through learning integration — and that's what separates agency from competence theater.
do_not_use_when: The user wants to evaluate a specific technical portfolio project for code quality or architecture decisions, not what the project reveals about problem-ownership capability.
The user is designing competency assessments for a role where execution fidelity matters more than initiative, such as compliance, safety, or regulated clinical work.
The user is asking how to coach a junior person through a specific, bounded technical skill gap rather than diagnosing a structural agency deficit.
The user wants to understand why a high-agency employee is burning out or creating chaos, where more agency demonstration is the wrong prescription.
frameworks.description_original: A five-stage model for demonstrating high-agency problem-solving that employers actually evaluate, moving from identifying problems through execution to teaching the pattern to others.
steps_original: Problem Recognition: See issues others ignore before they are named as problems
Solution Design: Imagine a better state and articulate what it looks like
Resource Marshaling: Gather what is needed — tools, knowledge, and people — without waiting for permission
Execution: Navigate from the current broken state to the better state, handling what breaks along the way
Learning Integration: Update your models based on what worked and what failed, then teach others the pattern

frameworks.name: Pascal's Wager of Tech Careers
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is weighing skill development strategies under uncertainty about AI's trajectory. Evaluate each strategy by mapping its outcomes across both futures — AI dominates and humans remain essential — then identify which strategy produces transferable value even in the wrong scenario. The deciding factor is asymmetry in downside risk, not probability. Push back on any framing that treats this as a hedge; the dominant strategy wins in both scenarios, not just the more likely one.
when_to_apply: I keep going back and forth between learning AI/ML tools deeply versus building broader leadership and strategy skills — I can't do both well
A junior engineer is asking me whether they should specialize in prompt engineering or invest in understanding business problems and stakeholder management
Someone is arguing they should wait to see how AI shakes out before committing to a career development direction
I'm trying to explain to my team why soft skills investment isn't a hedge — it's actually the dominant strategy regardless of AI trajectory
Two career paths look equally promising right now but I suspect one has a much worse downside if AI progresses faster than expected
principles: Map outcomes across both possible futures (AI dominates / humans remain essential) for each strategy
Identify which strategy has a positive expected outcome in both scenarios vs. only one
The dominant strategy is the one where even the 'wrong' bet still produces transferable value
Asymmetry in downside risk — not probability — is the deciding factor
Market behavior (hiring patterns, investment flows) provides real-world signal to calibrate which scenario is more likely

source_posts.title: The Kids Will be Ok: How To Skip the Jobs AI Doom Spiral and Actually Prepare for the Age of AI: A Tech Career Manifesto

frameworks.example_application: The payoff matrix is asymmetric and one strategy dominates. If you invest in human-judgment-intensive skills — strategic thinking, stakeholder navigation, ambiguity resolution — and AI fully automates technical execution, those skills become MORE valuable because you're the human steering AI systems. If AI stalls out and humans remain essential for execution, those same judgment skills still compound your career because every technical role rewards the person who can also navigate organizational complexity. The competing strategy — doubling down on narrow technical execution — only pays off in the scenario where AI doesn't displace it. That's a bet on one future; judgment skills pay in both.
do_not_use_when: The user is choosing between two specific job offers with defined salaries and roles, not evaluating long-term skill development strategies.
The user is a late-career specialist with 20+ years in a niche field where retraining is economically impractical regardless of AI trajectory.
The user is deciding which AI tool to purchase for their team this quarter, not which human capabilities to develop over time.
The user is asking about career preparation in a regulated profession like medicine or law where licensing constraints make the AI-dominance scenario legally implausible.
frameworks.description_original: A 2x2 asymmetric payoff matrix for evaluating career preparation strategies under uncertainty about AI's impact, showing that preparing for human-judgment-intensive work dominates regardless of which AI future arrives.

frameworks.name: Narrow Pipe → Large Engine (6-Step Process)
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user's AI summaries, digests, or automated outputs are producing noise instead of actionable output. Challenge their assumption that the tool is the problem — the likely culprit is a mixed-purpose input stream. Push them to prove they have a single inlet with a two-line policy before touching any model settings. What generic advice misses: upstream discipline compounds; downstream cleanup never does.
when_to_apply: Our Slack AI summaries or Notion AI outputs are garbage and I'm not sure if the tool is bad or we're feeding it wrong
The same customer info keeps getting retyped across three different tools and nobody has a single source of truth
We want to use built-in AI features but our channels and databases are too noisy and mixed-purpose
I'm spending hours cleaning up or triaging information that should have arrived in usable form
We're about to set up a new automated reporting or digest workflow and I want it to actually produce actionable output from day one
principles: Repetition of the same facts across workflows signals a hidden pipe begging to be narrowed
The minimal 'decision-grade' payload is rarely more than three fields
A single inlet with a clearly stated two-line policy is sufficient infrastructure
Upstream discipline (a few seconds of nudging) prevents downstream cleanup costs (hours of effort)
If the first AI output is not actionable, tighten the pipe further before adding complexity
steps: Identify repetitive information hotspots — scan workflows for places where the same facts get rewritten or forwarded across teams or tools. This matters because repetition of the same facts across tools is the signal that a hidden pipe exists; the author argues that the real leverage comes from fixing data inputs, not waiting for a smarter model to sort through the mess — skipping this step means you never find the pipe that's begging to be narrowed.

Define the minimal 'decision-grade' core — determine the smallest payload that lets a stakeholder act without chasing links (typically no more than three fields). This matters because the author insists the value is in 'actually thinking about how we handle data inputs to AI, but that takes work'; this step forces that thinking by distinguishing the few fields a stakeholder truly needs from the bulk that creates noise — without it, you feed the model everything and mistake volume for value. (inferred)

Carve a single inlet and label it loudly — create one dedicated channel, database, or sheet with a pinned two-line policy stating what belongs and what does not. This matters because the author's core argument is that 'the best model in careless hands is worse than useless' — a single, clearly labeled inlet is the minimum infrastructure that turns careless hands into disciplined ones, and skipping it guarantees the mixed-purpose input stream that makes AI output read like a random grab bag.

Police the boundary upstream, not downstream — nudge off-topic contributions back to general channels the moment they appear. This matters because the author observes that downstream cleanup never compounds while upstream discipline does; a few seconds of nudging prevents hours of triage, and this step is where human judgement — which the author says we need more of, not less — is applied at the cheapest possible point in the workflow.

Turn on the bundled model and inspect the first output — if the digest is not actionable, tighten the pipe further by shortening the payload, removing formatting noise, or splitting the stream. This matters because the author explicitly warns against chasing model upgrades as the fix; this step distinguishes a data-input problem from a model-capability problem — if the output still isn't actionable, the diagnosis is always 'tighten the pipe,' not 'wait for o3 Pro.'

Let improvements in the engine compound automatically — once the pipe is clean, every platform upgrade improves output without additional integration work. This matters because the author's central thesis is that 'if we took 50% of the passion we put into the latest model and put it into getting our data inputs right we'd get twice the leverage'; a clean pipe is what converts each new model release from hype into free, compounding gains — skipping upstream discipline means every upgrade requires yet another round of integration work.

source_posts.title: Stop Waiting for New AI Models: Here's How to Use Data to Make AI at Work, WORK

frameworks.example_application: The team's Slack channel AI summary is useless — it reads like a random grab bag because the channel mixes project updates, watercooler chat, and client escalations. The same client name and status gets restated across Slack, email, and a shared doc. That repetition is the signal: there's a hidden pipe. The decision-grade payload is three fields — client name, issue type, and current status. A dedicated #client-escalations channel with a two-line pinned policy ('Only post: client name, issue summary, and severity. Everything else stays in #general.') carves the inlet. After one week, Slack's built-in summarize feature produces a daily digest that's immediately actionable — no downstream triage, no manual reformatting — and when Slack ships its next AI upgrade, the output gets better for free.
do_not_use_when: The user's AI output quality problem stems from a poorly configured LLM prompt or wrong model choice, not from mixed-purpose input data.
The user needs to consolidate tools entirely because the organization has too many overlapping platforms, not just narrow what flows into them.
The user is dealing with a one-time data migration or audit, not a recurring workflow where pipe discipline compounds value over time.
The noise in the user's channels is caused by team behavior or culture issues that require change management, not structural data routing fixes.
frameworks.description_original: A six-step process for applying the Narrow-Pipe Law to any repetitive workflow, converting noisy mixed-purpose data sources into clean, single-purpose input streams that maximize the value of bundled AI tools.

Police the boundary upstream, not downstream — nudge off-topic contributions back to general channels the moment they appear

frameworks.name: Second-Use Litmus
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is misreading early AI adoption signals as product-market fit. Challenge their assumption that launch-day enthusiasm proves lasting value — first-use curiosity is cheap. Push them to prove second-use loyalty by examining Day-2, Week-2, and Month-1 cohort retention, and force the question: would users scream if this feature disappeared tomorrow, or did they build a press release?
when_to_apply: Our AI feature had a huge launch week but usage is dropping off a cliff and I'm not sure if it's a retention problem or a product problem
Leadership wants to scale our AI pilot based on strong early adoption numbers, but I'm skeptical the engagement is real
I need to set success metrics for an AI product launch that actually predict long-term value, not just hype
Users say they love our AI tool in surveys but the usage data tells a different story — trying to figure out what's actually happening
We're debating whether to invest more in an AI feature that got great press coverage but I want to know if it's actually sticky
principles: First-use curiosity is cheap; second-use loyalty is expensive — measure the latter
By session two, the bar shifts from 'Can it do something cool?' to 'Will it remove real friction every time?'
A product must deliver a 10× job improvement, not a 10-second magic show
Reliability must be proven before dependence is asked for
Measure retention in cohorts (Day-2, Week-2, Month-1), not anecdotes
If users wouldn't scream if the feature disappeared tomorrow, you built a press release, not a product

source_posts.title: Six AI Product Principles No One Tells You—And How I'm Applying Them in My Build

frameworks.example_application: The AI writing assistant launched to 5,000 users and hit 73% activation on Day 1 — but that's first-use curiosity, not signal. Day-7 cohort retention is 9%, and of the users who came back, session depth dropped 60%. The product delivered a magic trick, not a workflow improvement. The core job — 'help me write faster without sacrificing my voice' — isn't being done reliably enough for users to trust it with real work. The fix isn't better onboarding or more features; it's making the base generation accurate enough on the second draft that users stop reverting to their old process.
do_not_use_when: The AI product has no repeat-use design by nature (e.g., a one-time onboarding wizard), so second-use retention is structurally irrelevant.
Usage drop is already explained by a known external cause (seasonal demand, discontinued marketing spend), not product-market fit ambiguity.
The team needs to decide whether to build the AI feature at all, not evaluate an existing product's stickiness post-launch.
The 'AI product' is a B2B workflow tool with 6-month procurement cycles where Day-2 retention metrics are contractually and operationally meaningless.
frameworks.description_original: A test that evaluates whether an AI product delivers lasting utility by measuring whether users return after novelty wears off, rather than judging success by launch-day metrics.

frameworks.name: Trust Loops
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user's AI product is leaking trust after launch. Evaluate their design against four criteria: does the system show its work, escalate without friction, allow instant rollback, and measure regret? Push them to prove each criterion exists in the current build — most founders treat these as polish, not infrastructure, and that's where the credibility meter resets.
when_to_apply: Users are dropping off my AI feature after initial adoption and I can't figure out why engagement decays
We're about to ship an AI-powered feature and I need to decide which transparency and safety controls actually matter for the MVP
Our AI product works well 90% of the time but the 10% failure cases are destroying user confidence
I'm replacing a human-staffed workflow with AI automation and need to design for the moments when the AI gets it wrong
Support tickets are spiking around our AI feature and users keep saying they don't trust the outputs
principles: Every interaction with an LLM can reset the credibility meter, so trust loops must be built first, not added later
Show its work: citations, retrieval breadcrumbs, or source peeks
Escalate without friction: one-click handoff to a human with full context preserved
Allow instant rollback: version history and undo must be as prominent as the primary action
Measure regret: every correction, escalation, or abandoned session feeds back into improvement and KPI dashboards
Trust isn't a milestone; it's a heartbeat you have to keep nudging

source_posts.title: Six AI Product Principles No One Tells You—And How I'm Applying Them in My Build

frameworks.example_application: This AI draft-writing tool scores poorly on the Trust Loop dimensions. Show-its-work: zero — it produces outputs with no citations or reasoning trace, so users can't distinguish a confident hallucination from a grounded answer. Escapability: weak — escalating to a human editor requires opening a separate support ticket, which means context is lost and friction is high. Rollback: nonexistent — there's no version history, so a user who hits 'apply suggestions' on a bad rewrite has no recovery path. Regret measurement: absent — the team tracks adoption and session length but has no signal on corrections, abandoned outputs, or escalation frequency. The result is predictable: the product feels magical in demos but bleeds users after week two, because the first wrong answer has no trust infrastructure to absorb the shock.
do_not_use_when: The AI feature has never launched yet and the trust concern is hypothetical, making the framework's feedback-loop mechanics premature and irrelevant.
User drop-off is caused by a pricing or onboarding UX problem unrelated to AI outputs, so trust-loop instrumentation won't address the actual retention failure.
The AI system operates fully autonomously in a closed industrial process with no human-facing interface, so transparency and escalation controls have no surface to attach to.
The leader is evaluating whether to build an AI product at all, requiring a build-vs-buy or ROI framework rather than design requirements for a system that doesn't exist.
frameworks.description_original: A four-part design requirement for AI products that maintains user trust across probabilistic interactions by making the system's reasoning visible, escapable, reversible, and self-correcting.

frameworks.name: Show the Invisible Delta
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user's AI product is delivering value that stakeholders can't see or articulate. Shift their framing from "how do we report ROI" to "how does the product surface the delta in real time at the point of use." Push them to instrument the UI to display time saved, errors prevented, and cognitive load reduced — session by session — so the product proves its own worth without a slide deck.
when_to_apply: Our AI feature is saving people hours per week but leadership keeps asking what it actually does
Designing the in-product experience for an AI tool and deciding what the user should see after each interaction
An AI product just got cut from the budget despite strong usage — trying to figure out what went wrong
Building an enterprise AI product and need to preempt the 'prove your ROI' conversation before renewal
Users say they like the AI tool but can't articulate why when asked by their manager
principles: Hidden value gets cut; surface the delta in real time at the point of use
Instrument the product to display time saved, errors prevented, and revenue protected — in the UI, not just the slide deck
If the product can't prove its own worth at the point of use, it hasn't earned the second use
Users internalize value when they see the scoreboard tick upward session by session
Much AI ROI lies in shaved cognitive load that never appears in a payroll spreadsheet unless surfaced explicitly

source_posts.title: Six AI Product Principles No One Tells You—And How I'm Applying Them in My Build

frameworks.example_application: The conventional read is that ROI measurement is a finance problem — you gather the data, build the dashboard, present it quarterly. That's wrong here because by the time someone opens a spreadsheet to justify the tool's cost, the user who benefited has already forgotten the value and the budget holder never felt it. The fix is structural: the product itself must surface 'You just saved 14 minutes' or 'This caught 3 errors your team would have shipped' directly in the workflow, every session. When the CFO asks whether to renew, the answer isn't in a slide deck — it's in the muscle memory of forty users who watched a scoreboard tick upward every day. The invisible cognitive load reduction — the thing that never shows up on a payroll line — only becomes defensible spend when the product makes it visible at the moment it happens.
do_not_use_when: The AI tool is a back-end data pipeline with no user-facing interface, so there is no UI surface to instrument for real-time value display.
Leadership already has dashboards showing ROI clearly but distrusts the underlying model assumptions — a measurement visibility problem, not a surfacing one.
The product is in early prototype with fewer than 10 users, and adding value-display instrumentation would consume engineering cycles needed to validate core functionality first.
The budget cut was caused by a vendor contract dispute, not by stakeholders failing to perceive value, so reframing the in-product experience won't address the actual decision.
frameworks.description_original: Reframes AI ROI measurement by requiring the product itself to surface its own impact in real time at the point of use, rather than leaving value invisible until a quarterly finance review.

frameworks.name: Memetic Defense
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user is reacting to an AI claim before consulting primary sources. Challenge their assumption that emotional resonance is a signal of credibility — the meme lands before the evidence does. Push them to prove the claim across three axes: proof of work, proof of cost, and proof of time to utility. What generic skepticism misses is the announcement-to-reality gap and the missing baseline.
when_to_apply: A headline about an AI breakthrough is making me feel either excited or anxious and I haven't looked at any primary sources yet
A vendor or executive is quoting a dramatic efficiency gain but I can't find a reproducible demo or independent verification
I keep seeing the same AI success story repeated across outlets but no one links to actual data or follow-up coverage
Media coverage of an AI risk — energy consumption, job displacement, existential threat — feels urgent but I don't know what baseline they're comparing against
I'm about to share or act on a claim and realize I haven't asked myself what evidence would change my mind about it
principles: The meme lands before the evidence does — slow down the emotional response before forming a judgment
Always ask for a real baseline and what is being compared, not just the absolute claim

Demand proof across three axes: proof of work (demos, not declarations), proof of cost (real implementation costs, not launch slides), and proof of time to utility (honest timelines, not transformation myths)
Distinguish real case studies from repeated memes by checking whether outcomes are reproducible and whether announcements were later retracted or quietly revised
Practice constructive skepticism: explicitly ask 'what would make me change my mind?' to stay open to new evidence while resistant to unexamined narrative momentum
Build filters, not walls — the goal is faster understanding, not blanket rejection of new ideas
steps: Notice the emotional trigger: identify when a claim is landing in your 'lizard brain' before you've had a chance to think. This matters because the author identifies that AI hype is memetic — the emotionally gripping narrative lands first and short-circuits our ability to think well, so if you don't catch the emotional hit before it becomes a judgment, the meme has already infected your reasoning.

Demand a baseline: ask what the claim is being compared to and what context is missing. This matters because the author shows that without a real baseline, distortions persist — most people vastly overestimate AI energy use while underestimating familiar activities like watching an NFL game, not because of data, but because the meme sticks before anyone asks 'what's the real baseline? What's being compared? What's missing?'

Apply the three-axis proof test: evaluate whether the claim provides proof of work (demo or reproducible result), proof of cost (full implementation cost, not just launch), and proof of time to utility (realistic timeline to measurable value). This matters because the author argues that slides and sizzle reel videos carry more weight than reproducible outcomes unless you explicitly demand demos not declarations, real implementation costs not launch tweets, and honest timelines not transformation myths — skipping any axis lets success theater pass as evidence.

Check the announcement-to-reality gap: look for follow-up coverage, retractions, or quieted claims that contradict the original narrative. This matters because the author highlights the Klarna case — they announced replacing 700 CS agents with AI only to quietly backtrack when results didn't materialize — showing that gaps between announcement and reality aren't just footnotes but crucial checkpoints that distinguish real case studies from repeated memes.

State your update condition: articulate what evidence would cause you to change your mind, ensuring your skepticism remains constructive and open rather than reflexively dismissive. This matters because the author calls this the true heart of memetic defense — surfacing the specific evidence you'd need to shift your view builds epistemic resilience and keeps you open to new information while resistant to unexamined narrative momentum, building filters rather than walls.

source_posts.title: There is Too Much AI Hype—This is How To Defend Your Brain and Stay Calm

frameworks.example_application: The claim that Company X 'replaced 80% of its customer service team with AI' fails all three proof axes. Proof of work: no demo or reproducible benchmark, just a CEO quote in a press release. Proof of cost: no mention of the integration costs, hallucination remediation, or human escalation layer they certainly still run. Proof of time to utility: the announcement is three weeks old with zero follow-up confirming sustained results. This is success theater — a meme optimized for LinkedIn virality, not an evidence-backed case study. The update condition: if they publish six-month CSAT scores and net cost data with methodology, the claim becomes evaluable.
do_not_use_when: The user has already reviewed primary sources and peer-reviewed benchmarks and needs help interpreting technical methodology, not filtering hype.
The user is a researcher who produced the study being cited and needs help communicating findings accurately, not auditing their own work for meme propagation.
The user must make an irreversible procurement decision in hours and already has verified vendor data — skepticism scaffolding will delay action without adding information.
The user is emotionally distressed about job loss from automation they already experienced — applying epistemic filters to their lived situation would be dismissive and clinically inappropriate.
frameworks.description_original: A structured approach to building cognitive immunity against viral narratives and hype by demanding evidence across three axes before accepting a claim.
steps_original: Notice the emotional trigger: identify when a claim is landing in your 'lizard brain' before you've had a chance to think
Demand a baseline: ask what the claim is being compared to and what context is missing

Apply the three-axis proof test: evaluate whether the claim provides proof of work (demo or reproducible result), proof of cost (full implementation cost, not just launch), and proof of time to utility (realistic timeline to measurable value)
Check the announcement-to-reality gap: look for follow-up coverage, retractions, or quieted claims that contradict the original narrative
State your update condition: articulate what evidence would cause you to change your mind, ensuring your skepticism remains constructive and open rather than reflexively dismissive

frameworks.name: Three-Zone Wall Map
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user suspects their codebase has fake boundaries — folders that suggest layered architecture but don't enforce it. Challenge their assumption that working code means sound architecture. Push them to prove every hop crosses a new color zone, that SQL is confined to orange, and that no interface layer imports directly from storage — the violations worth finding are the ones hiding behind clean folder names.
when_to_apply: I generated a whole app with an LLM and it works, but I have no idea if the architecture is actually sound or just a pile of working code
Our codebase has folders named 'services' and 'repositories' but I suspect components are reaching across layers anyway
I'm about to split a monolith into services and need to know where the real boundaries are versus where we pretend they are
A PR touches five different layers and I need a fast way to check if it's violating architectural boundaries without reading every line
SQL queries or HTTP calls keep showing up in places they shouldn't be and I want to systematically find every instance
principles: Every hop should cross into a new color zone — same-zone jumps or zone skips are smells
Config files (docker-compose, serverless.yml) reveal which external systems exist; each should map to a thin adapter folder
Direct imports from storage into interface layers (e.g., UI importing DB calls) indicate a missing wall
A boundary violation is a design smell even if the code works today
Boundaries matter more than elegant function bodies
steps: Take your breadcrumb trail from the datum safari and color-code each hop: Blue = Interface, Green = Business Logic, Orange = Storage. This matters because autocomplete can flood a project with thousands of lines overnight, but it can't tell you whether a silent failure is hiding in that flood — color-coding each hop forces you to actually see the structure you've created rather than assuming it's sound.

Plot the hops left-to-right on paper or a whiteboard. This matters because reading code means making invisible structure visible; a spatial layout reveals zone skips and same-zone loops that are impossible to spot when you're just scrolling files, and skipping this step lets cosmetic folder names substitute for real understanding. (inferred)

Scan the repo directory tree and label folders with the corresponding colors. This matters because the author warns that working code and clean folder names create false confidence — labeling folders forces you to confront whether the 'architecture' is cosmetic (like the example's empty service/ folder) or actually participates in the request path.

Compare: does every hop traverse a new color? Flag any Orange → Blue or Blue → Orange direct jumps. This matters because a boundary violation is a design smell even if the code works today — the example shows an Express route handler (blue) importing Prisma directly (orange), skipping business logic entirely, which is exactly the kind of brittle bridge the author says reading skill lets you spot before it causes a future outage.

Check config files for external systems and verify each has a corresponding thin adapter folder. This matters because config files like docker-compose reveal which external systems actually exist; the example shows Redis and S3 connections with no adapter folders, meaning those clients are instantiated inline across dozens of files — skipping this step hides the surgery cost of any future swap. (inferred)

Run a grep for cross-zone imports (e.g., UI importing from db/) to confirm or deny wall integrity. This matters because the author's core argument is that being able to scan lines and spot the brittle bridge is now the rare skill — a mechanical grep catches direct storage-to-interface imports that hide behind clean folder names and that manual reading alone might miss.

Ask three boundary-stress questions: Is auth centralized in one layer? Is SQL confined to the storage zone? Are HTTP calls absent from business logic? This matters because boundaries matter more than elegant function bodies — these questions force you to prove structural integrity rather than assuming it, embodying the author's principle that reading code to understand its actual behavior is profoundly more valuable than trusting that working output equals sound design.

source_posts.title: Taming the Genie: How to Read the Code You Just Wished Into Existence

frameworks.example_application: Coloring the hops from the API controller through to the database reveals the problem: the Express route handler (blue) imports the Prisma client directly (orange), skipping the business logic layer entirely. There's no green hop in between. The service/ folder exists but nothing in the request path touches it — the 'architecture' is cosmetic. Meanwhile, docker-compose shows Redis and S3 connections, but neither has an adapter folder; those clients are instantiated inline wherever they're needed, which means swapping storage backends later will require surgery across dozens of files.
do_not_use_when: The user has a single-file script or small utility under ~500 lines where layered architecture would add ceremony with no benefit.
The codebase is a data pipeline or ETL job where storage-to-storage hops are intentional and zone-crossing is expected by design.
The user is diagnosing a performance bottleneck or memory leak, not an architectural boundary problem, despite mentioning 'layers' feeling slow.
The user is evaluating whether to rewrite the codebase in a new language or framework, making current boundary violations irrelevant to the decision.
frameworks.description_original: A color-coded boundary audit that classifies each folder and hop in a codebase as Interface (blue), Business Logic (green), or Storage (orange), then checks whether data ever jumps zones illegally.
steps_original: Take your breadcrumb trail from the datum safari and color-code each hop: Blue = Interface, Green = Business Logic, Orange = Storage
Plot the hops left-to-right on paper or a whiteboard
Scan the repo directory tree and label folders with the corresponding colors
Compare: does every hop traverse a new color? Flag any Orange → Blue or Blue → Orange direct jumps
Check config files for external systems and verify each has a corresponding thin adapter folder
Run a grep for cross-zone imports (e.g., UI importing from db/) to confirm or deny wall integrity
Ask three boundary-stress questions: Is auth centralized in one layer? Is SQL confined to the storage zone? Are HTTP calls absent from business logic?

frameworks.name: Three-Question Bridge Drill
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user needs a fast risk picture across service boundaries without reading business logic. Push back on the assumption that silent failures are rare — the common blind spot is empty catch blocks and unguarded calls hiding on revenue-critical paths. What this reveals that generic advice misses: a labeled heatmap of Clean & Loud, Synchronous Gamble, and Silent Drop bridges before any fixes are attempted.
when_to_apply: I just generated a bunch of code with AI and need to quickly find where it might fail silently across service boundaries
We have multiple microservices calling each other and I want a fast risk picture without reading every line of business logic
After an incident where something failed silently, I need to audit all the boundary crossings in the affected path
I'm preparing for a design review and need to surface which integrations are missing error handling, timeouts, or input validation
Our codebase has grown through rapid prototyping and I suspect there are empty catch blocks and unguarded API calls hiding everywhere
principles: Ask three questions per bridge: Is input validated before the hop? Is there a timeout or retry if the next hop stalls? How does failure surface to the caller or user?
Label each bridge with a three-word verdict: 'Clean & Loud,' 'Synchronous Gamble,' or 'Silent Drop'
An empty catch block is the clearest signal of a Silent Drop
A synchronous network call with no timeout is a Synchronous Gamble regardless of how rarely it fails
The goal is a heatmap of bridges, not a fix list — surface first, solve later
steps: List every arrow (hop) in your breadcrumb trail. This matters because autocomplete can flood a project with thousands of lines overnight and you can't spot a brittle bridge if you haven't first mapped every boundary where code crosses from one service to another — the silent failures hide in the hops you never enumerated.

For each hop, ask: Is input validated before crossing? (search for validate, schema, regex near the call). This matters because without validation, malformed data flows silently downstream — as in the example where the tax API response feeds directly into the invoice generator with no schema validation, causing invoices to render with zero tax and no alert. Skipping this step leaves you blind to the exact entry point where bad data poisons a revenue-critical path.

For each hop, ask: Is there a timeout or retry wrapper? (search for timeout, retry, backoff near the call). This matters because a synchronous network call with no timeout is a Synchronous Gamble regardless of how rarely it fails — as the author illustrates, if the tax service stalls, the checkout thread blocks indefinitely. This step distinguishes hops that can hang your system from those that fail fast.

For each hop, ask: How does failure surface? (look for error return, log call, or catch block — flag empty catch blocks). This matters because an empty catch block is the clearest signal of a Silent Drop — the single silent failure hiding in the flood that autocomplete can't tell you about, which the author identifies as the core danger of AI-generated code that nobody reviewed.

Label each bridge: 'Clean & Loud' (validation + timeout + clear error), 'Synchronous Gamble' (no timeout/retry), or 'Silent Drop' (missing validation and empty catch). This matters because the three-word verdict forces a concrete distinction between bridges that fail safely, bridges that can hang, and bridges that swallow errors — preventing the common blind spot where developers assume silent failures are rare and skip straight to fixes without understanding the failure mode.

Compile the labels into a risk heatmap and identify which Silent Drops are on revenue-critical paths. This matters because the goal is a heatmap of bridges, not a fix list — surface first, solve later. As the author argues, being able to scan lines, spot the brittle bridge, and ask the one question that saves a future outage is the rare skill; this step channels that skill into prioritization by pairing failure mode with business impact, as in the example where two flawed bridges on the payment-to-invoice path demand immediate attention before a traffic spike.

source_posts.title: Taming the Genie: How to Read the Code You Just Wished Into Existence

frameworks.example_application: The payment service calls the tax calculation API, and that call has no timeout — if the tax service stalls, the checkout thread blocks indefinitely. That's a Synchronous Gamble on a revenue-critical path. Worse, the response from the tax API feeds directly into the invoice generator with no schema validation and an empty catch block wrapping the whole thing — that's a Silent Drop. If the tax API returns malformed data, the invoice silently renders with zero tax and nobody gets alerted. Two bridges, both on the critical path, both need immediate attention before the holiday traffic spike.
do_not_use_when: The user has a monolithic single-process application with no network calls or service boundaries, making bridge classification meaningless.
The user wants to fix a known silent failure immediately, not map risk across boundaries — the heatmap output delays the remediation they need.
The user is auditing data privacy compliance across microservices, where regulatory and data-flow concerns require a different lens than error-handling classification.
The user is evaluating whether to migrate from a monolith to microservices, so boundaries don't yet exist and cannot be interrogated.
frameworks.description_original: A rapid three-question interrogation applied to every boundary crossing (bridge) in a codebase to classify each as 'Clean & Loud,' 'Synchronous Gamble,' or 'Silent Drop,' producing a risk heatmap without parsing algorithmic code.
steps_original: List every arrow (hop) in your breadcrumb trail
For each hop, ask: Is input validated before crossing? (search for validate, schema, regex near the call)
For each hop, ask: Is there a timeout or retry wrapper? (search for timeout, retry, backoff near the call)
For each hop, ask: How does failure surface? (look for error return, log call, or catch block — flag empty catch blocks)
Label each bridge: 'Clean & Loud' (validation + timeout + clear error), 'Synchronous Gamble' (no timeout/retry), or 'Silent Drop' (missing validation and empty catch)
Compile the labels into a risk heatmap and identify which Silent Drops are on revenue-critical paths

frameworks.name: Proxy Signal Reading
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user needs to assess structural risk in a codebase without reading logic. Challenge their assumption that architectural health requires deep code review — push them to prove the problem exists first using ERROR log frequency, network-to-retry ratio, import cycles, and field blast radius. These four signals reveal what generic advice misses: coupling and resilience failures that are invisible until something breaks.
when_to_apply: I just inherited a large codebase and need to know where the structural risks are before I start changing anything
My team has been using AI to generate a lot of code and I'm worried the architecture is quietly degrading
I need hard numbers to bring to a meeting about technical debt — not just a feeling that things are messy
I want a repeatable weekly health check I can run on a growing codebase without spending hours in the code
I'm reviewing a repo I can't run locally and need to assess its resilience and coupling from the source alone
principles: Signals are language-free and fast — they surface patterns in minutes, not hours
Four signals: ERROR log frequency (observability), network calls vs. retry wrappers (resilience), dependency graph cycles (coupling), and field search hit count (blast radius)
Numbers travel better in meetings than vibes — quantify every signal
Multiple signals singing the same song constitute strong evidence even without reading functions
Use browser search and the project's own tooling; no terminal required for the core technique
steps: Run the app and search logs for ERROR — count frequency and note which components produce them. This matters because the author insists that autocomplete can flood a project with thousands of lines overnight but 'can't tell you whether a single silent failure is hiding in that flood' — ERROR log frequency is the fastest way to surface those silent failures without reading a single function.

Count network calls (search for fetch, axios, http.get) vs. explicit retry wrappers (search for retry, backoff) — compute the ratio. This matters because the example application shows a 16:1 ratio meaning '94% of network calls will fail hard on any transient issue' — this ratio reveals resilience gaps that are completely invisible in normal operation and only catastrophic when something breaks. (inferred)

Pull the dependency graph (using a tool like depcruise or the IDE's built-in view) and look for red cycles between boundary zones. This matters because the author's core argument is that reading code is about being able to 'spot the brittle bridge and ask the one question that saves a future outage' — import cycles are exactly those brittle bridges, revealing structural coupling that guarantees cascading failures when one module changes.

Pick one field from your datum safari and count how many files reference it — this is its blast radius. This matters because the example shows a single email field appearing in 31 files across 4 boundary zones, making 'any schema change to that field a guaranteed multi-team incident' — this step quantifies the hidden cost of a change that no amount of function-level reading would reveal as quickly. (inferred)

Summarize all four signals in one sentence: '[N] outbound calls, [M] retries, [X] import cycles, field referenced in [Y] places — risk profile: [high/medium/low]'. This matters because the author emphasizes that 'numbers travel better in meetings than vibes' and that 'multiple signals singing the same song constitute strong evidence even without reading functions' — collapsing all four into one sentence gives you a defensible, quantified risk profile you can present to a team instead of a gut feeling.

source_posts.title: Taming the Genie: How to Read the Code You Just Wished Into Existence

frameworks.example_application: Scanning a 60k-line Node.js repo reveals 47 outbound fetch/axios calls but only 3 retry wrappers — a 16:1 ratio that means 94% of network calls will fail hard on any transient issue. The dependency graph shows two red cycles between the auth module and the data layer, confirming tight coupling. The user's email field appears in 31 files across 4 boundary zones, so any schema change to that field is a guaranteed multi-team incident. Risk profile: high — resilience is nearly absent, coupling is structural, and blast radius on core fields is dangerously wide.
do_not_use_when: The codebase is a single-file script under 500 lines with no external dependencies, where graph and retry-wrapper analysis would find nothing meaningful.
The user wants to assess architectural risk in a data pipeline that has no network calls or retry logic, making resilience and observability signals inapplicable.
The concern is about business logic correctness or domain model accuracy, not structural coupling — signals can't reveal whether the code does the right thing.
The repo is brand-new with fewer than two weeks of commits, so log noise and dependency patterns haven't had time to form meaningful baselines.
frameworks.description_original: A set of four language-agnostic signals (log noise, dependency graph shape, field blast radius, and retry coverage) that reveal architectural health without reading source code logic.
steps_original: Run the app and search logs for ERROR — count frequency and note which components produce them
Count network calls (search for fetch, axios, http.get) vs. explicit retry wrappers (search for retry, backoff) — compute the ratio
Pull the dependency graph (using a tool like depcruise or the IDE's built-in view) and look for red cycles between boundary zones
Pick one field from your datum safari and count how many files reference it — this is its blast radius
Summarize all four signals in one sentence: '[N] outbound calls, [M] retries, [X] import cycles, field referenced in [Y] places — risk profile: [high/medium/low]'

frameworks.name: Break-It-Watch-It Runtime Fieldwork
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user has an architectural suspicion but lacks runtime proof. Challenge their assumption that static analysis or demo behavior is sufficient evidence — the system has not failed in front of them yet. Push them to run the three core experiments (network offline, throttled resource, malformed input) and package each outcome as a screenshot plus two numbers before drawing conclusions.
when_to_apply: I traced the architecture and spotted what looks like a synchronous dependency with no fallback, but I need proof it actually breaks at runtime
Stakeholders don't believe the system is fragile because it works fine in demos — I need a concrete failure I can show them
An AI tool generated an integration and I want to verify error handling actually exists before merging it
The app has no observability and I want to find out what happens when a downstream service goes silent
I can see validation code in the frontend but I'm not sure whether bad data is also being caught before it hits the database
principles: Three core experiments: network offline (graceful degradation), throttled database (synchronous bottleneck), and malformed input (validation layer placement)
An infinite spinner with no log output is proof of both a synchronous bottleneck and weak observability simultaneously
Silence after sabotage is as informative as an error — it means the team is flying blind
Map runtime failures back to your breadcrumb diagram with red exclamation marks — learning by scar tissue
Screenshot + two numbers (e.g., '0 retries, 25-second hang') is sufficient evidence for non-technical audiences
steps: Experiment A — Network Offline: Open the app in a browser, enable Offline mode in DevTools, submit the target form, observe whether the response is a graceful error banner or an infinite spinner with no logs. This matters because an infinite spinner with no log output is proof of both a synchronous bottleneck and weak observability simultaneously — it reveals exactly the kind of 'silent failure hiding in the flood' that the author warns autocomplete cannot detect for you, and that only surfaces when you force the system to break at runtime.

Experiment B — Throttled Resource: Limit your database container CPU (e.g., docker update --cpus='.2'), submit several requests quickly, observe response times in the Network tab for timeout behavior vs. async acceptance; revert after. This matters because this step distinguishes synchronous bottlenecks from properly async architectures — without it you'd never know whether a dependency slowdown cascades into a user-facing hang, which is the 'brittle bridge' the author says you must spot before it causes a future outage. (inferred)

Experiment C — Malformed Input: Submit invalid data (e.g., not-an-email in an email field), then check the database viewer to determine whether the bad data was stored (validation in wrong layer) or rejected (interface wall working). This matters because it reveals whether validation lives in the right architectural layer or is silently absent — the author emphasizes that AI-generated code can look correct on the surface while hiding structural flaws, and skipping this step means you'd miss bad data flowing past what you assumed was a boundary.

Map each failure outcome back to the specific breadcrumb hop where the break occurred. This matters because the author's core argument is that reading and understanding the structures you've created is the compounding skill — mapping runtime failures to specific architectural hops transforms a vague 'something broke' into precise knowledge of which connection is the brittle bridge, turning scar tissue into durable understanding.

Package evidence as a screenshot + two numbers and a sentence starting 'If X fails, Y happens…'. This matters because the author frames code-reading as the rare skill that bridges technical reality and decision-making — a screenshot plus two concrete numbers (e.g., '0 retries, 45-second hang') translates a silent failure that only you can see into evidence legible to non-technical audiences, ensuring the finding actually drives action rather than getting dismissed as a hunch.

source_posts.title: Taming the Genie: How to Read the Code You Just Wished Into Existence

frameworks.example_application: The checkout form depends on a third-party payment API, and the code shows no retry logic or timeout handling. After toggling DevTools to Offline mode and submitting an order, the UI hangs on an infinite spinner for 45 seconds with zero log output — confirming both a synchronous bottleneck and complete observability blindness. The evidence package is a screenshot showing the frozen spinner plus '0 retries, 45-second hang' — that's enough to make the case to the product lead that this integration needs a circuit breaker and fallback UX before launch.
do_not_use_when: The user wants to stress-test a production system at scale — deliberate sabotage risks real user harm and requires load-testing tools instead.
The system isn't running yet and only exists as design documents, so there is no live runtime to sabotage or observe.
The suspected fragility is in a third-party SaaS API the team doesn't control, making component-level sabotage impossible and vendor SLA review more appropriate.
The user already has distributed tracing and error logs confirming the failure point — evidence exists and diagnosis is complete, so no sabotage experiment is needed.
frameworks.description_original: A structured method of deliberately sabotaging one component of a running application (network, database, input validation) to convert static architectural suspicions into hard runtime evidence.
steps_original: Experiment A — Network Offline: Open the app in a browser, enable Offline mode in DevTools, submit the target form, observe whether the response is a graceful error banner or an infinite spinner with no logs

Experiment B — Throttled Resource: Limit your database container CPU (e.g., docker update --cpus='.2'), submit several requests quickly, observe response times in the Network tab for timeout behavior vs. async acceptance; revert after

Experiment C — Malformed Input: Submit invalid data (e.g., not-an-email in an email field), then check the database viewer to determine whether the bad data was stored (validation in wrong layer) or rejected (interface wall working)
Map each failure outcome back to the specific breadcrumb hop where the break occurred
Package evidence as a screenshot + two numbers and a sentence starting 'If X fails, Y happens…'

frameworks.name: Friction-to-Agent Recognition Pattern
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user recognizes repetitive work but can't identify which tasks are realistic automation candidates. Challenge their assumption that judgment-heavy tasks are the bottleneck — the blind spot is usually that their highest-value targets begin with "Gather," "Check," "Compare," or "Remind" and consume attention without consuming judgment. Push them to prove repetition exists before expanding to volume.
when_to_apply: I just finished my weekly review and realized half my hours went to repetitive information-gathering that didn't require real thinking
A teammate keeps spending hours on 'check this' and 'compare that' tasks and I want to figure out which ones an AI workflow could handle
We have a recurring sync meeting that exists only because someone needs to manually collect and report status updates
I know AI agents could save me time but I don't know which of my actual tasks are realistic candidates versus ones that need too much judgment
I've done the same task identically three weeks in a row and I'm starting to resent it
principles: Any task beginning with 'Gather…', 'Check…', 'Compare…', or 'Remind…' is a strong candidate for automation
Repetitive tasks that consume attention but not judgment are the highest-value targets
The ability to notice friction and translate it into a living prompt is a competitive advantage, not just a productivity tactic
Reliability of one agent beats volume of many; stabilize before expanding
steps: Run one agent today on the task that stings most. This matters because the author's biggest insight is that the leap from reasoning to workflow happens by actually deploying an agentic workflow — not by planning one — and starting with the task that 'stings most' mirrors his principle that reliability of one agent beats volume of many; you prove the concept on the sharpest pain before expanding.

For seven days, log minutes not spent on the chore and note decisions that happened sooner because the agent's note landed unprompted. This matters because the author demonstrates that the real value of agentic workflows is time compression (he compressed a 6-hour task to 1 hour), and logging freed minutes and faster decisions reveals the compounding effect that chat alone never delivered — the shift from 'chat' to 'workflow' the author calls the biggest single jump.

At week's end, scan the previous week's meetings and to-dos for items beginning with 'Gather…', 'Check…', 'Compare…', or 'Remind…'. This matters because the author's core claim is that people underestimate what these models can do, and this scan exposes the blind spot: tasks that consume attention without consuming judgment are hiding in plain sight, disguised as necessary human work, exactly like the rote analysis the author used to spend 6 hours on before agents could one-shot it.

Flag each identified item as a workflow candidate. This matters because without explicitly flagging these items, they stay embedded in to-do lists as 'just part of the job' — the same assumption the author challenges when he shows that models have moved from chat to reasoning to workflow and the biggest gains come from recognizing which tasks belong in that last category. (inferred)

For each candidate, write the four-block spec and deploy one at a time. This matters because the author shows that the most powerful aspect of current models is agentic workflows where inputs, logic, and output destination are already obvious from how the task was done manually — writing a spec forces that clarity, and deploying one at a time mirrors his principle that stabilizing one reliable agent before expanding is what turns a prompt into a durable product rather than a one-off trick.

source_posts.title: Turn ChatGPT into a Sushi Conveyor Belt: 5 Prompts to Automate Workflows that (Seriously) Save Hours

frameworks.example_application: Scanning last week's to-do list reveals three items starting with 'Check…' (check vendor pricing updates, check whether Q3 data landed in the dashboard, check team PTO conflicts for the offsite) and one 'Gather…' (gather competitor feature announcements). None of these required judgment — they consumed attention purely to produce an information payload someone else then acted on. The vendor pricing check stings most: it took 40 minutes Tuesday and delayed a procurement decision by a day. That's the first agent to deploy. The four-block spec writes itself because the inputs, logic, and output destination are already obvious from how the task was done manually.
do_not_use_when: The user's repetitive task requires nuanced stakeholder judgment each iteration, making automation a trust or accountability risk rather than an efficiency opportunity.
The user is asking which AI tools to purchase or evaluate, not which of their existing tasks to automate with prompt workflows.
The recurring meeting exists due to team misalignment or unclear ownership, not information-gathering inefficiency, so restructuring roles would solve it faster than an agent.
The user is a solo founder doing each task only once as part of a one-time product launch, so no true repetition pattern exists to target.

frameworks.name: D-T-R Framework (Distribution, Tokenization, Reward)
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user needs to assess how defensible their AI product is against hyperscaler replication. Score their position across Distribution, Tokenization, and Reward Clarity on a 1–5 scale, then compare against the hyperscaler default of T=5, R=5. Identify which single lever they can realistically max first, push them to commit to widening that gap rather than chasing all three simultaneously — that path is a burn-rate trap.
when_to_apply: OpenAI or Google just announced a feature that overlaps with my product and I need to figure out if we're dead or differentiated
I'm deciding which dimension of my AI product to invest in over the next quarter to maximize defensibility
We're choosing between two market verticals and need to assess which one a hyperscaler is less likely to commoditize
My startup has strong distribution but the underlying AI capability is getting cheaper every month — how do I stay ahead?
I'm evaluating whether to go VC-backed or bootstrapped and need to understand how fast I need to build competitive distance
principles: Distribution (D): Measure how many target users can adopt without a new vendor approval or procurement cycle; score 1–5
Tokenization (T): Measure what fraction of raw data is instantly model-readable text or code; score 1–5
Reward Clarity (R): Measure whether success can be auto-graded without a human in the loop; score 1–5
Hyperscalers default to T=5 and R=5; their Distribution advantage depends on existing channel embeds (e.g., GitHub, Gmail, iOS)
Defensibility requires outscoring the giant on at least one lever, then widening that gap faster than they can close it
Maximize one lever to 5 quickly; raise a second to ≥3 within two quarters; hedge the third with portability
Trying to max all three levers simultaneously is a burn-rate trap

source_posts.title: We killed your startup, lol—what to build when Sam Altman keeps shipping better models
Why the Pipes Suddenly Matter

frameworks.example_application: This startup scores D=4, T=2, R=3. Their distribution is strong — they're embedded in Slack workflows and users adopt without procurement. But their core data is messy clinical notes (T=2), which is actually their defense: hyperscalers default to T=5 domains first, so they won't prioritize this vertical for 18+ months. The play is to lock in distribution to 5 and raise reward clarity to 4 by building auto-grading against clinical outcome codes. Trying to also clean up tokenization right now would be a burn-rate trap — the low T score is a moat, not a weakness.
do_not_use_when: The user's company is not an AI product — they sell physical goods or traditional SaaS and are asking about generic competitive threats from large tech entrants.
The user is asking whether to acquire or partner with a competitor, not how to defend their product's technical dimensions against hyperscaler replication.
The user's startup has no product yet and is still validating a problem space, making defensibility scoring premature and potentially distorting early focus.
The user faces a hyperscaler threat in a heavily regulated industry where distribution is legally restricted, making the D-T-R scoring assumptions about frictionless adoption structurally invalid.
frameworks.description_original: A three-dimensional scoring rubric that assesses how defensible a startup's product is against hyperscaler competition by rating Distribution access, Tokenization readiness, and Reward clarity on a 1–5 scale.

frameworks.name: King Kong Test
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user needs to stress-test defensibility against a hyperscaler entering their space. Challenge their assumption that execution speed is a moat by forcing an honest D-T-R self-score before they score the giant. Push them to prove they outscore on at least one lever — Distribution, Tokenization, or Reward Clarity — because speed without exclusivity is acceleration into a wall.
when_to_apply: OpenAI or Google just announced something uncomfortably close to what we're building and I need to figure out if we're dead
I'm pitching investors next week and need to honestly assess whether our AI product has any defensibility beyond execution speed
We're an AI wrapper startup trying to figure out what we actually own that a platform can't replicate
I need to decide whether to double down on our current product direction or pivot before a hyperscaler enters our vertical
Our competitive moat argument feels hand-wavy and I want a concrete, scoreable stress test
principles: Assume the threat is real and immediate — 'OpenAI ships your product free today'
Score yourself on D-T-R honestly before scoring the giant
Giants automatically get T=5 and R=5; their D score depends on their existing distribution channels
Your defensible beachhead is only the lever where you still outscore them
Speed without exclusivity is acceleration into a wall
Pivot the roadmap — not the pitch deck — when advantage shrinks
steps: Step 1 — Give yourself a brutally honest D-T-R score: rate your Distribution (user activation without vendor approval), Tokenization (fraction of raw data that is model-ready), and Reward Clarity (auto-gradable success) each on a 1–5 scale. This matters because the author warns that builders need a deliberate frame to fall back on when the next model drops and 'changes the game, again' — scoring yourself first prevents the self-delusion that execution speed alone is a moat, revealing where you are genuinely weak before you even look at the giant (as the dental example shows, a hidden T=2 means your data pipeline is trivially replicable).

Step 2 — Clone the giant's likely score: assign T=5 and R=5 to the hyperscaler by default, and estimate their realistic Distribution score based on existing channel embeds. This matters because the author frames the threat as immediate and real — 'Sam Altman keeps shipping better models' and the slide literally says 'we killed your startup' — so defaulting the giant to T=5 and R=5 forces you to internalize that compute-rich players will always out-tokenize and out-label you, and only their distribution gap is uncertain.

Step 3 — Circle the lever where you still outscore them: identify the single D, T, or R dimension where you have a structural advantage. This matters because the author says we're playing 'a board game where a few people are changing the game unpredictably' but 'we can find our own spaces' — this step distinguishes your defensible beachhead from mere feature differentiation, revealing the one dimension where rules don't get reset every time a new model drops. (inferred)

Step 4 — Design a moat-widening sprint: define what you can ship in 90 days to make that lever at least twice as hard to copy (e.g., lock a design partner, deploy edge devices, collect a proprietary reward dataset). This matters because the author insists on thinking 'deliberately' rather than reacting to each model release, and as the dental example shows, even a D=4 advantage decays to commodity within two platform update cycles unless you convert it into a structural asset — speed without exclusivity is acceleration into a wall.

Step 5 — Schedule a re-test trigger: re-run the test quarterly or whenever a major platform files about your vertical; if your advantage shrinks, pivot the roadmap. This matters because the author describes an environment where 'the most important rules' keep getting reset by model drops from OpenAI, Gemini, or DeepSeek — a scheduled re-test prevents you from clinging to a stale advantage, and pivoting the roadmap (not the pitch deck) forces an operational response rather than a narrative one. (inferred)

source_posts.title: We killed your startup, lol—what to build when Sam Altman keeps shipping better models

frameworks.example_application: This startup's D-T-R scores are D=4 (embedded in 200 dental clinics via hardware), T=2 (using generic medical NLP), R=3 (decent outcome labels). The giant's scores: D=2 (no dental channel), T=5, R=5. The surviving lever is Distribution — the physical clinic integration. But T=2 means the product's data pipeline is trivially replicable once a giant partners with a dental SaaS. The 90-day sprint must lock exclusive data-sharing agreements with those 200 clinics and deploy edge inference on-prem, converting distribution access into a proprietary tokenization asset. Without that, the D=4 advantage decays to commodity within two platform update cycles.
do_not_use_when: The user is a solo developer building a niche internal tool for their own company, where there is no commercial competitive threat to stress-test.
The user wants to assess defensibility against a well-funded startup rival, not a hyperscaler, making the giant-vs-startup scoring assumptions structurally invalid.
The user's product is a regulated healthcare or legal AI application where moat analysis is secondary to compliance barriers that platforms cannot easily replicate anyway.
The user has already decided to shut down or pivot and needs acquisition or wind-down advice, not a defensibility diagnostic that assumes the fight is worth having.
