frameworks.name: Mountain Pass Scouting Framework
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user needs to determine whether a vertical niche has structural friction that makes it genuinely defensible against hyperscalers. Challenge their assumption that messiness or regulation alone creates a moat — push them to prove at least two D-T-R levers score hard before they claim the pass is real. What generic advice misses is that temporary underservice looks identical to structural friction until you run the five-test field checklist.
when_to_apply: I have a startup idea in a vertical but I'm worried OpenAI or Google will just ship this as a feature — how do I know if the niche is actually safe?
We're choosing between two industry verticals to build our AI product in and need to figure out which one has real structural friction versus just being underserved temporarily
An investor asked me why a hyperscaler can't replicate what we're building in six months and I don't have a rigorous answer
I'm looking at a messy, regulated industry and trying to figure out if the messiness is a moat or just a sign the market isn't worth entering
My co-founder wants to build a general-purpose AI tool but I think we should go narrow and vertical — I need a framework to evaluate which verticals are actually defensible
principles: Hyperscalers hesitate where data is messy, compliance is thorny, or reward loops require specialist human judgment
A valid mountain pass must have at least one D-T-R lever that is structurally hard for a hyperscaler (D<3, T≤2, or R≤2)
The sector TAM should be large enough to matter (e.g., >$500M) but the wedge small enough for a tiny team to ship fast
Answering 'yes' to any two of the three scouting questions signals defensible terrain
If the map stays flat (no friction answers), keep walking — don't build on open plains
steps: Ask the Distribution Friction question: Where do decision-makers sit behind fragmented channels, procurement hoops, or political approval? This matters because hyperscalers optimize for massive, uniform distribution channels — if reaching buyers requires domain warm intros and navigating fragmented purchasing paths (like the veterinary clinic owner who barely checks email), the go-to-market complexity itself becomes a structural moat that platform companies won't replicate, since they need scale economics that fragmented channels destroy. (inferred)

Ask the Data Stubbornness question: Which critical inputs refuse to convert to clean text — sensors, proprietary file formats, photo or thermal blends? This matters because the author warns that the game resets every time a better model drops, but messy, non-text data like DICOM thermal overlays from eight different ultrasound machines requires custom ETL where 30%+ of raw data fails without it — this is terrain where a foundation model improvement alone cannot collapse your value, since the bottleneck is data ingestion, not intelligence. (inferred)

Ask the Outcome Ambiguity question: Where does quality still require a licensed human to approve — IRB boards, underwriters, compliance officers? This matters because the author frames the core threat as Sam Altman shipping ever-better models that absorb product value — but when a board-certified specialist must sign off for malpractice or compliance reasons, raw model capability gains cannot eliminate the human-in-the-loop cost structure, so a 10x cheaper model barely dents your price and the reward loop stays structurally defended. (inferred)

If two or more answers are 'yes,' run the five-test field checklist: Channel Test (domain warm intros required), Converter Test (30%+ of raw data fails without custom ETL), Oracle Test (removing licensed reviewer drops accuracy below tolerance), Token-Shock Test (10x cheaper model barely dents your price), Exit-Clause Test (customer cannot swap to a hyperscaler in <30 days without retraining or refiling). This matters because the author's central insight is that temporary underservice looks identical to structural friction until you pressure-test it — the field checklist distinguishes a genuine mountain pass from open plains by quantifying switching costs, data pipeline lock-in, and price insensitivity to model improvements, preventing you from building on terrain that evaporates when the next model drops and changes the game again.

source_posts.title: We killed your startup, lol—what to build when Sam Altman keeps shipping better models

frameworks.example_application: The pass is real for this veterinary radiology AI startup. Distribution friction is high — every clinic buys through a different practice management vendor with unique integrations, and the buying committee includes a practice owner who barely checks email. Data stubbornness is severe — the core inputs are DICOM thermal overlays from eight different ultrasound machines, and 30%+ of raw scans fail without custom ETL. Outcome ambiguity is locked in — a board-certified veterinary radiologist must sign off on every diagnosis for malpractice reasons. That's three out of three scouting questions answered yes. Running the field checklist confirms it: Token-Shock Test passes because a 10x cheaper foundation model doesn't change the $85 per-read price driven by specialist review costs, and the Exit-Clause Test passes because switching requires re-filing with state veterinary boards and retraining on clinic-specific DICOM pipelines — that's a 90+ day migration, not a weekend swap.
do_not_use_when: The user is evaluating whether to enter a market where a hyperscaler is already dominant and the question is how to compete, not whether structural friction exists.
The user's startup is a consumer app targeting individuals, where distribution friction and data tokenization barriers are irrelevant because no enterprise compliance layer exists.
The user already has paying customers and traction in a vertical and needs go-to-market or pricing advice, not validation that the niche is structurally defensible.
The user is at a large enterprise deciding whether to build or buy an AI capability internally, where hyperscaler dominance is irrelevant because the product won't be sold externally.
frameworks.description_original: A three-question scouting method for identifying market niches where structural friction in distribution, data tokenization, or reward clarity makes the terrain too costly for hyperscalers to dominate, paired with a five-test field checklist to confirm the pass is real.
steps_original: Ask the Distribution Friction question: Where do decision-makers sit behind fragmented channels, procurement hoops, or political approval?
Ask the Data Stubbornness question: Which critical inputs refuse to convert to clean text — sensors, proprietary file formats, photo or thermal blends?
Ask the Outcome Ambiguity question: Where does quality still require a licensed human to approve — IRB boards, underwriters, compliance officers?

If two or more answers are 'yes,' run the five-test field checklist: Channel Test (domain warm intros required), Converter Test (30%+ of raw data fails without custom ETL), Oracle Test (removing licensed reviewer drops accuracy below tolerance), Token-Shock Test (10x cheaper model barely dents your price), Exit-Clause Test (customer cannot swap to a hyperscaler in <30 days without retraining or refiling)

frameworks.name: Three Bottleneck Framework (Compute, Context, Integration)
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user suspects their AI tool needs an upgrade or replacement. Classify their frustration into exactly one of three bottlenecks — Compute, Context, or Integration — before any tier comparison occurs. Challenge the user's assumption that paying more solves the problem; push them to prove which constraint actually blocks them. The common blind spot is Integration: copy-paste friction masquerading as a compute or context problem.
when_to_apply: I'm hitting limits on my AI tool and I'm not sure if I need a bigger plan or a different tool entirely
I keep copy-pasting data between my apps and ChatGPT and the whole workflow feels broken
My AI chat keeps forgetting what I said earlier in long sessions and I'm wondering if upgrading will fix that
I'm comparing AI subscription tiers and the feature differences all sound the same — I can't tell which one solves my actual problem
I'm paying for multiple AI tools and suspect I'm solving the same problem twice with none of them doing it well
principles: Every AI failure traces to one primary bottleneck: Compute (how many heavy requests you get), Context (how much content the model can hold at once), or Integration (proximity of AI to your data and tools)
Pay to lift the bottleneck that actually blocks you; paying for anything else adds cost without unlocking value
Fix Integration first when multiple bottlenecks appear — moving AI next to your data often eliminates perceived compute and context pain
Compute pain is time-of-day sensitive (vanishes at off-peak hours); context pain is document-size sensitive; integration pain is workflow-topology sensitive
Each pricing tier is designed to relieve one specific constraint — identify which constraint matches your problem before choosing a tier
steps: Observe your AI friction for one day: tally each complaint under C (compute), Cx (context), or In (integration). This matters because with over $700/month in plausible AI costs, you have to say no to something — tallying reveals your actual pattern of pain rather than letting you impulse-upgrade based on a vague sense that your current tool isn't working (inferred).

Check compute: Did you wait for a capacity timer this week? If yes, compute is your bottleneck. This matters because compute pain is time-of-day sensitive and vanishes at off-peak hours — this test distinguishes genuine rate-limit constraints from transient congestion, preventing you from paying more for a problem that might dissolve with a schedule change.

Check context: Did you split a file into parts or lose chat memory mid-session? If yes, context is your bottleneck. This matters because document-size sensitivity is the telltale sign of context limits — as the example shows, a user splitting long contracts into chunks and losing conversation history is experiencing context pain, not compute pain, and upgrading API call volume would waste money.

Check integration: Did copy-paste steal more than 10 minutes a day? If yes, integration is your bottleneck. This matters because integration is the common blind spot — copy-paste friction masquerades as compute or context problems, and as the example application shows, moving AI next to source files (e.g., Copilot embedded in a document management system) can dissolve perceived context pain entirely.

Match your identified bottleneck to the vendor tier that specifically addresses it using the compute-context-integration grid. This matters because each pricing tier is designed to relieve one specific constraint — the author emphasizes that paying for anything other than the bottleneck that actually blocks you adds cost without unlocking value, which is critical when plausible costs exceed $700/month and you have to say no to something.

Apply the ROI formula: (hourly rate × hours saved per month) ÷ monthly plan cost — upgrade only if result exceeds 2×, lock in at 4×. This matters because the author's core question is 'how do you know if you're paying too much or too little?' — this formula converts the bottleneck diagnosis into a concrete spend/don't-spend decision, preventing both overpaying ($200/month for ChatGPT Pro when it's unwarranted) and underpaying when the upgrade would clearly pay for itself (inferred).

source_posts.title: You Will Choose Wisely: The Definitive Guide to Picking (and Paying for) an AI Plan in Q2 2025

frameworks.example_application: The frustration here is context, not compute. The user keeps splitting long contracts into chunks and losing prior conversation history mid-analysis — that's document-size sensitivity, not rate-limit pain. Upgrading to a plan with more API calls per hour would waste money; the fix is a tier (or tool) that extends the context window. Before even spending on that, though, check integration: if they're copy-pasting those contract chunks from a document management system into ChatGPT manually, moving to Copilot embedded in their existing workflow might dissolve the context pain entirely by keeping the AI next to the source files.
do_not_use_when: The user's frustration stems from poor prompt quality or misuse of the tool, not a platform constraint — diagnosis should precede any tier comparison.
The user is evaluating whether to adopt AI at all, not optimizing an existing deployment — bottleneck analysis assumes commitment already made.
The user's bottleneck is organizational (team adoption resistance, governance policy, legal approval) rather than any technical or pricing constraint.

The user needs a completely different AI tool category (e.g., switching from a chat model to a fine-tuned domain-specific system) — tier upgrades within the current tool won't resolve a fundamental capability mismatch.

frameworks.name: AI Subscription ROI Quick-Math
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user questions whether a specific AI subscription is financially justified. Score their situation against the 2×/4× ROI thresholds using their actual hourly rate and hours saved — not vague productivity feelings. Push them to prove the hours-saved number; that's where self-reporting breaks down. This reveals whether they're paying for capability they've stopped using.
when_to_apply: I'm paying for ChatGPT Plus, Claude Pro, and Copilot and I'm not sure which ones are actually worth it
My AI subscription just raised prices and I need to decide if the new cost is still justified
The project that made me subscribe to this AI tool is over and I'm not sure I still need it
I'm considering upgrading from a free tier to a paid AI plan and want to know if the math works
It's end of quarter and I want a quick sanity check on whether my AI tool spending makes sense
principles: ROI = (hourly rate × hours saved per month) ÷ monthly plan cost
Below 2× ROI: downgrade or cancel
Between 2× and 4× ROI: keep but re-evaluate next quarter
Above 4× ROI: lock in; consider switching to annual billing
Re-run the test every quarter because GPU prices fall and context windows expand, changing the denominator and numerator over time
steps: Estimate your effective hourly rate (billing rate for professionals, or time-value estimate for others). This matters because without a concrete dollar-per-hour anchor, ROI devolves into 'vague productivity feelings' — the exact trap the framework exists to prevent; the example application hinges on a specific $150/hour rate to expose that Pro's savings are negligible relative to its cost.

Track hours saved per month attributable to the specific plan. This matters because self-reporting of hours saved is where the math breaks down — people overestimate how much time a tool actually reclaims; skipping this step lets you pay for capability you've stopped using, which is precisely what the $200/month Pro subscription example reveals.

Divide (hourly rate × hours saved) by the monthly plan cost. This matters because this single ratio distinguishes a tool that's earning its keep from one that merely sounds compelling; in the example, this calculation exposes that Pro delivers only 1.4× ROI while Plus would deliver 10×+ — a difference invisible without the math.

Compare the result to the 2×/4× thresholds to make the keep/cancel/upgrade decision. This matters because with over $700/month in plausible AI costs, 'you have to say no to something' — the thresholds force a concrete keep/cancel/downgrade verdict instead of letting subscriptions accumulate; the example shows the right move isn't canceling AI entirely but downgrading and redirecting the $180/month difference.

Repeat the calculation each quarter. This matters because GPU prices fall and context windows expand, changing both the denominator (plan costs shift) and the numerator (capabilities that once required a premium tier get absorbed into cheaper plans), so a plan that scored 4× last quarter may score below 2× this quarter — or vice versa (inferred).

source_posts.title: You Will Choose Wisely: The Definitive Guide to Picking (and Paying for) an AI Plan in Q2 2025

frameworks.example_application: The ChatGPT Pro subscription at $200/month scores 1.4× ROI. At a $150/hour effective rate, it's saving roughly 1.9 hours per month — but the Plus plan at $20/month covers 90% of the same use cases and would score 10×+ ROI on even a single hour saved. The right move isn't canceling AI entirely; it's downgrading to Plus and redirecting the $180/month difference. The Pro-exclusive features (extended thinking, higher rate limits) sound compelling but aren't hitting real workflow hours.
do_not_use_when: The user is evaluating an enterprise AI platform contract with procurement, legal, and IT stakeholders involved, where hourly-rate math drastically understates organizational value.
The user is a student or hobbyist with no billable hourly rate, making time-value ROI calculations meaningless as the core assumption doesn't apply.
The user needs to decide between two AI tools for a specific one-time task this week, where quarterly re-evaluation cycles and thresholds are irrelevant to the immediate decision.
The user's AI subscription cost is trivial relative to their income but they're asking whether the tool produces accurate outputs, which is a quality question not a financial one.
frameworks.description_original: A simple formula and threshold system for deciding whether to keep, upgrade, or cancel an AI subscription based on time-value return.
steps_original: Estimate your effective hourly rate (billing rate for professionals, or time-value estimate for others)
Track hours saved per month attributable to the specific plan
Divide (hourly rate × hours saved) by the monthly plan cost
Compare the result to the 2×/4× thresholds to make the keep/cancel/upgrade decision
Repeat the calculation each quarter

frameworks.name: AI Resume Failure Catalog (9 Categories)
frameworks.description: Apply this catalog when a user can't diagnose why their AI resume isn't landing or can't articulate what they actually did. Check their resume language against the nine failure modes — tool-dumper, buzzword blender, inflated generalist, prompt-as-product illusionist, and the rest — and name which pattern is present. Most users assume the problem is underselling; surface whether they're actually over-owning, disconnecting wins from AI's role, or signaling curiosity without evidence of application.
when_to_apply: I've listed AI tools and projects on my resume but I'm not getting callbacks and I can't figure out why
I'm reviewing a candidate's resume and their AI experience feels impressive but I can't tell what they actually did
I helped build an AI feature at work but I'm not sure how to describe my specific contribution without overclaiming or underclaiming
My resume mentions GPT, LangChain, and RAG but a mentor told me it reads like a buzzword list
I did real AI work but it was a side project, not enterprise-scale — how do I present it without inflating it?
principles: Vague observers describe interest or curiosity without any evidence of application
Tool-dumpers list names without explaining the problem solved or outcome achieved
Inflated generalists use enterprise-scale language for individual or side projects
Undersold real workers did valuable things but described them too generically to be legible
Generic contributors use soft verbs like 'collaborated' without specifying their actual contribution
Buzzword blenders stack jargon to sound technical without clarifying what the AI actually did
Over-owners claim sole credit for team work, which breaks trust in interviews
Disconnected wins cite business outcomes without explaining what role AI played
Prompt-as-product illusionists frame a one-off manual prompt as a shipped product

frameworks.example_application: The active failure mode is 'disconnected wins.' The bullet reads 'Drove 30% increase in customer retention using AI-powered analytics' — but there's no trace of what the AI actually did, what model or tool was involved, or what the candidate's role was in building versus consuming it. The business outcome is real but completely decoupled from any legible AI contribution. The fix isn't removing the metric — it's inserting the mechanism: what AI system, what it did, and what this person specifically built or configured to make it work.

The user is a recruiter asking how to write a job posting that attracts genuine AI talent, not how to read or write a resume.
The user's resume is getting callbacks but they are failing technical screens, making this a skills-gap or interview-prep problem rather than a resume-framing one.

frameworks.name: AI-Assisted Resume Refinement Process
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user wants AI help improving resume content but is getting generic, hollow output. Challenge their assumption that better prompting alone will fix it — the real blind spot is that they're feeding AI polished-but-vague input instead of honest, unpolished substance. Push them to prove the raw material exists before touching any tool.
when_to_apply: I pasted my resume into ChatGPT and everything came back sounding like corporate word soup
I know what I did at work but I can't figure out how to make it sound impressive without lying
I want to tailor the same experience for different job postings without rewriting from scratch each time
I'm preparing for interviews and want to identify the narrative threads across my resume bullets
I'm worried my AI-polished resume will get flagged as generic or trigger AI detection concerns
principles: AI is a writing coach, not a ghostwriter — it needs tight input to produce useful output
Start with honest, unpolished substance before giving anything to an AI tool
Constrained, specific prompts produce better results than open-ended ones like 'make this better'
Use AI to generate optionality (multiple framings) then select and polish manually
The final voice must remain the author's — AI should sharpen, not replace, human expression
Never let AI fabricate outcomes or metrics you did not actually achieve
steps: Write out what you actually did in plain, honest language — no polish, no performance, just the real description as you'd explain it to a colleague. This matters because AI has made it very easy to create a very polished resume, so polish is no longer a signal of quality — starting with honest, unpolished substance is the only way to ensure the raw material contains real differentiating detail rather than the inflated, generic tokens that now flood the talent market.

Give the AI tool specific, constrained instructions naming the desired output format, the role context, and explicit requirements (tool used, task completed, measurable outcome, appropriate tone). This matters because constrained, specific prompts prevent the AI from producing the same hollow, polished-but-vague output that makes every resume look perfect at first glance — naming the tool, task, and measurable outcome forces the kind of concrete specificity that actually stands out when recruiters have seen thousands of AI-era resumes.

Ask the AI to generate 2–3 alternate framings of the same content (e.g., one more technical, one more impact-focused) to find the best fit for the target role. This matters because generating optionality reveals dimensions of your work you might not surface on your own — as shown in the example, the impact framing uncovered a pattern of building self-serve tools that remove bottlenecks, a theme the candidate would have missed with a single polished bullet. (inferred)

Use the AI reflectively: feed in multiple bullets and ask it to identify themes, patterns, or what they reveal about how you work — use this for narrative summaries and interview prep. This matters because in a market where every resume mentions AI and every bullet looks polished, what makes a candidate stand out is a coherent narrative about how they work — this step synthesizes discrete accomplishments into a differentiated story that signals genuine quality beyond the cheap tokens AI has flooded the talent market with.

source_posts.title: The AI Resume Survival Guide (for 2025 and Beyond)

frameworks.example_application: The raw input is 'I built a dashboard in Looker that the sales team used to track pipeline.' Step one produced honest substance. Step two constrains the AI: 'Rewrite this as a resume bullet for a data analyst role. Include the tool (Looker), the task (pipeline visibility for sales), and a measurable outcome (reduced weekly reporting time by 3 hours). Use a direct, non-corporate tone.' Step three generates three framings — one technical ('Designed and deployed a Looker dashboard integrating CRM data...'), one impact-focused ('Eliminated 3 hours/week of manual reporting for a 12-person sales team...'), one hybrid. The technical version fits the target role best but the impact framing surfaces a theme — this person consistently builds self-serve tools that remove bottlenecks. That theme, identified in step four, becomes the backbone of the summary section and a ready-made interview narrative.
do_not_use_when: The user is a recruiter or hiring manager trying to evaluate AI-generated resumes they've received, not improve their own.
The user needs to build a resume from scratch with no prior work history, so the framework's assumption of existing raw material doesn't hold.
The user is asking about optimizing a LinkedIn profile or portfolio site, where tone, format, and platform conventions differ fundamentally from resume bullets.
The user's concern is purely about ATS keyword parsing and formatting rules, not writing quality or voice authenticity.

frameworks.name: AI Detector Risk Mitigation Checklist
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user suspects their resume will be flagged by AI screening tools. Challenge their assumption that polish is the problem — the real issue is low perplexity and low burstiness, not quality. Push them to prove their verbs reflect actual struggle, not safe defaults, and expose where structural repetition is killing rhythm variation in ways generic writing advice would never surface.
when_to_apply: I used ChatGPT to help write my resume and I'm worried it reads like AI wrote it
I ran my resume through an AI detector and it came back flagged — how do I fix it without starting over?
My resume bullets all sound the same — polished but generic — and I'm applying to companies that use automated screening
I want to make sure my resume sounds like me and not like averaged professional prose
Every bullet on my resume follows the same structure and uses words like 'leveraged' and 'utilized'
principles: AI detectors flag predictability (low a search-augmented model) and uniformity (low burstiness), not actual AI use
Overly polished, safe writing scores worse on these metrics than messy, varied human writing
Never paste AI-generated text directly into a resume — always rewrite in your own words
Verb choice is a key signal: tactile, specific verbs (rebuilt, debugged, scrapped) score better than safe ones (leveraged, utilized, enhanced)
Sentence rhythm variation — mixing short punchy phrases with longer complex clauses — increases burstiness
A little imperfection builds credibility; perfect polish raises suspicion
Re-exposing yourself to pre-AI human writing (old blogs, essays, novels) helps recalibrate your natural voice
steps: Run the final resume draft through a publicly available text-classification tool before submitting. This matters because AI has made it trivially easy to produce polished resumes, so recruiters are actively using AI checkers to catch them — you need to see what they'll see before they see it.

Identify which sections scored lowest on perplexity or burstiness. This matters because the problem is rarely the whole resume — it's concentrated in specific sections (like the experience section in the example), and pinpointing where predictability clusters lets you surgically fix what's actually triggering the detector instead of rewriting everything.

Check for structural repetition: are multiple bullets following the same 'Built X using Y to achieve Z' pattern? This matters because AI detectors flag uniformity (low burstiness), and identical syntactic structures across bullets — like 'Leveraged X to enhance Y, resulting in Z% improvement' repeated throughout — are exactly the kind of predictable patterning that signals AI-generated text, not human writing.

Replace safe, generic verbs (leveraged, utilized, developed, enhanced) with verbs that reflect real action and struggle (rebuilt, debugged, restructured, scrapped, retrained). This matters because AI has inflated the supply of cheap, polished tokens — safe verbs are the default output of every AI tool, so they no longer act as a signal of quality; tactile, specific verbs that reflect actual struggle distinguish a real candidate from an AI-generated facade.

Vary sentence rhythm deliberately: mix short fragments with longer, winding clauses; break uniform pacing. This matters because burstiness — the variation between short punchy phrases and longer complex clauses — is a core metric detectors use, and uniform pacing is precisely what AI-polished writing produces; breaking rhythm (e.g., 'Scrapped the old pipeline. Started over.') is what drops the score from flagged to human-passing.

Rewrite any AI-drafted sections in your own voice before finalizing. This matters because the author's core argument is that AI has made every resume look perfect at first glance, destroying the resume's function as a quality signal — pasting AI output directly preserves exactly the low-perplexity, low-burstiness patterns detectors catch, while rewriting in your own voice reintroduces the natural imperfection and variation that builds credibility.

source_posts.title: The AI Resume Survival Guide (for 2025 and Beyond)

frameworks.example_application: The resume scores 87% AI-likelihood. The problem is concentrated in the experience section: every bullet follows 'Leveraged X to enhance Y, resulting in Z% improvement' — identical syntactic structure, safe verbs, no variation in sentence length. Replacing 'leveraged' with 'rebuilt,' 'enhanced' with 'overhauled,' breaking two bullets into short fragments ('Scrapped the old pipeline. Started over.'), and varying clause length drops the score to 31%. The perplexity issue was structural repetition, not content quality.
do_not_use_when: The user wants to improve their resume's content and relevance for a specific role, not fix AI-detection flags — rewriting for burstiness won't address weak qualifications.
The user wrote their resume entirely themselves but worries it sounds generic, making AI-detector mechanics irrelevant since the real problem is weak differentiation and word choice.
The user is submitting to a company that explicitly bans AI-assisted applications and needs ethical or policy guidance, not technical tricks to evade detection.
The user is a hiring manager asking whether their ATS flags AI-written resumes, requiring evaluation of detector tooling rather than candidate-side mitigation advice.
frameworks.description_original: A structured set of checks and interventions to reduce the probability that a resume is falsely flagged as AI-generated by automated screening tools, by diagnosing low-perplexity and low-burstiness signals.

Vary sentence rhythm deliberately: mix short fragments with longer, winding clauses; break uniform pacing

frameworks.name: AI Leverage Map
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user needs to diagnose where their AI strategy actually has structural leverage. Classify their situation into one of three positions — distribution, middleware, or workflow — by sorting their claims about competitive advantage against each definition. Push them to prove which position their strategy is anchored in; if they can't, the strategy is a wish, not a position.
when_to_apply: We have multiple AI initiatives running but can't articulate why any of them are defensible
Our AI roadmap feels like a list of features rather than a coherent strategic position
We're debating whether our advantage is in our data, our integrations, or our understanding of the user problem
A competitor just shipped a similar AI feature and leadership is panicking — I need to explain why our position is or isn't at risk
We're trying to decide whether to invest in acquiring users, building better AI infrastructure, or going deeper into domain-specific workflows
principles: Advantage in the AI era comes from distribution, middleware, or workflow—not model access
These three positions are distinct but interdependent: distribution provides data, middleware converts data into behavior, workflow is where value is delivered
A strategy must be anchored in at least one of the three or it is merely a wish

Distribution advantage = existing user surfaces and trust; Middleware advantage = ability to turn model output into reliable system behavior; Workflow advantage = deep knowledge of user friction points

source_posts.title: You Don't Need Better Models—You Need a Better Strategy

frameworks.example_application: This company's AI play sits entirely in the middleware layer — they've built reliable orchestration that turns noisy model output into consistent, auditable decisions for regulated industries. That's real. But they have no distribution advantage: they're selling through partners who own the customer relationship and the data feedback loop. The workflow layer is also thin — they're operating on generic templates, not deep domain-specific friction knowledge. The strategic move isn't to improve model quality; it's to acquire a distribution surface (even a narrow one) so the middleware advantage compounds through proprietary data instead of decaying as competitors replicate the orchestration patterns.
do_not_use_when: The company has no AI initiatives yet and needs to decide whether to adopt AI at all, not which position to defend.
The competitive threat is a pricing war or sales execution gap, not a capability or product differentiation problem.
The user is evaluating a specific vendor or build-vs-buy decision for a single AI tool, not diagnosing strategic positioning.
The company operates in a regulated market where AI deployment is blocked pending compliance approval, making positioning questions premature.
frameworks.description_original: A classification of three structural positions where AI can create compounding competitive advantage, used to diagnose where a company actually has strategic leverage.

frameworks.name: AI Strategy Kernel
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user has AI activity but no coherent strategy—scattered features, shifting roadmaps, or launches that don't compound. Challenge their assumption that more AI output equals progress; the blind spot is usually confusing feature volume with leverage. Push them to prove each initiative reinforces the next, and surface where diagnosis, guiding policy, or coherent action sequencing has broken down.
when_to_apply: We have a dozen AI features in flight and no principled way to decide which ones to keep funding
Our AI roadmap changes every time a new model drops — we need a strategy that's durable across capability shifts
We're shipping AI that gets good reactions in demos but isn't creating any compounding advantage
Leadership wants to go from scattered AI experiments to a coherent AI product strategy with clear bets
Our AI initiative has lots of activity and launches but feels like it's not building toward anything
principles: Diagnosis narrows the problem space by identifying where leverage actually exists, not what is theoretically possible
Guiding policy is a directional filter—a posture about what game you are playing—not a roadmap or feature list
Coherent actions reinforce one another and compound over time; disconnected AI features do not constitute a strategy
Start with the smallest possible wedge that fits the guiding policy and creates a feedback loop
Kill features that don't compound leverage, regardless of how well they demo
Treat strategy as a repeating loop, not a one-time planning exercise
steps: Diagnose your leverage position: Map your business honestly against distribution, middleware, and workflow to identify where you have an unfair advantage in deploying AI. This matters because without diagnosis you default to building wherever AI demos well rather than where you actually have leverage—as the example shows, the summarizer demoed well but compounded nothing, while the real advantage was hidden in the proprietary workflow data flowing through the middleware layer. (inferred)

Set a guiding policy: Articulate a posture that commits to one or more leverage positions and explicitly rules out directions that don't fit—this acts as a filter for all future decisions. This matters because the author argues good strategy maintains clarity regardless of model-of-the-day news and hype; a guiding policy is what lets you distinguish news you need to pay attention to from news you can safely ignore, preventing every new model release from scrambling your roadmap.

Identify coherent actions: Choose a thin starting wedge aligned to the guiding policy, then sequence subsequent builds so each reinforces the last and creates a feedback loop. This matters because disconnected AI features do not constitute a strategy—the example team shipped a summarizer, classifier, and chatbot that shared no data and fed nothing into each other, creating zero switching costs; coherent sequencing is what turns individual AI features into compounding leverage rather than scattered output. (inferred)

Observe system behavior: Watch deployed AI tools in production, collect signals, and use findings to sharpen middleware, UX, prompts, and fallback logic. This matters because the author emphasizes that good strategy requires durability and adaptation beyond initial planning; without production observation you cannot build the feedback loops—like classifier corrections retraining the model weekly—that make your middleware layer progressively harder to replicate. (inferred)

Repeat the loop: Revisit diagnosis regularly (at least quarterly), recommit to or explicitly update the guiding policy, and ship new wedges that reflect current learning. This matters because the author warns that model noise is going to happen all the time—new releases, new capabilities, shifting hype—and treating strategy as a repeating loop rather than a one-time planning exercise is what lets you absorb that turbulence while maintaining clarity about what actually deserves your attention.

source_posts.title: You Don't Need Better Models—You Need a Better Strategy

frameworks.example_application: The team has shipped an AI summarizer, an AI classifier, and an AI chatbot across three different product surfaces in six months. None share data, none feed each other, and none have created switching costs. The diagnosis reveals the real leverage is in the proprietary workflow data flowing through the middleware layer — not in any individual AI feature. The guiding policy becomes: every AI capability must plug into and enrich the shared workflow graph. The chatbot stays because it generates structured interaction data that improves the classifier. The summarizer gets killed — it demos well but operates on public documents and compounds nothing. The next wedge is a feedback loop where classifier corrections from users retrain the model weekly, making the middleware layer progressively harder to replicate.
do_not_use_when: The team needs to evaluate a single, already-scoped AI feature for build-vs-buy, not choose among competing strategic bets.
The organization is pre-product and hasn't shipped anything yet, so there's no activity pattern to diagnose or prune toward leverage.
Leadership is asking how to communicate an existing, already-decided AI strategy to employees, not how to form one.
The user is a solo founder with one AI product and two weeks of runway, where prioritization survival trumps compounding leverage logic.
frameworks.description_original: An adaptation of Rumelt's diagnosis-guiding policy-coherent action framework applied specifically to AI product strategy, forcing teams to narrow focus and build compounding leverage rather than scattered features.
steps_original: Diagnose your leverage position: Map your business honestly against distribution, middleware, and workflow to identify where you have an unfair advantage in deploying AI
Set a guiding policy: Articulate a posture that commits to one or more leverage positions and explicitly rules out directions that don't fit—this acts as a filter for all future decisions
Identify coherent actions: Choose a thin starting wedge aligned to the guiding policy, then sequence subsequent builds so each reinforces the last and creates a feedback loop
Observe system behavior: Watch deployed AI tools in production, collect signals, and use findings to sharpen middleware, UX, prompts, and fallback logic
Repeat the loop: Revisit diagnosis regularly (at least quarterly), recommit to or explicitly update the guiding policy, and ship new wedges that reflect current learning

frameworks.name: AI Execution Architecture Audit
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user's AI strategy looks sound on paper but execution keeps breaking down across teams. Run the four diagnostic questions in sequence, but push back on the assumption that coordination failures are a people or process problem — the real blind spot is usually architectural. Force the user to prove that ownership, quality language, feedback loops, and kill criteria actually exist as named, functioning structures.
when_to_apply: We have a solid AI strategy but teams keep stepping on each other and nothing compounds
AI features ship once and then never meaningfully improve — they just sit there
Nobody can tell me who actually decides whether an AI feature is working or should be killed
Our AI quality conversations go in circles because everyone has a different definition of 'good enough'
The feedback loop from users back into model improvement feels impossibly slow given our org structure
principles: Most AI strategy failures are architectural, not intellectual—the structure doesn't support the strategy
Ownership of AI experimentation must be distinct from ownership of AI infrastructure
Quality evaluation for AI requires a different mental model than traditional QA because outputs are probabilistic
Iteration speed is a strategic variable; waterfall delivery structures are incompatible with AI compounding
Without a named decision-maker and clear criteria, failed AI features persist and erode trust
steps: Ask: Who owns AI experiments—specifically, who is trusted to put model-backed features in front of users and close the loop back into product? This matters because without a single trusted owner who spans from model to user to product feedback, work fragments across ML, product, and engineering teams—as the example shows, each group executes its slice but no one closes the loop, guaranteeing strategic drift regardless of how sharp the strategy doc is. (inferred)

Ask: Who judges quality and how—what shared language and benchmarks exist for evaluating AI feature performance in production? This matters because AI outputs are probabilistic, not deterministic, which means traditional QA mental models don't apply—without a shared language for 'good enough,' every review cycle devolves into subjective taste debates that stall iteration, exactly the kind of noise the author warns against when he argues that good strategy must maintain clarity amid constant model-level churn.

Ask: How fast can you close the feedback loop—are UX patterns designed to generate useful signals and can the team act on them without a full rewrite? This matters because iteration speed is a strategic variable and the author emphasizes that durable strategy requires the ability to act on signals quickly—if UX isn't designed to generate usable signals and retraining requires a full sprint, you've built a waterfall structure that prevents the compounding the author sees as essential to AI execution. (inferred)

Ask: When do you kill something—who owns the call and what criteria trigger it? This matters because without a named decision-maker and explicit kill criteria, failed AI features persist for months—as the example shows with two zombie features still live after eight months—eroding organizational trust and consuming resources that should compound toward the strategic priorities the author argues must remain clear amid constant AI noise. (inferred)

source_posts.title: You Don't Need Better Models—You Need a Better Strategy

frameworks.example_application: The strategy doc is sharp — embed AI across three product surfaces — but the audit exposes the real problem. Nobody owns the experiments end-to-end: the ML team builds models, product defines requirements, and engineering deploys, but no single person is trusted to put a model-backed feature in front of users and close the loop. Quality evaluation is ad hoc — the team has no shared language for 'good enough' probabilistic output, so every review cycle turns into a taste debate. The feedback loop takes six weeks because UX wasn't designed to generate usable signals, and retraining requires a full sprint. Two AI features launched eight months ago are still live despite poor engagement because no one has the authority or criteria to kill them. The strategy isn't the problem — the execution architecture has four structural fractures that guarantee drift.
do_not_use_when: The organization hasn't shipped any AI features yet and is still debating whether to invest in AI at all, making structural audit premature.
Coordination failures stem from a recent merger creating duplicate teams across all functions, not AI-specific ownership gaps requiring a different intervention.
A solo founder or two-person team is asking who owns AI quality, where org-design advice adds no value because there is no org to redesign.
The team's AI features are compounding poorly because the underlying models are genuinely inadequate, not because of structural bottlenecks the audit would surface.
frameworks.description_original: Four structured questions to determine whether an organization's structure can actually execute an AI strategy, surfacing ownership gaps, quality blind spots, and iteration bottlenecks.

frameworks.name: The Seven Tech Workflows
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user needs to locate AI leverage or assess job vulnerability by classifying their work into the seven recurring workflow motions. Sort their role or team's activities into each motion, then identify where AI amplifies clean motion versus multiplies confusion. Push them toward designing the motion itself — not optimizing isolated tasks — because task thinking is the trap this framework is built to expose.
when_to_apply: I want to use AI tools at work but I'm not sure which parts of my job they'd actually improve versus just add noise
My team is adopting Copilot/ChatGPT and we need to figure out where to point it first for maximum impact
I'm trying to explain to my manager why my role still matters even though AI can produce drafts of most of my deliverables
We have friction in how work moves through our team and I want to understand whether it's a people problem or a workflow design problem before layering AI on top
I keep hearing 'AI will replace knowledge workers' and I want a concrete way to audit which parts of my job are actually vulnerable
principles: Your job is not your title or output — it is a set of recurring workflow motions
AI amplifies clean, intentional motion and multiplies confusion in messy, unexamined motion
The parts of each workflow that are hardest to describe or tokenize are the parts most resistant to AI replacement (Polanyian tacit knowledge)
Each workflow has a distinct leverage point where AI can extend human capability without replacing judgment
Task thinking is a trap; designing the motion is the new competitive advantage

source_posts.title: If You're Worried AI Will Replace You, Read This First

frameworks.example_application: A product manager's job decomposes into seven motions: researching (gathering market signals), synthesizing (turning signals into a thesis), deciding (prioritizing the roadmap), communicating (writing specs and aligning stakeholders), coordinating (keeping cross-functional work in sync), creating (drafting narratives and decks), and reviewing (QA on output quality). AI has massive leverage on researching and first-draft creating — those are high-volume, tokenizable motions. But the synthesizing motion is where this PM's actual competitive value lives: the judgment call that three weak customer signals plus one churned enterprise account means the pricing model is broken, not the feature set. That insight is tacit, context-soaked, and nearly impossible to prompt for. Introducing AI into the coordinating workflow without first cleaning up the underlying motion — who owns what, what 'done' means — would multiply the existing confusion, not reduce it.
do_not_use_when: The user is a solo freelancer deciding whether to subscribe to a specific AI tool, not redesign how work moves through a team.
The user's friction is caused by a broken approval process or org politics, not workflow design, so taxonomy work won't surface the real fix.
The user is an executive evaluating a company-wide AI vendor contract, where the decision hinges on procurement and risk criteria, not job-motion analysis.
The user already knows which workflow they want to automate and just needs tool recommendations, not a classification exercise to find leverage points.
frameworks.description_original: A classification system that decomposes any knowledge work job into seven recurring workflow motions, enabling workers to identify where AI provides leverage and where human judgment remains irreplaceable.

frameworks.name: High-Performing AI Team Behaviors
frameworks.description: Apply this framework when a user's team is underperforming despite adequate AI tooling — the gap is almost always in coordination, not capability. Score their team against the eight dimensions, pressing them to distinguish surface-level adoption from genuine distributed cognition. Push back on the assumption that individual AI usage compounds into team intelligence — it doesn't without explicit prompt literacy norms, metadata transparency, and collective sense-making rituals.
when_to_apply: Two teams have the same AI tools and similar talent but one is dramatically more productive — I need to figure out what's actually different
My team members are all using ChatGPT individually but our collective output quality hasn't meaningfully improved
We're about to stand up a new AI-native team and I want to design their working norms from the start rather than retrofit them later
I'm running a retrospective focused on our AI practices and need a structured way to identify where we're weakest
People on my team are generating tons of AI content but we're drowning in options and losing track of what was human-validated versus raw AI output
principles: AI adoption at the team level requires reshaping coordination, not just individual productivity
Distributed cognition means team intelligence now lives partly in human-AI interactions, which must be managed explicitly
High performance requires both generating AI outputs AND maintaining rigorous human judgment over them
Prompt literacy is a team sport—variance in prompting quality across members degrades collective output quality
Async-first workflows unlock AI's full value by reducing coordination overhead and enabling continuous progress
Collective sense-making rituals are necessary because AI dramatically increases the volume of options and content teams must process
Trust and accountability require explicit metadata and transparency about who prompted, refined, and approved AI content
Velocity and iteration matter more than perfection, but only after foundational practices are in place

source_posts.title: Your Team is Using AI Wrong: The Hidden Pattern Behind High-Performing AI Teams

frameworks.example_application: This team scores high on individual prompt literacy (Dimension 3) — most members write solid prompts — but collapses on collective sense-making (Dimension 6) and attribution transparency (Dimension 7). The tell: everyone generates AI drafts independently, but meetings devolve into comparing five AI-generated options with no shared process for evaluating them, and nobody can trace which outputs were AI-generated versus human-refined. The highest-leverage fix isn't more AI training — it's installing a weekly synthesis ritual where AI-generated options are triaged against shared criteria, and requiring lightweight provenance metadata on all AI-assisted deliverables.

A solo founder or individual contributor is asking how to improve their own AI-assisted output with no team coordination involved.

frameworks.name: Low-Performing AI Team Pitfall Catalog
frameworks.description: Apply this catalog when a user's team has adopted AI but isn't seeing expected gains, or when collaboration, quality, or trust has degraded post-adoption. when_to_apply: My team adopted Copilot/ChatGPT months ago and our velocity hasn't improved — I can't tell if the tools are the problem or how we're using them
